overview.introHtml:
Digital SAT 1400+ Curriculum & Interactive Courseware

A complete, Bluebook-aligned 7-day intensive curriculum, 21-day exam preparation runway, and local-first interactive web courseware designed for international (ESL) students advancing from a 1200 baseline (560 Reading & Writing · 640 Math) to 1400+ (650–700+ R&W · 700–750+ Math).

Dimension Specification
Target Cohort International & non-native English speakers (December 5, 2026 SAT runway: Nov 14 – Dec 4)
Daily Study Load 4.0–5.0 effective active hours/day (32 hr 33 min audited across Days 1–7; ~56% R&W / ~44% Math)
Course Structure 1 Master Roadmap + 7 Self-Contained Daily Workbooks (10 guided steps per day = 70 total steps)
Original Practice Bank 232 SAT-Style Questions (125 R&W + 107 Math · 196 Multiple Choice + 36 Student-Produced Response)
Academic Word Core 60 High-Utility SAT Words taught via 3-Layer Profiles, Context-Clue Polarity, and Spaced Retrieval
Diagnostic & Mastery 35 Student Error Case Studies (E1–E10 & V1–V7 taxonomy) + 66 Closed-Notes Mastery Gate Checks

chapters.title: Executive Weekly Performance Dashboard
chapters.html:
Important Score-Interpretation Rule: Practice accuracy percentages below measure skill execution on untimed and timed practice sets; they do not translate mechanically into official scaled SAT scores. Because the Digital SAT uses two-stage module-level adaptation and item-level difficulty weighting, missing three questions in a harder Module 2 produces a very different scaled score than missing three easy questions in Module 1. Furthermore, a 200-point scaled score gain (1200 → 1400+) cannot be guaranteed within 7 days. This 7-day sprint builds the diagnostic clarity, grammar/vocabulary systems, and math reliability required to push into the 1280–1340+ range by Day 6 and reach 1400+ across the remaining 14 follow-up days before December 5, 2026.

A. Verified Official & Core Study Resources (Zero Fabricated Items)

  1. College Board Bluebook App (Active Practice Tests 4–11):
    • College Board retired Practice Tests 1–3; Practice Tests 4 through 11 (8 official adaptive exams) are active in Bluebook.
    • Test Preservation Rule: Complete Practice Test 4 on Day 1 (Diagnostic) and Practice Test 5 on Day 6 (End-of-Sprint Simulation). Preserve Practice Test 6 (Nov 28) and Practice Test 7 (Dec 1) for the two-week follow-up window, keeping Tests 8–11 untouched as unspoiled reserves. (If you already used Test 4 to obtain your 1200 baseline, shift every assigned test number up by 1: use Test 5 on Day 1, Test 6 on Day 6, Test 7 on Nov 28, and Test 8 on Dec 1.)
  2. College Board SAT Suite Question Bank:
    • Filter by Assessment: SAT → Section: Reading and Writing or Math → exact Domain, Skill, and Difficulty (Easy, Medium, Hard).
    • Mandatory Anti-Spoiler Rule: Always turn ON the "Exclude Active Questions" checkbox before generating practice sets so you never accidentally preview items from Bluebook Practice Tests 4–11.
  3. Khan Academy Official Digital SAT Prep:
    • Organized into Foundations, Medium, and Advanced tiers (plus Challenge) across SAT Reading and Writing (Information and ideas, Craft and structure, Expression of ideas + standard English conventions) and SAT Math (Algebra, Problem-solving and data analysis, Advanced math, Geometry and trigonometry).
    • Use short concept articles/videos only to repair a diagnosed rule gap (5–10 minutes max), then move immediately to active solving.
  4. Personalized SAT Vocabulary Notebook: Vocabulary-Notebook-and-Spaced-Review.md
  5. SAT Diagnostic Error Log & Reflection Workbook: SAT-Error-Log-and-Daily-Reflections.md

chapters.title: Special Academic Vocabulary System for International Students
chapters.fullTitle: 3. Special Academic Vocabulary System for International Students
chapters.html:
A. What Vocabulary Actually Appears on the Digital SAT

Do not download archaic 1990s SAT word lists (obsequious, defenestrate, lugubrious). Digital SAT passages are 25–150-word academic excerpts drawn from peer-reviewed science, economics, sociology, history, and literary prose. High-return vocabulary falls into six functional groups:

  1. Argument & Evidence Verbs: substantiate, corroborate, undermine, bolster, refute, assert, posit, concede, reconcile, extrapolate, scrutinize, entail.
  2. Epistemic Certainty & Caution Modifiers: plausible, tentative, speculative, definitive, inconclusive, compelling, dubious, empirical.
  3. Nuance, Clarity & Complexity Adjectives: ambiguous, nuanced, overt, subtle, disparate, homogeneous, conventional, novel, ubiquitous.
  4. Polysemous Words (Everyday Words with Secondary Academic Meanings): qualify ("limit/moderate a claim"), check ("restrain/slow down"), arrest ("halt"), observe ("follow a rule" or "remark"), appreciate ("understand fully" or "increase in value"), afford ("provide"), compromise ("weaken/endanger").
  5. Logical Pivot & Concession Connectors: nevertheless, notwithstanding, albeit, conversely, consequently, moreover, inasmuch as, hitherto, contingent on.
  6. Author Attitude & Rhetorical Purpose Verbs: critique, lament, underscore, qualify, contextualize, repudiate, commemorate, vindicate.

B. Three-Layer Vocabulary Instruction Model

Every new word studied during this week is learned through three progressive layers—never bare translation:

Model Demonstration: Reconcile (verb)

  • Layer 1 — Simple English Meaning:
    To find a way for two ideas, facts, or groups that seem to disagree to fit together without contradiction.
  • Layer 2 — SAT Academic Context:
    "Paleoclimatologists struggled for decades to reconcile geological evidence of tropical glaciers with computer models predicting high carbon dioxide levels during the same era."
    How it works in the sentence: Notice the tension between tropical glaciers (extreme cold) and high carbon dioxide (warming). Reconcile expresses the scientists' effort to make those two conflicting facts fit into a single coherent explanation.
  • Layer 3 — Independent Application:
    1. Contextual MCQ Check: In the sentence "To ______ the museum's mission of public access with the fragility of ninth-century silk scrolls, curators display high-resolution replicas alongside rotating originals," why does reconcile work while substantiate fails? (Because the curators are balancing two competing goals—access vs. preservation—not proving a claim true.)
    2. Productive Output: Write one original sentence in Vocabulary-Notebook-and-Spaced-Review.md connecting two competing priorities in your own life or academic studies.
    3. Transfer Check: Recognize the negative adjective irreconcilable ("irreconcilable differences between the two datasets") three days later without hints.

C. Repeatable 5-Step Context-Clue Method (Use on Every Words in Context Question)

  1. Identify the Passage's Core Claim: Strip away adjectives and side clauses—who or what is the main subject, and what is the central point?
  2. Spot the Logical Signal: Circle punctuation and pivot markers:
    • Colon (:) or Em-Dash (—): Restates, defines, or illustrates the exact same idea (Clause A = Clause B).
    • Support / Continuation (moreover, indeed, similarly, consequently, thus): Blank matches the direction/tone of the adjacent evidence (+ → + or - → -).
    • Contrast / Concession (although, nevertheless, notwithstanding, whereas, yet, instead of, far from): Blank flips the direction/tone (+ → - or - → +).
  3. Predict a Simple Plain-English Word First: Cover choices A–D with your hand or cursor and put a simple English phrase in the blank (e.g., "weaken," "prove," "unclear," "temporary").
  4. Test All Four Choices Against Context (Never Familiarity):
    • Do not pick a word just because you know it if it misses your prediction.
    • Do not eliminate an unfamiliar word if the three words you do know clearly contradict your prediction!
  5. Verify Author Meaning & Tone Precision: Re-read the sentence with your chosen word inserted. Confirm that both logical direction and degree of certainty match (e.g., tentative fits cautious early data; irrefutable is too extreme).

D. Language-Accessibility Rules for International Learners

  • Clause Stripping Before Translating: Long English academic sentences hide simple cores inside participial phrases and appositives. Train your eye to bracket Everything between paired commas or dashes first:
    The hypothesis [proposed by early marine biologists after brief coastal surveys] was undermined by deep-ocean sonar. → Core: The hypothesis was undermined by deep-ocean sonar.
  • Strategic First-Language (L1) Rule: Never translate whole passages into your native language during practice—translation cuts reading speed in half and breaks English syntax intuition. During untimed review only, if an abstract English concept (like concession or empirical) feels fuzzy after reading the simple English definition, check your L1 equivalent for 5 seconds, then close the dictionary and write your example sentence in English.
  • Zero Simplification During Timed Sets: Timed practice always uses authentic SAT sentence complexity; scaffolding happens strictly during instruction and post-set analysis.

E. Spaced Vocabulary Retention Schedule (Days 1–7 + Extension to Dec 5)

Target: Study 8–12 high-value words/expressions daily (48–58 total across Days 1–6, consolidated on Day 7), achieving at least 3 retrieval touches per priority word and 80%+ delayed recall accuracy without notes:

  • Day 1 (Nov 14): Encode 10 foundational academic words + log 8–10 unfamiliar words from Bluebook Test 4 using the 7-column notebook.
  • Day 2 (Nov 15): Closed-notes retrieval of Day 1 words (cover meanings, state simple English definition + polarity) + encode 10 new SEC/WIC academic words.
  • Day 3 (Nov 16): Re-test "sticky" Day 1 words inside fresh SAT-style sentences + retrieve Day 2 words + encode 10 reasoning/argument words.
  • Day 4 (Nov 17): Cumulative Mixed Retrieval & Synonym-Discrimination Quiz (Days 1–3 pool) + encode 10 medium/hard tone & concession words.
  • Day 5 (Nov 18): Timed Contextual Vocabulary Drill (45 seconds/question across Days 1–4 words in unfamiliar contexts) + encode 8 high-utility expressions.
  • Day 6 (Nov 19): Capture 8–10 authentic unfamiliar words encountered during Bluebook Practice Test 5 (no heavy memorization post-exam).
  • Day 7 (Nov 20): Consolidated 7-Day Functional Vocabulary Assessment across all 48–58 studied words (>=80% threshold across recognition, contextual meaning, clue spotting, synonym discrimination, simple-English explanation, and new-passage application).
  • Days 8–20 (Nov 21–Dec 3 Extension): Add reduced daily batches (5–7 words/day from Question Bank misses) while running 10-minute spaced retrieval quizzes every 3rd day (Nov 23, Nov 26, Nov 29, Dec 2). Stop adding new words after December 3 so December 4 stays calm and consolidated.

chapters.title: Diagnostic Error-Log & End-of-Day Reflection Systems
chapters.html:
A. Daily Error-Log Protocol (15–20 Minutes Every Morning)

Every missed or uncertain question goes into SAT-Error-Log-and-Daily-Reflections.md using this exact 7-column schema:

Date Section Topic Question Type Why I Missed It Correct Rule/Method What I Will Do Next Time

Mandatory Vocabulary & Language Error Sub-Labels:

  1. Did not know word meaning
  2. Knew word but selected the wrong meaning (polysemy / secondary academic sense trap)
  3. Misunderstood sentence structure (lost subject-verb core in dense clauses)
  4. Missed a contrast or cause-and-effect clue (ignored pivot words or colons)
  5. Confused similar answer choices (close synonym or degree-of-certainty trap)
  6. Misunderstood the author's tone (confused neutral description with praise/criticism)
  7. Failed to connect evidence to the claim (picked true-sounding text that proves the wrong variable)

How to Apply the 3+ Recurring Pattern Rule Accurately:

  • Count underlying cognitive/linguistic failure mechanisms, not broad College Board domain labels.
  • False Grouping: Missing one Words in Context item (Did not know word meaning), one Text Structure item (Misread question), and one Cross-Text item (Timing problem) all fall under Craft and Structure, but they require three completely different fixes.
  • True Priority Pattern (Flag at >=3): Missing three items because you failed to spot a comma splice with a conjunctive adverb (, however,), OR missing three items across different skills because you overlooked a concession word (albeit / notwithstanding). Any root mechanism hitting 3 occurrences automatically becomes the opening 15-minute repair drill of your next session.

B. Daily 15-Minute End-of-Day Reflection Routine

Every evening study session closes with a strict 15-minute audit recording all 11 required progress metrics in SAT-Error-Log-and-Daily-Reflections.md:

  1. Total questions attempted · 2. Overall accuracy % · 3. R&W accuracy % · 4. Math accuracy % · 5. Words studied · 6. Vocabulary retrieval accuracy % · 7. Main mistakes · 8. New concepts learned · 9. Most difficult topic · 10. Topics needing review · 11. One specific, behavioral improvement target for tomorrow.

chapters.title: High-Return Score-Improvement Strategy (1200 → 1400+)
chapters.html:
A. Reading & Writing: Climbing from 560 toward 650–700+

For an international student at 560 R&W, trying to "read faster and memorize 1,000 words" is the slowest path to points. Instead, attack R&W in order of rule predictability and speed return (subject to Day 1 diagnostic confirmation):

  1. Standard English Conventions (~26% of R&W, Q15–Q21 range): Finite, mechanical rules. Even if 3 nouns in a science sentence are unfamiliar, you can still identify the grammatical subject, check singular/plural verb agreement, and test whether two clauses are independent! Moving SEC from ~58% to 92%+ both banks fast points and saves 4–5 minutes per module for dense reading passages.
  2. Transitions (~7–10% of R&W): Pure logical polarity (Support/Addition, Contrast/Concession, Cause/Effect, Example/Specification). Strip Clause 1 and Clause 2 to short summaries, ignore the underlined transition, label the logical bridge, and eliminate any two transitions in the same functional family (e.g., Furthermore and Moreover cannot both be right).
  3. Rhetorical Synthesis (Bullet-Point Notes, last 2–4 Qs of each module): Do not even read the bullet points until you dissect the exact goal in the question stem ("emphasize a difference," "introduce the researcher's method to an unfamiliar audience," "illustrate a practical limitation"). Often 2–3 choices are grammatically fine and factually true from the notes, yet fail half of the prompt's rhetorical goal.
  4. Words in Context (~15–19% of R&W, Q1–Q5): Apply the 5-Step Context-Clue Method so punctuation and contrast markers carry 70% of the weight before vocabulary recall even starts.
  5. Central Ideas and Details: Anchor on the main claim + scope; eliminate choices that elevate a minor supporting example into the central thesis or introduce extreme quantifiers (always, exclusively, never, prove conclusively).
  6. Command of Evidence (Textual & Quantitative): Identify the exact two-part hypothesis (Variable A causes/correlates with Outcome B under Condition C). Eliminate data choices that misread the table/graph OR report accurate numbers about the wrong variable.
  7. Inferences (Blank at the End of a Dense Paragraph): Treat SAT inferences like strict logical deductions (Premise 1 + Premise 2 → Necessary Conclusion), never creative storytelling. Every word in the winning inference must be licensed by stated constraints in the passage.
  8. Text Structure & Purpose / Cross-Text Connections: Track structural shifts (Common Belief → New Challenge → Qualified Synthesis) and map exact point of agreement vs. disagreement between Text 1 and Text 2 before reading choices.

How Grammar, Vocabulary, Structure, and Logic Interact for Non-Native Readers:
Many "reading comprehension" misses by international students are actually syntax-boundary misses: misreading a participial modifier ("Long dismissed by classical economists, behavioral models...") as the author's own rejection rather than an outdated view the author is overturning! Mastering Boundaries & Modifiers on Day 2 directly unlocks Main Ideas, Inferences, and Text Purpose on Days 3–5.

B. Math: Climbing from 640 toward 700–750+

A 640 Math baseline means your foundational arithmetic and basic algebra exist, but points leak in three places: (1) 1–3 preventable careless/misread errors in Module 1 that either cap your routing or waste cushion, (2) medium/hard nonlinear functions, systems with constants (no solution / infinitely many solutions), and percent-change traps, and (3) slow manual algebra where Desmos solves in 15 seconds.

  • Zero-Leak Module 1 Rule: Treat Questions 1–15 of Module 1 with surgical verification (box the final target expression; check units/axes). Hitting 20–22 / 22 in Module 1 unlocks the full 700–800 ceiling.
  • High-Frequency Algebra & Advanced Math Mastery: Drill linear parameters (slope = rate of change, y-intercept = initial value, parallel/perpendicular slopes, infinite/zero solutions in systems), quadratic forms (standard, factored/roots, vertex, discriminant b² - 4ac), and exponential models (a(1 ± r)^(t/k)).
  • Strategic Desmos Fluency: Use Desmos instantly for systems of equations (linear or nonlinear intersections), parameter/constant problems via sliders, equivalent expressions (graph f(x) and choices to test identical curves, checking domain edge cases!), and table regressions (y_1 ~ m x_1 + b or y_1 ~ a x_1^2 + b x_1 + c). Keep crisp manual algebra for symbolic isolation ("solve for r in terms of p and q") and discriminant inequalities where Desmos sliders need algebraic framing first.

How Digital SAT Module Adaptation Works (Evidence-Based Reality, Not Myths):
The Digital SAT adapts between Module 1 and Module 2, never question-by-question inside a single module. Module 1 mixes Easy, Medium, and Hard questions. Strong overall performance across Module 1 routes you to the harder Module 2, which unlocks the full 650–800 score ceiling; weaker Module 1 performance routes you to the easier Module 2, which places a ceiling on your maximum possible section score even if you answer every Module 2 question right. College Board does not publish an exact cutoff number, and question weights vary—so do not try to count how many questions you "can afford to miss." Instead:

  1. In Module 1: Prioritize clean accuracy on every Easy and Medium question using a two-pass strategy so careless slips never jeopardize upper-tier routing.
  2. In Harder Module 2: Expect dense academic vocabulary and multi-step Math! Do not panic if 3–4 questions feel intense—getting routed to Harder Module 2 is good news, and flagging the 2–3 toughest time-sinks while banking the other 24 R&W / 19 Math questions cleanly already puts you squarely in 700+ territory.

A. Five Highest-Priority Weaknesses (Pre-Diagnostic Hypotheses to Confirm on Day 1)

Important Diagnostic Framing: The five weaknesses below are evidence-based hypotheses representing the highest-probability score leaks for an international student scoring 560 in Reading & Writing and 640 in Math. Confirm or replace each hypothesis using your actual Day 1 Bluebook Practice Test 4 error log.

Hypothesis 1: Sentence-Boundary & Modifier Blindness Masked by Dense Academic Vocabulary (R&W)

  • Why It Matters: Standard English Conventions accounts for 26% of R&W (13–15 questions per test). International students scoring 560 often lose 5–7 points here—not because punctuation rules are vast, but because unfamiliar academic nouns and long participial phrases disguise where one independent clause ends and the next begins (causing comma-splice and subject-verb agreement traps). These are the fastest, highest-certainty points on the entire exam.
  • How to Diagnose It: On Day 1 Practice Test 4, count misses in Standard English Conventions (Boundaries and Form, Structure, and Sense) and check whether your average time per grammar item exceeded 50 seconds.
  • Official Resource to Use: Khan Academy Official Digital SAT Prep (Medium and Advanced: Expression of ideas + standard English conventions) paired with College Board SAT Suite Question Bank (Section: Reading and Writing → Domain: Standard English Conventions → Skills: Boundaries and Form, Structure, and Sense → Difficulty: Medium, Hard → Exclude Active Questions: ON).
  • What Mastery Looks Like: 90–95%+ accuracy on mixed Medium/Hard SEC sets at an average speed of 35–45 seconds per question, isolating the grammatical subject and main verb even when technical nouns are unfamiliar.

Hypothesis 2: Contextual Vocabulary & Concession-Marker Misinterpretation (R&W)

  • Why It Matters: Words in Context (15–19% of R&W) and Transitions (7–10% of R&W) directly test academic vocabulary and logical connectors (notwithstanding, albeit, conversely, substantiate, tentative, qualify). Non-native speakers frequently pick a familiar word with the wrong polarity or an everyday meaning instead of a secondary academic meaning (V2), or miss a concession pivot (V4).
  • How to Diagnose It: Count Day 1 misses tagged V1 (unknown word), V2 (wrong secondary meaning), V4 (missed contrast/cause clue), or V5 (confused close synonyms) across Words in Context and Transitions.
  • Official Resource to Use: College Board SAT Suite Question Bank (Domain: Craft and Structure → Skill: Words in Context and Domain: Expression of Ideas → Skill: Transitions, Medium/Hard, Exclude Active Questions: ON) + Personalized SAT Vocabulary Notebook using the 5-Step Context-Clue Method.
  • What Mastery Looks Like: Predicting a plain-English word and + / - logical polarity before looking at choices A–D, achieving 80%+ accuracy on Medium/Hard WIC and 90%+ on Transitions, with 80%+ delayed recall on studied vocabulary.

Hypothesis 3: Evidence-to-Claim Mismatch & Dense Clause Overload on Inferences / Command of Evidence (R&W)

  • Why It Matters: International readers at 560 often read every word carefully yet miss Inferences and Command of Evidence items because multi-clause academic sentences overload working memory (E3), causing them to select a choice that repeats familiar keywords from the passage (recycled-language trap) rather than proving the specific causal link in the prompt (V7).
  • How to Diagnose It: Check Day 1 performance on Information and Ideas (Inferences and Command of Evidence), specifically comparing untimed cold re-solve accuracy against timed test accuracy.
  • Official Resource to Use: College Board SAT Suite Question Bank (Domain: Information and Ideas → Skills: Inferences and Command of Evidence, Medium/Hard, Exclude Active Questions: ON) + Khan Academy (Medium/Advanced: Information and ideas).
  • What Mastery Looks Like: Bracketing non-essential clauses automatically, stating the exact 2-variable hypothesis before reading A–D, and reaching 75–82%+ accuracy on Medium/Hard Information and Ideas questions within 75–90 seconds per passage.

Hypothesis 4: Preventable Module 1 Math Leaks & English-Wording Traps in Linear/Percent Models (Math)

  • Why It Matters: At 640 Math, students typically understand core algebra yet drop 2–4 questions per test due to target misreads (solving for x instead of 3x - 2), linear-system parameter traps (no solution vs. infinitely many solutions), or subtle English phrasing in Problem-Solving and Data Analysis ("decreased by 15%" vs. "is 15% of", "percent greater than", conditional probability denominators).
  • How to Diagnose It: Audit every Day 1 Module 1 Math miss and every Algebra / Problem-Solving and Data Analysis miss using codes E4 (misread question), E7 (careless slip), and E1 (concept gap).
  • Official Resource to Use: College Board SAT Suite Question Bank (Domain: Algebra → Systems of two linear equations & Linear functions; Domain: Problem-Solving and Data Analysis → Percentages & Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units, Medium/Hard, Exclude Active Questions: ON).
  • What Mastery Looks Like: 95%+ accuracy on Math Module 1 (21–22 / 22), boxing the exact target expression on every question before entering the answer, and translating percent/rate sentences into algebraic multipliers (1.15x, 0.85x) with zero hesitation.

Hypothesis 5: Nonlinear Advanced Math Bottlenecks & Under-Using Desmos Under Time Pressure (Math)

  • Why It Matters: Breaking from 640 into 700–750+ requires conquering Harder Module 2 items in Advanced Math—quadratic discriminants (b² - 4ac), vertex/intercept translations, exponential growth/decay intervals (a · b^(t/k)), and nonlinear systems—while using Desmos to solve graphing/intersection/slider items in 20 seconds so you preserve 6–8 minutes for the final five problems.
  • How to Diagnose It: Check Day 1 Advanced Math accuracy on Medium/Hard items and count how many missed or >2-minute Math problems could have been solved in <30 seconds via Desmos graphing, sliders, or y_1 ~ m x_1 + b regression (E9).
  • Official Resource to Use: Khan Academy (Medium/Advanced: Advanced math) + College Board SAT Suite Question Bank (Domain: Advanced Math → Nonlinear functions, Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems, Equivalent expressions, Medium/Hard, Exclude Active Questions: ON) + Desmos Graphing Calculator.
  • What Mastery Looks Like: Instant 5-second classification (Manual vs. Desmos), 75%+ accuracy on Hard Advanced Math, and finishing 22-question Math modules with 3–4 minutes left to verify flagged items.

B. Realistic Score Progression (1200 → 1400+ Trajectory)

A 200-point scaled score increase is an ambitious, multi-week transformation—never an automatic 7-day guarantee. Distinguish three separate layers of progress so you stay objective and motivated:

  1. Short-Term Skill Improvement (Visible Within Days 2–5):
    • Immediate, measurable jumps in topic-level practice accuracy: Standard English Conventions rising from ~58% to 85%+, Transitions hitting 85–90%, Words in Context climbing via the 5-Step Method, and Desmos eliminating 2-minute algebraic stalls.
  2. Official Bluebook Practice-Test Progress (Across the 21-Day Window):
    • Scaled scores move in steps rather than smooth straight lines—especially when you cross the threshold into Harder Module 2 for the first time (where raw questions feel much tougher even as your scaled score climbs!).

Official SAT Sat, Dec 5, 2026 Official Exam 650–700+ Goal 700–750+ Goal 1400+ Target Full execution under rested conditions
  1. Exam-Day Score Uncertainty:
    • Every official SAT carries a natural measurement band of roughly ±30–40 total points due to test-day passage topics, sleep/nerves, and whether a borderline guess lands on a high-weight item. Building a 1410–1430 rehearsal ceiling on fresh Bluebook tests is the safest buffer to protect a 1400+ official score.

  • Phase 2 & Phase 3 — Subsequent 14-Day Consolidation, Stamina & Taper Window: Saturday, Nov 21 – Friday, Dec 4, 2026 (Days 8–21). Maintain 3.5–4.5 effective hours/day during Days 8–18 (with one lighter recovery day on Sunday, Nov 22), then taper volume sharply on Days 19–21 (Dec 2–4) so your brain peaks on Saturday morning, December 5.

EXAM Sat, Dec 5 — OFFICIAL DIGITAL SAT: 10-min morning warm-up (2 previously solved grammar Qs + 2 easy linear Qs at home before leaving) → Execute calmly!

D. Full Bluebook Practice Test Strategy (Preserving Official Assessments)

Out of the 8 active full-length adaptive tests in Bluebook (Practice Tests 4–11), 4 full exams is the optimal number for a 21-day window:

  1. Diagnostic Test — Practice Test 4 (Day 1: Saturday, Nov 14): Unspoiled baseline + language/timing profiling.
  2. Post-Sprint Benchmark — Practice Test 5 (Day 6: Thursday, Nov 19): Validates gains from intensive Grammar, Vocab Foundations, Algebra/Adv Math repair, and Split-Order pacing.
  3. One-Week-Out Simulation — Practice Test 6 (Day 15: Saturday, Nov 28): Taken at the exact clock hour of your real December 5 test center reporting time to synchronize biological alertness.
  4. Final Dress Rehearsal — Practice Test 7 (Day 18: Tuesday, Dec 1): Final verification 96 hours before test day—close enough for peak sharpness, early enough for full neural recovery.
  5. Unspoiled Reserves — Practice Tests 8–11: Keep untouched! Taking 7–8 full tests in three weeks steals 25+ hours away from targeted error repair and causes severe reading fatigue. Reserve Test 8 only if Test 4 was already used previously (or in the event of a future retake).

E. Efficient College Board SAT Suite Question Bank Usage

Follow this exact 5-step workflow every time you open the Question Bank so your practice is surgical and spoiler-free:

  1. Set Core Filters First:
    • Assessment: SAT
    • Section: Reading and Writing or Math
    • Checkbox — "Exclude Active Questions": CHECKED (ON) (Non-negotiable until after December 1 so Bluebook Tests 4–7 remain 100% unseen!)
  2. Filter by Exact Domain & Skill (Match Your Error Log):
    • R&W Domains/Skills:
      • Information and Ideas → Central Ideas and Details | Command of Evidence | Inferences
      • Craft and Structure → Words in Context | Text Structure and Purpose | Cross-Text Connections
      • Expression of Ideas → Rhetorical Synthesis | Transitions
      • Standard English Conventions → Boundaries | Form, Structure, and Sense
    • Math Domains/Skills:
      • Algebra → Linear equations in one variable | Linear functions | Linear equations in two variables | Systems of two linear equations in two variables | Linear inequalities in one or two variables
      • Advanced Math → Nonlinear functions | Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables | Equivalent expressions
      • Problem-Solving and Data Analysis → Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units | Percentages | One-variable data | Two-variable data | Probability and conditional probability | Inference from sample statistics and margin of error | Evaluating statistical claims
      • Geometry and Trigonometry → Area and volume | Lines, angles, and triangles | Right triangles and trigonometry | Circles
  3. Select Difficulty Strategically:
    • Repairing a Concept Gap or Grammar Rule? Start with Medium (8–10 Qs), then switch to Hard (8–10 Qs) once accuracy hits >=80%.
    • Training for 650–750+ Module 2? Filter strictly Medium + Hard (with 60% Hard on Days 4, 10, 11, 13, 17).
  4. Export / View Without Answers Visible: Hide answer keys and rationales while solving in batches of 10–15 questions.
  5. Prevent Answer Memorization When Re-Using Items:
    • Never judge a revisited question right just because you recognize "the answer was C." To count a re-solved question as mastered, you must state out loud (or write in one line): (a) the exact structural clue or formula, (b) why your original wrong choice fails, and (c) what would make a different choice right if one word or sign in the stem changed. Wait at least 48–72 hours before re-testing a missed Question Bank item.

F. Surgical Khan Academy Official Digital SAT Prep Usage

Khan Academy is a repair scalpel, not a Netflix playlist:

  • Never spend 90 minutes watching videos from top to bottom. Passive video watching creates an illusion of fluency (especially for non-native English speakers listening to clear explanations without doing the syntactic work themselves).
  • The 10-Minute Micro-Lesson Rule: Open Khan Academy only when your Error Log flags E1 (Concept gap) or E6 (Grammar rule forgotten):
    1. Read the short Lesson Article (faster and easier to scan for academic terms than video) or watch one 4–6 minute worked-example video at the Medium or Advanced tier.
    2. Immediately pause before the instructor solves the example—try solving it on scratch paper yourself.
    3. Complete the 4-question Khan skill check right underneath (aim for 4/4).
    4. Transfer immediately to 10–12 fresh College Board SAT Suite Question Bank items on that same skill.

G. Digital SAT Pacing & Adaptive Module Strategy

1. Reading & Writing Pacing (32 Minutes · 27 Questions · ~71 Seconds/Question Average)

International students lose the most points when they get bogged down on dense Inferences and Command of Evidence passages around Questions 10–14 and then rush easy Grammar, Transitions, and Rhetorical Synthesis points at Questions 15–27! Use the Split-Module Two-Pass Order:

Pass / Question Block Question Types Target Time Budget Countdown Clock Remaining Tactical Rule
Step 1: Jump straight to Q15 (first SEC item) → Solve Q15–Q27 Standard English Conventions, Transitions, Rhetorical Synthesis (~12–13 Qs) 10–11 minutes (~45–50 sec/Q) 21:00–22:00 left Bank mechanical grammar, transition polarity, and goal-first bullet notes while your brain is fresh!
Step 2: Click Q1 → Solve Q1–Q7 Words in Context + Text Structure / Cross-Text (~6–7 Qs) 7–8 minutes (~60–65 sec/Q) 13:00–15:00 left Apply 5-Step Context-Clue prediction; do not stare at an unknown word past 65 seconds—eliminate wrong polarities, mark, and move!
Step 3: Solve Q8–Q14 (Densest Reading Core) Central Ideas, Command of Evidence, Inferences (~7–8 Qs) 11–12 minutes (~85–95 sec/Q) 2:00–3:00 left You now know for certain how much time you have left with Q15–27 already banked! Bracket extra clauses, match exact claim scope.
Step 4: Flagged Buffer Review Any 2–3 marked items (never leave blanks—no guessing penalty!) 2–3 minutes 0:00 Confirm every single question 1–27 has a selected bubble by the 01:00 warning.

Emergency Unknown-Vocabulary Rule Under Timed Conditions:

  1. Unfamiliar Word in the Passage: Ignore the exact noun/adjective unless it is the core predicate; replace it mentally with "X-thing" or "[positive/negative trait]" using surrounding modifiers and keep moving.
  2. Two Unfamiliar Answer Choices in Words in Context: Test the two words you DO know strictly against your 5-Step prediction.
    • If one known word matches both logic and tone → Pick it confidently (never pick an unknown word just because it "sounds fancy"!).
    • If both known words clearly violate your prediction → Eliminate both immediately! You just jumped from a 25% guess to a 50% shot; use prefix/suffix polarity (un-, in-, cor-, -ous) to pick between the remaining two in 10 seconds, flag, and move on.

2. Math Pacing (35 Minutes · 22 Questions · ~95 Seconds/Question Average)

Questions inside each Math module generally climb from Easy → Medium → Hard (Q1–Q7 easiest, Q19–Q22 hardest):

Checkpoint Block Target Duration Countdown Clock Remaining Tactical Rule
Questions 1–10 10–11 minutes (~60 sec/Q) 24:00–25:00 left Fast, clean execution—box the target phrase (x vs 2x + 1) on every question so zero easy points leak.
Questions 11–17 11–12 minutes (~95 sec/Q) 12:00–14:00 left Run the 5-Second Desmos Check: if graphing intersections, sliders, or regression beats manual algebra, open Desmos immediately.
Questions 18–22 (Hardest 5) 9–10 minutes (~110–120 sec/Q) 2:30–3:00 left 90-Second Bailout Rule: If after 90 seconds you have neither a clear equation nor a Desmos setup, mark for review, enter your best strategic estimate, and try the next question (Q21 may fit your strengths much better than Q19!).
Final Verification Pass 2.5–3 minutes 0:00 Double-check SPR formatting (fractions/decimals, negative signs) and verify flagged Module 1/2 items via Desmos plug-in.

H. 1400+ Readiness Checklist (Pre-Exam Sign-Off Before December 5, 2026)

Check off each competency only when demonstrated under timed conditions on fresh official material:

  • Grammar Reliability: Consistently scoring 90%+ on mixed Boundaries and Form, Structure, and Sense sets at <=45 seconds/question, unaffected by technical vocabulary.
  • Reading Comprehension & Clause Stripping: Able to bracket modifiers/appositives in dense 100-word academic sentences and state the core Subject + Verb + Claim on the first read without translating into L1.
  • Contextual Vocabulary Independence: Achieving 80%+ on Medium/Hard Words in Context using the 5-Step Prediction Method and retaining 85%+ of your personal 90–110 high-utility vocabulary deck on delayed closed-notes checks.
  • Disciplined Inference: Eliminating "too extreme," "half-true," and "recycled-keyword" distractors to reach 75–80%+ on Medium/Hard Inferences.
  • Evidence-Based Reasoning: Identifying both halves of a scientific/historical hypothesis before scanning quotes or quantitative tables (80%+ accuracy on Command of Evidence).
  • Math Foundation Shield: Hitting 20–22 / 22 (91–100%) on Math Module 1 across two consecutive Bluebook tests with zero target-misread errors (x vs x + y).
  • Advanced Math & Data Mastery: Solving quadratic discriminants, vertex/intercept forms, exponential intervals, circle equations, and percent-change multipliers at 75%+ accuracy on Medium/Hard sets.
  • Desmos Fluency: Entering linear/nonlinear systems, constant sliders, and y_1 ~ m x_1 + b regressions cleanly in <25 seconds while knowing when symbolic isolation is faster by hand.
  • Timed Module Composure: Finishing 32-minute R&W and 35-minute Math modules with a 2–3 minute buffer and zero single-question stalls exceeding 2 minutes.
  • Error-Pattern Elimination & Score Stability: Zero unresolved 3+ recurring root weaknesses in SAT-Error-Log-and-Daily-Reflections.md, and scoring 1380–1430+ on at least one fresh, unspoiled Bluebook simulation (Test 6 or Test 7) prior to December 5, 2026.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: How Digital SAT Reading & Writing Works for International Students
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 1.1: How Digital SAT Reading & Writing Works for International Students
lessons.html:
A. The One-Passage, One-Question Advantage

Unlike older paper exams with 800-word passages and 10 questions each, every Digital SAT Reading & Writing module gives you 27 short passages (25–150 words) with exactly ONE question per passage, always arranged in a predictable sequence:

  1. Craft and Structure (~Q1–Q7): Words in Context first, followed by Text Structure and Purpose and Cross-Text Connections.
  2. Information and Ideas (~Q8–Q14): Central Ideas and Details, Command of Evidence (Textual & Quantitative), and Inferences.
  3. Standard English Conventions (~Q15–Q21): Boundaries (punctuation between clauses) and Form, Structure, and Sense (verbs, pronouns, modifiers, plurals/possessives).
  4. Expression of Ideas (~Q22–Q27): Transitions and Rhetorical Synthesis (bulleted research notes).

B. Why International Students Lose Points at 560 (And Why Memorizing Dictionaries Fails)

Non-native speakers often blame every wrong answer on "my English vocabulary is too small." In reality, diagnostic audits of 550–580 scorers reveal four distinct bottlenecks:

  • Trap 1 — Word-by-Word Mental Translation: Translating a 95-word astrophysics paragraph into your native language takes 75 seconds before you even read the choices, leaving 10 seconds to guess.
  • Trap 2 — Secondary Meaning Blindness (Polysemy): You know the everyday word qualify ("qualify for the World Cup"), so you miss its academic SAT meaning ("make a claim less absolute by adding conditions").
  • Trap 3 — Modifier Overload: English academic prose loves placing long descriptive phrases before the subject or between the subject and verb. If you lose track of who agrees or disagrees with what, you pick the exact opposite of the author's point.
  • Trap 4 — Leaving Mechanical Points Late: Spending 3 minutes on Question 12 (Hard Inference) forces you to guess on Questions 23–27 (Transitions and Bullet Notes)—questions you could have solved in 35 seconds each with 95% accuracy!

Worked Example 1.1 (Diagnostic Root-Cause Identification)

Sample Passage: Long celebrated by urban historians as spontaneous hubs of civic equality, nineteenth-century coffeehouses in port cities frequently enforced unspoken commercial hierarchies that excluded dockworkers from merchant tables.

Student's Mistake: Asked for the main idea, the student chose: "Nineteenth-century port coffeehouses were celebrated because they promoted civic equality among merchants and dockworkers."

  • Diagnostic Analysis: Did the student miss an obscure vocabulary word? No—every word (celebrated, civic, equality, enforced, excluded) was familiar. The student missed english participial modifier structure (E3 / V3): "Long celebrated by urban historians as X, [Subject] actually did Y." In academic English, opening phrases like "Long celebrated as X," "Often assumed to be X," or "Once dismissed as X" introduce an old belief that the main clause is about to overturn!

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 1.1 (Check answers in Section 8 after completing all checks)

  • CC-RW-1: In a Digital SAT R&W module of 27 questions, why is jumping to Question 15 (Standard English Conventions) at 32:00 safer for an international student than solving strictly Q1 → Q27 in numerical order?
  • CC-RW-2: In the sentence "Widely regarded by early botanists as parasitic organisms, epiphytic orchids actually obtain moisture and nutrients from rain and airborne dust rather than from their host trees," what is the author's main claim—that epiphytic orchids are parasitic, or that they are not parasitic? Which structural phrase signals the old mistaken belief?

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Reading Dense Academic Sentences Without Translating & The 5-Step Context-Clue Method
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 1.2: Reading Dense Academic Sentences Without Translating & The 5-Step Context-Clue Method
lessons.html:
A. The 3-Step Clause-Stripping Technique

Whenever an SAT sentence looks intimidatingly long, do not translate it. Strip it in 3 visual moves:

  1. Bracket Interrupting Phrases: Mentally put [brackets] around phrases set off by paired commas, paired em-dashes (— ... —), parentheses, or prepositional chains (of ..., in ..., across ...).
  2. Read Only the Skeleton (Subject + Main Verb + Object/Complement): Get the core action in plain English first.
  3. Circle Polarity & Pivot Signals: Mark + (support/agreement/benefit), - (criticism/limitation/doubt), and logical turn signals (although, despite, notwithstanding, yet, whereas, far from, rather than).

Worked Example 1.2A (Clause Stripping in Action)

Original SAT-Level Sentence (44 words):
"The hypothesis—advanced by paleoclimatologists after examining boron isotopes in Pacific coral cores—that tropical sea temperatures remained utterly static throughout the Miocene epoch has been complicated by newly recovered sediment records from the Indian Ocean."

  • Step 1 (Bracket Supplements):
    The hypothesis [—advanced by paleoclimatologists after examining boron isotopes in Pacific coral cores—] [that tropical sea temperatures remained utterly static throughout the Miocene epoch] has been complicated by newly recovered sediment records [from the Indian Ocean].
  • Step 2 (Read the 7-Word Skeleton):
    The hypothesis has been complicated by new records.
  • Step 3 (Polarity):
    Old idea = tropical seas stayed static. New Indian Ocean data = challenges/complicates (-) that simple story! Notice you did not need to know what boron isotopes or the Miocene epoch are to understand 100% of the logic!

B. The 5-Step Context-Clue Method for Words in Context

  1. Find the Core Idea using Clause Stripping.
  2. Spot the Connector:
    • : or — or that is or specifically → Same-Direction Restatement (=)
    • although, though, despite, notwithstanding, whereas, while, however, yet → Opposite-Direction Contrast (≠)
    • because, since, consequently, therefore, thus, accordingly → Cause-and-Effect (→)
  3. Predict Your Own Simple English Word before looking at A–D.
  4. Eliminate Polarity & Meaning Mismatches (never choose a word merely because it looks familiar or sophisticated).
  5. Plug Back In to verify both meaning and tone intensity.

Worked Example 1.2B (5-Step Method)

Original SAT-Style Example:
While early reviewers praised the documentary for its vivid archival footage, labor historians noted that its explanation of the 1912 textile strike was frustratingly ______: by focusing almost exclusively on two charismatic union speakers, the filmmaker ignored wage records, mill-floor safety inspections, and immigrant mutual-aid networks.

A) exhaustive
B) reductive
C) impartial
D) corroborated

  • Step 1 & 2 (Core Idea + Signal): Opening While contrasts praise (+ vivid footage) with historians' criticism (- frustratingly ______). Next comes a colon (:), which defines the blank! After the colon: the filmmaker looked only at two speakers and ignored three complex economic/social factors.
  • Step 3 (Simple Prediction): "oversimplified / too narrow / incomplete."
  • Step 4 (Evaluate A–D):
    • A) exhaustive = complete, covering everything → exact opposite of ignoring key factors!
    • B) reductive = presenting a complex subject in an overly simple, narrow way → matches "oversimplified"! (Even if you only partially knew "reduce = make smaller," root + context points straight here!)
    • C) impartial = fair, neutral → positive/neutral tone, contradicts "frustratingly" and ignoring evidence.
    • D) corroborated = confirmed by evidence → contradicts historians' critique.
  • Step 5 (Verify): "frustratingly reductive" fits both the negative tone and the colon explanation cleanly. Correct: B.

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 1.2

  • CC-RW-3: Strip this sentence to its 6–8 word core skeleton: "Microbial communities thriving near hydrothermal vents—environments devoid of sunlight and subjected to crushing hydrostatic pressure—synthesize organic compounds through chemosynthesis."
  • CC-RW-4: Predict a simple English word for the blank before thinking of fancy words: "Far from being ______, the architect's choice of porous volcanic stone served three practical functions: regulating indoor humidity, absorbing street noise, and reducing structural weight."

lessons.title: Lesson 1.3: Diagnostic Playbook Across All Four Digital SAT R&W Domains
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 1.3: Diagnostic Playbook Across All Four Digital SAT R&W Domains
lessons.html:
Use these compact, high-precision rules whenever solving or reviewing questions across the four domains:

Domain 1: Information and Ideas (Central Ideas, Command of Evidence, Inferences)

  • Central Ideas & Details Rule: Your winning choice must cover the primary topic + exact claim scope of the entire paragraph. Eliminate:
    • Too Narrow: True detail from one sentence that misses the main point.
    • Too Broad / Extreme: Uses words like all, never, only, completely disproved, impossible when the passage says often, may, suggests.
    • Wrong Comparison: Invents a "better than / more important than" comparison never stated in the passage.
  • Command of Evidence (Textual & Quantitative) Rule:
    1. Box the exact claim in the question stem first (usually Factor X leads to Result Y).
    2. For data tables/graphs: Read title, column headers, units, and footnotes for 5 seconds first. Eliminate any choice that misstates a number (False to Data) OR states a true number from the table that fails to prove the specific claim (True to Data, Irrelevant to Claim—the #1 Hard trap!).
  • Inferences Rule: The blank at the end of the passage ("most logically completes the text") must follow necessarily from combining the passage's premises. Never add outside world knowledge or emotional leaps.

Domain 2: Craft and Structure (Text Structure & Purpose, Cross-Text Connections)

  • Text Structure / Overall Purpose Rule: Read for functional moves, not small facts. Label Sentence 1 ([Introduces conventional hypothesis]), Sentence 2 ([Describes new experiment]), Sentence 3 ([Explains why results challenge Sentence 1]). Match the active verb in choices A–D ("question an assumption," "illustrate a mechanism," "qualify an earlier claim").
  • Cross-Text Connections Rule: Write a 4-word summary of Text 1's claim and Text 2's claim + + (agrees), - (disagrees), or ± (agrees with phenomenon, offers a limitation/alternative cause). Most right answers on the SAT are nuanced partial agreements or scope limitations (±), not angry total rejections!

Domain 3: Expression of Ideas (Transitions, Rhetorical Synthesis)

  • Transitions Rule: Physically ignore the transition currently in the blank. Summarize Sentence A → Sentence B, pick one of the 4 Core Logical Bridges:
    1. Addition / Continuation: Moreover, Furthermore, In addition, Similarly, Likewise
    2. Contrast / Concession: However, Nevertheless, Still, Conversely, On the other hand, Granted
    3. Cause / Result: Therefore, Consequently, Thus, Accordingly, As a result
    4. Specification / Example / Restatement: Specifically, For instance, In other words, Indeed, In fact
    • Shortcut: If two answer choices are exact functional synonyms (e.g., Therefore and Consequently in the same question), cross out both immediately—the SAT never forces you to split hairs between identical transitions!
  • Rhetorical Synthesis Rule: Read ONLY the question prompt first; underline every constraint (e.g., "emphasize a similarity between the two telescopes to an audience already familiar with Hubble"). Test choices A–D strictly against that checklist before reading the bulleted notes (read the notes only if two choices satisfy the prompt and you need to check factual accuracy).

Domain 4: Standard English Conventions (Boundaries & Form, Structure, and Sense)

Glance at choices A–D first to see what changes:

  1. Punctuation Changes (Boundaries)? Test Independent Clauses (IC)!
    An IC has a main subject + finite tense verb (is, were, analyzes, discovered — never bare -ing like analyzing!) and stands alone as a complete thought.
    • IC . IC = Legal
    • IC ; IC = Legal (including before conjunctive adverbs: ; however,, ; nevertheless,, ; therefore,)
    • IC , FANBOYS IC = Legal (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so)
    • IC : [Explanation / Noun Phrase / List / IC] = Legal (Left of a colon MUST be a complete IC!)
    • IC , IC (including , however,!) = ILLEGAL COMMA SPLICE!
    • Dependent Clause , IC = Legal (e.g., Although the sensor failed, the satellite landed safely.)
  2. Verb Endings Change? Check Subject-Verb Agreement & Tense!
    Cross out prepositional phrases (of the paintings in the gallery) between subject and verb: The restoration [of the paintings] WAS (singular restoration, not plural paintings). Notice the 3-versus-1 Odd-One-Out Hint: if three choices are plural (are, have been, remain) and one is singular (is), check immediately whether the true subject is singular!
  3. Opening Participial Phrase (Walking into the archive, _____)? Check Dangling Modifiers!
    Whatever noun touches the comma must be the person/thing doing the opening action (Walking into the archive, the historian noticed... — NOT the letters caught the historian's eye!).

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 1.3

  • CC-RW-5 (Boundaries): Why is "The spectrometer detected trace methane, however, researchers cautioned against claiming biological activity" grammatically wrong on the SAT, and what are two ways to fix it?
  • CC-RW-6 (Transitions Shortcut): On a Transitions question, Choice A is Furthermore, Choice B is Moreover, Choice C is Nevertheless, and Choice D is For example. Which two choices can you eliminate in 2 seconds without even reading the passage, and why?
  • CC-RW-7 (Modifiers): Which noun must immediately follow the comma in: "Having analyzed sediment cores from twelve alpine lakes, ______" — (a) evidence of industrial lead appeared earlier than expected OR (b) geochemists concluded that industrial lead appeared earlier than expected?
  • CC-RW-8 (Rhetorical Synthesis): What should you read first on a bulleted-notes question, and why?

checks.promptHtml: Why is "The spectrometer detected trace methane, however, researchers cautioned against claiming biological activity" grammatically wrong on the SAT, and what are two ways to fix it?
checks.answerHtml: It is a comma splice (IC , however , IC — however is a conjunctive adverb, NOT a FANBOYS conjunction). Two valid fixes: (1) ...methane; however, researchers... or (2) ...methane. However, researchers... (or ...methane, but researchers...).

checks.promptHtml: On a Transitions question, Choice A is Furthermore, Choice B is Moreover, Choice C is Nevertheless, and Choice D is For example. Which two choices can you eliminate in 2 seconds without even reading the passage, and why?
checks.answerHtml: Eliminate A (Furthermore) and B (Moreover) immediately because both are exact additive transitions (+ addition); on the Digital SAT, two functionally identical transitions cannot have one right and one wrong.

checks.promptHtml: Which noun must immediately follow the comma in: "Having analyzed sediment cores from twelve alpine lakes, ______" — (a) evidence of industrial lead appeared earlier than expected OR (b) geochemists concluded that industrial lead appeared earlier than expected?
checks.answerHtml: (b) geochemists concluded... — Only human geochemists can "have analyzed sediment cores." Placing "evidence" right after the comma creates an illogical dangling modifier claiming evidence analyzed the cores!

checks.promptHtml: What should you read first on a bulleted-notes question, and why?
checks.answerHtml: Read only the final question stem first and underline every rhetorical goal constraint (e.g., similarity vs. difference, cause vs. result, familiar vs. unfamiliar audience), because 2–3 choices will be factually true according to the notes yet violate the specific goal.

subSections.title: A. Day 1 Core Academic Vocabulary (10 High-Utility SAT Words)
subSections.titleHtml: A. Day 1 Core Academic Vocabulary (10 High-Utility SAT Words)
subSections.html:
Study each word using all three layers. After completing the exercises below, verify your entries in Vocabulary-Notebook-and-Spaced-Review.md.

1. substantiate (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To prove or support a claim with concrete facts, data, or evidence.
  • Alternative / Related Forms: substantiation (n. — proof), unsubstantiated (adj. — lacking proof; rumor-like), substantial (adj. — Watch out! Substantial usually means "large in size/amount," NOT "proven"!).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: verify, validate, confirm · Ant: disprove, refute, contradict.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "While coastal legends long described a submerged stone harbor, marine archaeologists could not substantiate those accounts until sonar mapping revealed carved breakwaters forty meters offshore."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Before sonar mapping, the harbor stories were just unverified legends; sonar provided solid physical proof to substantiate them.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing substantiate ("prove with evidence") with substantial ("large/significant") because they look nearly identical.
  • Short Application Activity: Replace the bracketed phrase in your head: "Without raw temperature logs, the team's claim remains [unproven]." → unsubstantiated.

2. undermine (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To weaken an argument, system, belief, or authority—often gradually or indirectly.
  • Alternative Meanings: Literally "to dig beneath a foundation so a wall collapses"; on the SAT, almost always metaphorical ("weaken credibility or effectiveness").
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: weaken, erode, subvert, compromise · Ant: bolster, strengthen, reinforce.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Discovery of widespread contamination in the laboratory's control vials undermined the study's conclusion that airborne microbes survived stratospheric radiation."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Dirty control vials do not necessarily prove the exact opposite is true, but they destroy the reliability of the experiment's conclusion.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Thinking undermine means "underestimate" ("guess too low") or "underline" ("emphasize"). Never confuse undermine (weaken) with underscore (emphasize)!
  • Short Application Activity: Contrast pair check—write + or - next to undermine (-) vs. underscore (+ / emphasize).

3. corroborate (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To confirm or give independent supporting evidence for a statement, theory, or finding.
  • Alternative / Related Forms: corroboration (n.), corroborative (adj.). Typically used when Source B independently backs up Source A.
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: confirm, verify, bear out · Ant: contradict, refute, challenge.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Tree-ring growth anomalies in Scandinavian pines corroborated seventh-century Byzantine chronicles describing two consecutive summers without warmth."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Two totally separate records—biological tree rings and written medieval histories—point to the same cooling event, so one confirms (corroborates) the other.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing corroborate ("confirm with evidence") with collaborate ("work together as teammates"). Tree rings cannot "work as teammates" with medieval historians, but they can confirm their reports!
  • Short Application Activity: Decide which word fits: "Two astronomers in Chile and Japan ______ [worked together] on the survey, and Hubble data later ______ [confirmed] their measurements." (collaborated / corroborated).

4. plausible (adjective)

  • Simple English Definition: Reasonable and believable enough that it could be true, based on what we currently know.
  • Degree-of-Certainty Nuance: Sits in the middle-positive zone—stronger than a wild guess, weaker than 100% proven fact!
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: credible, conceivable, reasonable · Ant: implausible, far-fetched, untenable.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Although direct fossil footprints are absent, seasonal river-delta flooding offers a plausible mechanism for how seed pods crossed the ancient strait."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: "Although direct... footprints are absent" tells us scientists lack 100% proof, yet river flooding is realistic and scientifically believable (plausible).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Treating plausible as meaning "praiseworthy / applause-worthy" (because it shares the Latin root plaudere, to clap) or treating it as "100% proven."
  • Short Application Activity: Rank from least certain (1) to most certain (3): definitive, implausible, plausible. (1 = implausible, 2 = plausible, 3 = definitive).

5. ambiguous (adjective)

  • Simple English Definition: Open to two or more valid interpretations; unclear or undecided in meaning.
  • Alternative / Related Distinction: Distinguish ambiguous (a statement/result whose meaning can be read multiple ways) from ambivalent (a person having mixed, conflicting feelings about something).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: equivocal, inconclusive, open-ended · Ant: unambiguous, explicit, clear-cut.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Because elevated silicon levels can stem from either volcanic ashfall or intensified continental weathering, the mineral layer's climatic signal remains ambiguous."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Notice "either X or Y"—two competing causes fit the exact same silicon data, making its meaning unclear (ambiguous).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Thinking ambiguous means "ambitious" (working hard for big goals) due to spelling similarity!
  • Short Application Activity: Spot the clue phrase in the sentence above that proves ambiguous is right ("either volcanic ashfall or intensified continental weathering").

6. infer (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To reach a logical conclusion by reasoning from clues and evidence rather than reading an explicit statement.
  • Alternative / Direction Nuance: A speaker/writer implies (puts clues in); a reader/scientist infers (draws the conclusion out).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: deduce, conclude, gather · Ant: state directly, speculate wildly.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Because obsidian blades unearthed on the island matched the chemical signature of a mainland quarry 200 kilometers away, anthropologists inferred that Neolithic residents maintained maritime trade networks."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Nobody left a written receipt saying "we traded by boat," yet mainland volcanic glass on an island logically proves sea exchange (inferred).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Thinking infer means "guess creatively using imagination." On the SAT, a valid inference is tightly bound to stated evidence.
  • Short Application Activity: State what you can strictly infer from: "Every novel submitted after Friday was disqualified, and Maya's novel won second prize." (Maya submitted her novel on or before Friday.)

7. reconcile (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To make two seemingly conflicting facts, theories, or groups fit together harmoniously.
  • Alternative Meanings: (1) Intellectual/scientific: resolve an apparent contradiction between two models/datasets; (2) Social: restore friendly relations after an argument; (3) Passive: reconcile oneself to X = reluctantly accept an unavoidable reality.
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: harmonize, integrate, resolve · Ant: polarize, alienate, clash.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "By accounting for thermal expansion in brass instruments during summer nights, the astronomer finally reconciled his meridian measurements with those recorded at the Greenwich observatory."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: The two observatories initially had conflicting numbers; factoring in heat expansion made both datasets agree (reconciled them).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Thinking reconcile simply means "reconsider" (think again). Reconcile almost always requires two things in tension (reconcile A with B).
  • Short Application Activity: Identify A and B being reconciled in the sentence above (his meridian measurements and those recorded at Greenwich).

8. nuanced (adjective)

  • Simple English Definition: Capturing subtle, careful shades of meaning or complexity rather than taking an extreme, one-sided position.
  • Related Form: nuance (n. — a subtle difference in meaning, tone, or condition).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: subtle, refined, qualified, balanced · Ant: simplistic, sweeping, crude, black-and-white.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Rejecting claims that automation uniformly destroys or uniformly creates employment, the economist presented a nuanced analysis showing how robotics raises wages for diagnostic technicians while displacing routine assembly roles."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Notice the contrast with "uniformly destroys or uniformly creates" (extreme, simplistic views). Showing different effects for different workers is nuanced.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Assuming nuanced means "confusing" or "indecisive." On the SAT, nuanced is nearly always a high-praise academic word describing rigorous scholarship!
  • Short Application Activity: Why would an SAT Cross-Text answer describing Text 2's response as "offering a more nuanced perspective" usually beat "completely refuting Text 1"? (Because scholars typically add conditions rather than claiming 100% of Text 1 is false.)

9. tentative (adjective)

  • Simple English Definition: Provisional, cautious, and not yet final—open to revision when stronger evidence arrives.
  • Alternative Meanings: Can also describe physical hesitation ("a tentative knock on the door"), but in SAT science/history passages it means "preliminary / not conclusive."
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: preliminary, provisional, cautious, guarded · Ant: conclusive, definitive, final, irrefutable.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Because the exoplanet passed in front of its host star only twice during the telescope's observation window, astrophysicists offered only a tentative estimate of its orbital period."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Two transits is a tiny dataset, so honest scientists present their calculation cautiously (tentative), awaiting future transits.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing tentative with attentive ("paying close attention")! Look closely at the spelling: attentive = focused; tentative = provisional/unconfirmed.
  • Short Application Activity: Pick which word fits cautious science: "With only six fossil fragments recovered, any reconstruction of the creature's gait must remain [tentative / attentive]." (tentative).

10. notwithstanding (preposition / adverb / conjunction)

  • Simple English Definition: In spite of; despite; nevertheless.
  • Syntactic Flexibility (Crucial for International Students!):
    • Before a noun phrase: "Notwithstanding the drought, wheat yields rose." (= Despite the drought...)
    • After a noun phrase! "The drought notwithstanding, wheat yields rose." (= Despite the drought... — unique English inversion that confuses non-native readers!)
    • As a transition adverb: "The soil was arid; notwithstanding, native shrubs flourished." (= nevertheless)
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: despite, regardless of, nevertheless · Ant: because of, owing to, consequently.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Its formidable mathematical complexity notwithstanding, Noether's theorem rapidly became an indispensable pillar of modern theoretical physics."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Notice the post-positioned structure (Its complexity notwithstanding = Despite its intense difficulty). Normally complexity slows adoption, yet the theorem became essential anyway.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Breaking the word literally into "not + standing" and guessing it means "collapsing," "unimportant," or "refusing to tolerate." It always means despite / nevertheless!
  • Short Application Activity: Rewrite "Her limited archival access notwithstanding, the biographer reconstructed the poet's correspondence" starting with Despite (Despite her limited archival access, the biographer...).
