subSections.html:
Exercise 4A: Original SAT-Style Words in Context Multiple Choice

VOC-Q1 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Easy]
Early ethnographers often portrayed high-altitude pastoral communities as isolated from lowland economies, yet recent isotopic analyses of bronze tools from Andean herding sites ______ that view by demonstrating regular metal exchange across three elevation zones.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) corroborate
B) undermine
C) substantiate
D) infer

VOC-Q2 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Medium]
Because early Renaissance workshop contracts rarely named individual apprentices, attributing an unsigned panel painting to a single young assistant rather than to the master's studio generally yields at best a ______ identification unless pigment spectroscopy or private letters provide independent proof.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) tentative
B) nuanced
C) unambiguous
D) mandatory

VOC-Q3 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Medium]
For decades, oceanographers struggled to ______ satellite altimetry readings showing steady sea-surface elevation in the basin with coastal tide-gauge logs indicating rapid local subsidence; only when vertical land motion from groundwater extraction was modeled did the two datasets align.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) undermine
B) infer
C) reconcile
D) assert

VOC-Q4 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Hard]
The playwright's depiction of industrial modernization is remarkably ______: rather than framing steam-powered mills purely as engines of prosperity or purely as instruments of alienation, her scenes trace how factory wages simultaneously expanded young women's civic autonomy and eroded traditional craft guilds.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) ambiguous
B) tentative
C) plausible
D) nuanced

Exercise 4B: Context-Clue Signal & Polarity Identification

For each sentence (VOC-Q5 to VOC-Q9), write down: (i) the exact signal word or punctuation mark guiding the logic, and (ii) whether the bracketed target word carries a Supporting/Confirming (+), Weakening (-), or Cautious/Unclear (?) function in context:

  • VOC-Q5: "Although the herbal extract reduced inflammation in cultured cells, clinical trials failed to [substantiate] any therapeutic benefit in human patients."
  • VOC-Q6: "Pollen grains preserved in bog peat [corroborated] monastic tax rolls: both sources pointed to an abrupt shift from barley cultivation to sheep grazing around 1350."
  • VOC-Q7: *"Severe funding shortages [notwithstanding], the municipal conservatory maintained free Saturday acoustics workshops for public-school students."*
  • VOC-Q8: "Because the inscription's final verb is weathered away, epigraphers remain divided over its [ambiguous] reference to a royal pardon."
  • VOC-Q9: "Given that nocturnal moths navigated accurately inside a magnetically shielded chamber, researchers considered reliance on Earth's magnetic field alone an [implausible] explanation."

Exercise 4C: Academic Sentence Completion

Fill each blank (VOC-Q10 to VOC-Q14) using the single most precise word from Day 1's 10-word bank (substantiate, undermine, corroborate, plausible, ambiguous, infer, reconcile, nuanced, tentative, notwithstanding — inflect verb tense if needed):

  • VOC-Q10: From variations in strontium ratios inside fossilized mammoth tusks, paleoecologists can ______ the seasonal migration routes individual animals traveled across Arctic tundra.
  • VOC-Q11: Even a single undisclosed financial conflict of interest can ______ public trust in an otherwise well-designed epidemiological survey.
  • VOC-Q12: Harsh subzero winds ______, automated weather stations on the Antarctic plateau transmitted uninterrupted barometric data for eighteen months.
  • VOC-Q13: While acoustic resonance offers a ______ hypothesis for why ancient builders curved the amphitheater's upper wall, engineers note that drainage considerations could also explain the design.
  • VOC-Q14: Independent radar measurements from the European orbiter ______ the ice-thickness estimates previously reported by NASA's polar lander.

Exercise 4D: Close-Synonym & Trap Discrimination

International students scoring 650+ must separate words that feel similar. Choose the exact right word in each pair (VOC-Q15 to VOC-Q18) and state in 5–10 words why the other fails:

  • VOC-Q15 (tentative vs. ambiguous): "The contract's wording regarding overtime pay was dangerously ______, allowing managers and union representatives to calculate two completely different hourly totals."
  • VOC-Q16 (corroborate vs. collaborate): "Three newly digitized ship logs from Lisbon ______ the chronicler's claim that monsoon winds arrived three weeks early in 1541."
  • VOC-Q17 (undermine vs. underscore): "Far from weakening her thesis, those regional exceptions actually ______ her central point that local water rights depended on soil permeability."
  • VOC-Q18 (substantiate vs. substantial): "Although the sociologist interviewed a ______ number of commuters, self-reported travel times alone could not ______ a citywide decline in transit delays." (Place both words in the correct order!)

Exercise 4E: Short Academic Passage Integrating Target Vocabulary

Read the 115-word passage below without using a dictionary, then answer VOC-Q19 to VOC-Q21:

Early maritime historians dismissed accounts of transoceanic drift voyages in balsa-wood rafts as implausible folklore, arguing that porous timber would waterlog and sink within weeks. Their skepticism notwithstanding, twentieth-century experimental crossings demonstrated that freshly felled balsa retains sap that slows water absorption, offering a plausible physical basis for prolonged buoyancy. Even so, contemporary archaeologists urge a nuanced interpretation: proving that a vessel could survive ocean currents does not by itself substantiate claims of regular pre-modern trade unless excavations unearth artifacts whose chemical origins corroborate two-way contact. Until coastal stratigraphy yields firmer evidence, any map of sustained drift-raft commerce remains tentative.

  • VOC-Q19: Strip Sentence 2 ("Their skepticism notwithstanding... prolonged buoyancy") to explain what experimental crossings proved and what obstacle/doubt they overcame.
  • VOC-Q20: Why do contemporary archaeologists call for a "nuanced" interpretation rather than saying experimental voyages proved ancient trade? (Point to the exact distinction between plausible and substantiate in the passage!)
  • VOC-Q21: Why does the passage end with tentative rather than ambiguous or implausible?

Exercise 4F: Closed-Notes Rapid Retrieval Quiz

Cover Section 4A completely! Without looking back, write a 3–6 word simple English meaning for each item (VOC-Q22 to VOC-Q31):

  • VOC-Q22: corroborate → __________________
  • VOC-Q23: notwithstanding → __________________
  • VOC-Q24: tentative → __________________
  • VOC-Q25: undermine → __________________
  • VOC-Q26: reconcile → __________________
  • VOC-Q27: nuanced → __________________
  • VOC-Q28: plausible → __________________
  • VOC-Q29: ambiguous → __________________
  • VOC-Q30: substantiate → __________________
  • VOC-Q31: infer → __________________

vocabulary.answerKeyHtml:
Exercise 4A (Words in Context MCQs)

  • VOC-Q1 → Correct: B (undermine)
    • Why B works: yet signals contrast between early ethnographers' claim (isolated) and new isotopic data (regular metal exchange across three zones). New data weakens (undermines) the isolation claim.
    • Why others fail: A (corroborate) and C (substantiate) mean confirm/prove (opposite polarity); D (infer) is an action a person performs from evidence—data itself does not "infer a view."
  • VOC-Q2 → Correct: A (tentative)
    • Why A works: Lack of apprentice names means any attribution without chemical/letter proof is provisional and unconfirmed (tentative).
    • Why others fail: B (nuanced) praises subtle balance rather than describing unconfirmed evidence; C (unambiguous) means 100% clear (contradicted by unless... provide proof); D (mandatory) means required.
  • VOC-Q3 → Correct: C (reconcile)
    • Why C works: Notice the pattern reconcile [Dataset A: steady sea surface] with [Dataset B: rapid local sinking], confirmed by "did the two datasets align."
    • Why others fail: A (undermine), B (infer), and D (assert) neither fit _____ X with Y grammar nor express making two conflicting datasets fit together.
  • VOC-Q4 → Correct: D (nuanced)
    • Why D works: The colon defines the blank: rejecting two one-sided extremes (purely prosperity vs. purely alienation) to show simultaneous benefits and losses = subtle, balanced (nuanced).
    • Why others fail: A (ambiguous) implies unclear/confusing writing rather than deliberate analytical subtlety; B (tentative) means provisional; C (plausible) means merely believable.

Exercise 4B (Signal & Polarity)

  • VOC-Q5: Signal = Although + failed to; Function of substantiate = Confirming/Proving (+), negated by failed to so overall clause shows negative outcome.
  • VOC-Q6: Signal = Colon (:) + both sources pointed to; Function of corroborated = Confirming (+).
  • VOC-Q7: Signal = Post-positioned notwithstanding; Function = Concession/Contrast (despite - obstacle → + outcome).
  • VOC-Q8: Signal = Because... weathered away + remain divided; Function of ambiguous = Unclear / Multiple Interpretations (?).
  • VOC-Q9: Signal = Given that [moths navigated without magnetic field]; Function of implausible = Unbelievable / Weakened (-).

Exercise 4C (Sentence Completion)

  • VOC-Q10: infer (deduce migration routes logically from chemical clues)
  • VOC-Q11: undermine (weaken/erode public trust)
  • VOC-Q12: notwithstanding (post-positioned = "Despite harsh subzero winds")
  • VOC-Q13: plausible (reasonable/believable, though drainage is another possible cause)
  • VOC-Q14: corroborated (or corroborate — independent European orbiter data confirmed NASA lander data)

Exercise 4D (Close-Synonym Discrimination)

  • VOC-Q15: ambiguous — The contract allows two competing interpretations, whereas tentative means temporary/cautious.
  • VOC-Q16: corroborate — Inanimate 16th-century ship logs confirm a claim with evidence; they cannot collaborate (work together socially like people).
  • VOC-Q17: underscore — "Far from weakening" requires the opposite of weaken: emphasize (underscore), never undermine (weaken)!
  • VOC-Q18: First blank = substantial (large in number); Second blank = substantiate (prove with hard evidence).

Exercise 4E (Academic Passage Synthesis)

  • VOC-Q19: Core meaning: Despite historians' skepticism, real raft voyages proved fresh balsa wood stays afloat long enough to cross oceans.
  • VOC-Q20: Showing a raft could float makes transoceanic contact plausible (physically possible/believable), but possibility alone does not substantiate (prove with hard evidence) that regular ancient trade actually happened.
  • VOC-Q21: Because rafts can float (not implausible), yet archaeological proof is still incomplete, any trade map is provisional and awaiting firmer data (tentative), rather than ambiguous (double-meaning wording).

Exercise 4F (Closed-Notes Retrieval Key — Score 1 point per accurate plain-English meaning)

  • VOC-Q22 (corroborate): Confirm with independent evidence.
  • VOC-Q23 (notwithstanding): Despite; in spite of; nevertheless.
  • VOC-Q24 (tentative): Provisional, cautious, not yet final.
  • VOC-Q25 (undermine): Weaken gradually or erode credibility.
  • VOC-Q26 (reconcile): Make two conflicting facts/ideas fit together.
  • VOC-Q27 (nuanced): Showing subtle, balanced distinctions (not simplistic).
  • VOC-Q28 (plausible): Reasonable and believable enough to be possible.
  • VOC-Q29 (ambiguous): Open to two or more meanings; unclear.
  • VOC-Q30 (substantiate): Prove or back up a claim with solid evidence.
  • VOC-Q31 (infer): Conclude logically from clues/evidence.

rwPractice.introHtml:
Explicit Origin Notice: All 18 items below (RW-D1-Q1 through RW-D1-Q18) are original SAT-style practice questions engineered to mirror Digital SAT item blueprints.
Timed Calibration Option: Set a strict countdown timer for 21 minutes (~70 seconds/question). Apply the Split-Order Strategy (solve Q12–Q18 first in ~6 minutes, then return to Q1–Q11 with 15 minutes remaining!). Do not view Section 8 until all 18 answers are recorded.

questions.stemHtml:
Unlike broadleaf deciduous trees that shed foliage seasonally, desert succulents open their leaf pores primarily at night; this nocturnal gas-exchange cycle enables the plants to ______ internal water reserves that would otherwise evaporate rapidly in midday heat.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: conserve
disperse
fabricate
exhaust

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why A works: Opening pores only at night prevents water from evaporating "in midday heat," meaning the plants save/preserve (conserve) internal water.
  • Why others fail: B (disperse) = scatter away; C (fabricate) = invent/manufacture from scratch; D (exhaust) = use up completely (the exact fate the plant avoids!).
  • Skill Assessed: Contextual vocabulary + otherwise contrast logic.
  • Next-Time Clue: "that would otherwise [be lost]" proves the blank must mean keep/protect.

questions.stemHtml:
When museum conservators examined the Flemish portrait using conventional infrared photography, the resulting chronology remained ______: dense lead-white pigment in the lower layer scattered light so unevenly that the underdrawing could plausibly date either to the artist's Antwerp apprenticeship in 1528 or to her later court commission in 1542.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: definitive
ambiguous
corroborated
overt

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: Look right after the colon (:): the underdrawing "could plausibly date either to... 1528 or to... 1542." Two equally plausible interpretations = ambiguous.
  • Why others fail: A (definitive) = 100% settled (opposite); C (corroborated) = confirmed; D (overt) = obvious/openly visible.
  • Skill Assessed: Academic vocabulary + colon definition structure.
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever a colon is followed by "either X or Y," predict unclear / ambiguous / inconclusive.

questions.stemHtml:
In her 2019 monograph, economic historian Nadia Al-Mansoor argued that seventeenth-century artisan guilds uniformly stifled technical innovation; after uncovering provincial town ledgers showing rural weavers adopting multi-shaft looms with guild subsidies, however, she ______ her earlier claim in a 2025 follow-up article, restricting it to capital-city luxury trades.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: substantiated
qualified
amplified
vindicated

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: In 2019 she made an absolute claim ("uniformly stifled"); after finding rural counter-evidence (however), she narrowed/limited (qualified) her claim "restricting it to capital-city luxury trades."
  • Why others fail: A (substantiated) & D (vindicated) mean proved her original sweeping 2019 claim completely right (ignoring however and restricting it); C (amplified) means expanded/made louder, opposite of restricting scope.
  • Skill Assessed: Secondary academic meaning (polysemy) of qualify (= moderate or limit an absolute statement).
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever a scholar shifts from "all/uniformly" to "only in certain cases," the SAT's favorite verb is qualify!

questions.stemHtml:
Municipal planners have long assumed that expanding open paved surface area in downtown plazas automatically fosters neighborhood social interaction. Yet time-lapse pedestrian mapping across fourteen renovated European squares reveals that vast, unshaded stone expanses remain largely deserted except as brisk transit corridors. By contrast, narrower plazas bordered by recessed shopfronts, movable seating, and continuous tree canopies recorded four times as many stationary conversations per hour.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.raw: To argue that historical European squares are too narrow to accommodate modern commuter traffic
choices.html: To argue that historical European squares are too narrow to accommodate modern commuter traffic

choices.raw: To question a widespread assumption in urban design and highlight physical features associated with higher social engagement
choices.html: To question a widespread assumption in urban design and highlight physical features associated with higher social engagement

choices.raw: To explain how time-lapse pedestrian mapping replaced resident surveys in municipal planning
choices.html: To explain how time-lapse pedestrian mapping replaced resident surveys in municipal planning

choices.raw: To advocate replacing paved city plazas entirely with forested suburban parks
choices.html: To advocate replacing paved city plazas entirely with forested suburban parks

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: Sentence 1 states a common assumption ("Municipal planners have long assumed..."); Sentence 2 overturns it with evidence ("Yet time-lapse... reveals..."); Sentence 3 identifies what actually drives lingering ("shopfronts, movable seating, and continuous tree canopies").
  • Why others fail: A reverses Sentence 3; C elevates a research tool (time-lapse mapping) into the main purpose and invents "replaced resident surveys"; D is an extreme fabrication ("forested suburban parks").
  • Skill Assessed: Text Structure and Purpose (Assumption → Empirical Refutation → Alternative Explanation).
  • Next-Time Clue: "have long assumed... Yet..." almost always maps to "question/challenge a common assumption."

questions.stemHtml:
Text 1
Geochemists studying the end-Triassic marine extinction have linked the abrupt collapse of coral-dominated reefs to volcanic carbon dioxide emissions from the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province. Rising atmospheric CO2​ lowered ocean surface pH, starving calcifying corals of the carbonate ions required to build skeletal frameworks.

Text 2
Carbonate chemistry undoubtedly stressed tropical scleractinian corals during the peak volcanic pulse. Nevertheless, stratigraphic cores from northern latitude basins show that siliceous sponge-microbial reefs—organisms far less sensitive to pH drops—suffered severe die-offs prior to the main carbon-isotope excursion, coinciding instead with a rapid regional drop in sea level that exposed continental-shelf habitats.

Based on the texts, how would the authors of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation presented in Text 1?

choices.raw: By disputing the claim that volcanic eruptions occurred in the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province during the late Triassic
choices.html: By disputing the claim that volcanic eruptions occurred in the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province during the late Triassic

choices.raw: By arguing that tropical scleractinian corals actually benefited from reduced carbonate ion concentrations
choices.html: By arguing that tropical scleractinian corals actually benefited from reduced carbonate ion concentrations

choices.raw: By acknowledging that ocean acidification harmed certain reef builders while contending that it cannot by itself explain the timing and ecological breadth of reef collapse
choices.html: By acknowledging that ocean acidification harmed certain reef builders while contending that it cannot by itself explain the timing and ecological breadth of reef collapse

choices.raw: By proposing that siliceous sponges caused the drop in ocean pH prior to volcanic emissions
choices.html: By proposing that siliceous sponges caused the drop in ocean pH prior to volcanic emissions

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Text 2 opens with a polite concession ("Carbonate chemistry undoubtedly stressed tropical... corals") and pivots via Nevertheless to show northern sponge reefs died earlier due to sea-level drop—meaning acidification hurt some reefs but cannot explain the timing and full breadth of collapse.
  • Why others fail: A & B falsely claim total disagreement (contradicting "undoubtedly stressed"); D scrambles cause and effect between sponges and pH.
  • Skill Assessed: Cross-Text Connections — partial concession + scope limitation (±).
  • Next-Time Clue: When Text 2 starts with "Undoubtedly / Granted / Certainly... Nevertheless," look for an answer starting with "Acknowledge X, but contend/question Y."

questions.stemHtml:
The following text is an original passage written in the style of nineteenth-century realist fiction.
Every Sunday afternoon, visitors from the provincial capital toured Uncle Mateo's glasshouse, marveling at the velvet-petalled Amazonian orchids arranged beneath brass misting pipes and gilt Latin plaques. Clara noticed, however, that once the iron gate latched behind the last carriage, her uncle walked past the prized tropical rows without a glance, pulling a low wooden stool beside a cracked terracotta pot of coastal rosemary he had carried as a boy from his grandmother's courtyard.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.raw: Despite public admiration for his rare botanical collection, Clara's uncle privately cherishes a modest plant connected to his personal history.
choices.html: Despite public admiration for his rare botanical collection, Clara's uncle privately cherishes a modest plant connected to his personal history.

choices.raw: Clara's uncle plans to sell his tropical orchids because brass misting pipes are too costly to maintain.
choices.html: Clara's uncle plans to sell his tropical orchids because brass misting pipes are too costly to maintain.

choices.raw: Visitors from the provincial capital prefer native coastal herbs to imported Amazonian orchids.
choices.html: Visitors from the provincial capital prefer native coastal herbs to imported Amazonian orchids.

choices.raw: Clara disapproves of her uncle's habit of locking the glasshouse gate on Sunday evenings.
choices.html: Clara disapproves of her uncle's habit of locking the glasshouse gate on Sunday evenings.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why A works: Captures both halves of the contrast (visitors marvel at rare orchids vs. however... her uncle privately sits beside childhood rosemary).
  • Why others fail: B (sell orchids / costly pipes), C (visitors prefer herbs), and D (Clara disapproves) all invent unsupported narrative claims.
  • Skill Assessed: Central Ideas and Details in literary prose.
  • Next-Time Clue: In fiction passages, track the contrast between public appearance and private character action.

questions.stemHtml:
As Arctic permafrost thaws, meltwater ponds accumulate both dissolved methane and humic organic acids leached from ancient peat. Under oxygen-poor conditions, specialized bacteria normally consume a substantial fraction of dissolved methane using iron minerals as electron acceptors before the gas can bubble into the sky. Recent fieldwork demonstrates, however, that humic acids bind tightly to dissolved iron ions, locking them into chemical complexes that methane-consuming bacteria cannot access.

According to the text, how do humic organic acids affect meltwater ponds?

choices.raw: They supply extra oxygen that accelerates bacterial consumption of peat.
choices.html: They supply extra oxygen that accelerates bacterial consumption of peat.

choices.raw: They react directly with atmospheric methane to form solid iron minerals.
choices.html: They react directly with atmospheric methane to form solid iron minerals.

choices.raw: They prevent permafrost from thawing during peak summer sunlight.
choices.html: They prevent permafrost from thawing during peak summer sunlight.

choices.raw: They bind with iron in a way that limits bacteria's ability to break down methane before it escapes.
choices.html: They bind with iron in a way that limits bacteria's ability to break down methane before it escapes.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why D works: Matches the final sentence directly: humic acids "bind tightly to dissolved iron ions, locking them into chemical complexes that methane-consuming bacteria cannot access," reducing bacterial breakdown of methane.
  • Why others fail: A says oxygen (passage says oxygen-poor and limits bacteria); B confuses humic-iron binding with atmospheric methane forming solid iron; C invents stopping permafrost thaw.
  • Skill Assessed: Central Ideas and Details + dense clause tracking in biogeochemistry.
  • Next-Time Clue: Trace the 3-link causal chain on scratch paper: Humic acid binds Iron → Bacteria lose Iron → Less Methane broken down.

questions.stemHtml:
Literary critic Helena Lindqvist contends that in the late lyric poems of Tomas Vane, memory is portrayed not as a passive vault preserving past experiences intact, but as an active craft that reshapes earlier moments to suit present emotional needs.

Which quotation from a poem by Vane would most effectively illustrate Lindqvist's claim?

choices.raw: *"Beneath the cellar stone the winter apples keep / their crisp October scent through January frost."*
choices.html: "Beneath the cellar stone the winter apples keep / their crisp October scent through January frost."

choices.raw: *"What we call yesterday is hammered new each dusk / upon the restless anvil of tonight's desire."*
choices.html: "What we call yesterday is hammered new each dusk / upon the restless anvil of tonight's desire."

choices.raw: *"The harbour clock strikes four—four measured brazen notes / across the empty pier where fishing skiffs are tied."*
choices.html: "The harbour clock strikes four—four measured brazen notes / across the empty pier where fishing skiffs are tied."

choices.raw: *"No chronicle records the mason's quiet name, / though arches raised by him still bear the bridge's weight."*
choices.html: "No chronicle records the mason's quiet name, / though arches raised by him still bear the bridge's weight."

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: Lindqvist's claim has two required parts: (1) memory is not passive preservation, and (2) memory actively reshapes the past for present feelings. Choice B's metaphor—"What we call yesterday is hammered new each dusk / upon the restless anvil of tonight's desire"—expresses both active remaking (hammered new) and present emotion (tonight's desire).
  • Why others fail: A depicts intact preservation (winter apples keeping October scent—the exact view Vane rejects!); C describes a harbor clock in the present; D discusses historical anonymity vs. enduring stone arches.
  • Skill Assessed: Command of Evidence (Textual) in poetry/literature.
  • Next-Time Clue: Check both halves of the critic's "not X, but Y" thesis; SAT traps often illustrate X instead of Y!

questions.stemHtml:
Winter Cover-Crop Effects on Nitrate Leaching and Subsequent Corn Yield (3-Year Field Mean)

Field Treatment Soil Nitrate Leaching (kg/ha) Subsequent Corn Yield (metric tons/ha)
Bare Soil (No Cover Crop) 48 8.9
Crimson Clover Only 34 9.8
Winter Rye Only 14 8.4
Clover–Rye Mixture 16 9.7

Agronomists investigating agricultural runoff in river watersheds note that planting winter rye alone dramatically curtails soil nitrate leaching relative to leaving fields bare, but farmers often hesitate to plant rye monocultures because immobilizing soil nitrogen in spring can slightly reduce subsequent corn harvests. Based on a three-year field trial, the researchers argue that seeding a mixture of crimson clover and winter rye resolves this trade-off.

Which data comparison from the table most effectively supports the researchers' argument?

choices.raw: Bare soil recorded $48\text{ kg/ha}$ of nitrate leaching, whereas crimson clover only recorded $34\text{ kg/ha}$.
choices.html: Bare soil recorded 48 kg/ha of nitrate leaching, whereas crimson clover only recorded 34 kg/ha.

choices.raw: Winter rye only produced a corn yield of $8.4\text{ metric tons/ha}$, which was lower than bare soil's $8.9\text{ metric tons/ha}$.
choices.html: Winter rye only produced a corn yield of 8.4 metric tons/ha, which was lower than bare soil's 8.9 metric tons/ha.

choices.raw: The clover–rye mixture kept nitrate leaching nearly as low as winter rye only ($16\text{ kg/ha}$ vs. $14\text{ kg/ha}$) while achieving a corn yield of $9.7\text{ metric tons/ha}$, well above both winter rye only and bare soil.
choices.html: The clover–rye mixture kept nitrate leaching nearly as low as winter rye only (16 kg/ha vs. 14 kg/ha) while achieving a corn yield of 9.7 metric tons/ha, well above both winter rye only and bare soil.

choices.raw: Crimson clover only achieved the highest corn yield in the study ($9.8\text{ metric tons/ha}$) while lowering nitrate leaching below $40\text{ kg/ha}$.
choices.html: Crimson clover only achieved the highest corn yield in the study (9.8 metric tons/ha) while lowering nitrate leaching below 40 kg/ha.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: To prove clover–rye "resolves this trade-off," the data must prove both (1) low nitrate leaching comparable to winter rye (16 vs. 14 kg/ha, far below 48) and (2) no corn-yield penalty (9.7 t/ha vs. 8.4 for rye and 8.9 for bare soil). Choice C cites both metrics accurately.
  • Why others fail: A & D omit the clover–rye mixture entirely! B proves the problem with winter rye alone, not the solution (clover–rye mixture).
  • Skill Assessed: Command of Evidence (Quantitative) (True-to-Table, Incomplete-for-Claim distractor elimination).
  • Next-Time Clue: When an argument claims Solution S fixes a trade-off between Metric 1 and Metric 2, eliminate any choice that mentions only one metric or omits Solution S!

questions.stemHtml:
In languages with grammatical gender, nouns are assigned classes—such as masculine or feminine—that differ arbitrarily across tongues; for example, the word for "bridge" is feminine in German (die Brücke) but masculine in Spanish (el puente). Psycholinguists asked fluent German–Spanish bilinguals to name pictured objects strictly in Spanish during an all-Spanish session with no German words spoken or displayed. Participants took an average of 42 milliseconds longer to name objects whose grammatical gender conflicted between German and Spanish than objects whose gender matched in both languages, suggesting that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.raw: grammatical properties of a bilingual speaker's unspoken language remain partially active even during single-language speech production.
choices.html: grammatical properties of a bilingual speaker's unspoken language remain partially active even during single-language speech production.

choices.raw: native Spanish speakers learn German noun genders more rapidly than native German speakers learn Spanish noun genders.
choices.html: native Spanish speakers learn German noun genders more rapidly than native German speakers learn Spanish noun genders.

choices.raw: bilingual speakers consciously translate every noun from their first language before pronouncing it in their second language.
choices.html: bilingual speakers consciously translate every noun from their first language before pronouncing it in their second language.

choices.raw: concrete nouns like "bridge" are harder to classify grammatically than abstract nouns in most European languages.
choices.html: concrete nouns like "bridge" are harder to classify grammatically than abstract nouns in most European languages.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why A works: Even in a 100% Spanish session with zero German spoken, conflicting German gender slowed Spanish naming by 42 ms—logically demonstrating that the unspoken language's grammar stays partially active in the background.
  • Why others fail: B invents language-learning speed between native groups; C is too extreme ("consciously translate every noun"—42 milliseconds is subconscious co-activation, not full conscious translation); D invents concrete vs. abstract difficulty (abstract nouns were never tested).
  • Skill Assessed: Inferences — disciplined empirical deduction vs. extreme overreach.
  • Next-Time Clue: Prefer hedged, mechanism-accurate wording ("partially active") over sweeping psychological claims ("consciously translate every noun").

questions.stemHtml:
When an exoplanet passes in front of its host star, astronomers analyze starlight filtering through the planet's limb; a flat, featureless transmission spectrum indicates one of three conditions: high-altitude photochemical hazes created by intense stellar ultraviolet (UV) radiation, high planetary surface gravity compressing atmospheric gases into a thin layer, or the near-total absence of a volatile atmosphere. Recent observations of exoplanet LHS-49b revealed a completely flat transmission spectrum. Mass and radius measurements confirm that LHS-49b has a low surface gravity comparable to Saturn's moon Titan, and decades of stellar monitoring show its host red dwarf emits negligible UV radiation, implying that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.raw: LHS-49b's host star likely experienced intense UV flares shortly before stellar monitoring began that permanently compressed the planet's crust.
choices.html: LHS-49b's host star likely experienced intense UV flares shortly before stellar monitoring began that permanently compressed the planet's crust.

choices.raw: transmission spectroscopy is incapable of detecting atmospheric gases around planets that orbit red dwarf stars.
choices.html: transmission spectroscopy is incapable of detecting atmospheric gases around planets that orbit red dwarf stars.

choices.raw: LHS-49b's surface gravity has increased substantially since its initial mass and radius were measured.
choices.html: LHS-49b's surface gravity has increased substantially since its initial mass and radius were measured.

choices.raw: LHS-49b most likely lacks a substantial volatile atmosphere rather than possessing a haze-obscured or gravity-compressed one.
choices.html: LHS-49b most likely lacks a substantial volatile atmosphere rather than possessing a haze-obscured or gravity-compressed one.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why D works: Pure disjunctive deduction (A or B or C):
    • Flat spectrum = (1) UV haze OR (2) high gravity OR (3) no volatile atmosphere.
    • Data rules out (2) (low surface gravity like Titan) and rules out (1) (negligible UV radiation).
    • Necessary conclusion: (3) lacks a substantial volatile atmosphere (D)!
  • Why others fail: A & C invent unstated historical changes that contradict the passage's measurements; B overgeneralizes to all red-dwarf planets.
  • Skill Assessed: Inferences (Hard deductive elimination).
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever a science passage lists "one of three conditions: X, Y, or Z" and then disproves two of them, the answer must affirm the remaining one!

questions.stemHtml:
Constructed in the fourth century BCE without electronic amplification, the theater at Epidaurus projected whispered dialogue to fourteen thousand spectators through two acoustic ______ stepped limestone seating rows that filtered low-frequency crowd murmur and a steeply raked stage basin that channeled high-frequency consonant sounds upward.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: innovations,
innovations;
innovations:
innovations and

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Left of the blank is a complete independent clause (...the theater at Epidaurus projected whispered dialogue to fourteen thousand spectators through two acoustic innovations). Right of the blank is a two-item noun-phrase explanation (stepped limestone seating rows... and a steeply raked stage basin...). Complete IC : Noun-Phrase Explanation requires a colon (:).
  • Why others fail: A (, ) loosely attaches a heavy compound explanation where a formal colon is needed to signal "namely"; B (;) is grammatically illegal because the right side has no main verb for rows or basin (filtered and channeled sit inside subordinate that-clauses, making the right side a fragment!); D (innovations and) falsely treats "two acoustic innovations" as a parallel list item alongside the two innovations themselves.
  • Skill Assessed: SEC: Boundaries (Colon IC : Fragment/List vs. Semicolon IC ; IC).
  • Next-Time Clue: "two [noun]s: [Item 1] and [Item 2]" is a classic SAT colon pattern—just verify the clause before the colon is complete!

questions.stemHtml:
The first transatlantic telegraph cable laid in 1858 suffered catastrophic insulation breakdown after just three weeks of ______ commercial syndicates in London and New York remained convinced of submarine telegraphy's economic promise and financed a heavier armored cable in 1865.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: operation, nevertheless,
operation; nevertheless,
operation, nevertheless
operation nevertheless

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: Left side = complete IC (The first... cable... suffered catastrophic insulation breakdown after just three weeks of operation). Right side = complete IC (commercial syndicates... remained convinced...). Because nevertheless is a conjunctive adverb (not FANBOYS), you must separate the two ICs with a semicolon (or period) before nevertheless, followed by a comma: operation; nevertheless,.
  • Why others fail: A and C are comma splices (IC , IC); D is a fused run-on sentence.
  • Skill Assessed: SEC: Boundaries (Conjunctive adverb comma-splice trap).
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever choices differ only by , word, vs. ; word,, check if both sides are complete ICs. If yes, , word, is an automatic comma splice!

questions.stemHtml:
Non-invasive legibility analysis of carbonized papyrus scrolls and fragile wax tablets recovered from volcanic ash at Herculaneum ______ high-energy X-ray phase-contrast tomography rather than mechanical unrolling, which would shatter the brittle layers.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: require
have required
are requiring
requires

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why D works: Strip the prepositional chain: Non-invasive legibility analysis [of carbonized papyrus scrolls and fragile wax tablets recovered from volcanic ash at Herculaneum] _____. The true grammatical subject is singular analysis, which takes singular requires!
  • Why others fail: A (require), B (have required), and C (are requiring) are all plural verbs lured by plural scrolls and tablets!
  • Skill Assessed: SEC: Form, Structure, and Sense (Subject-Verb Agreement across intervening prepositional phrases).
  • Next-Time Clue: Notice the 3-plural (A, B, C) vs. 1-singular (D) split! Whenever 3 verb options share number and 1 stands alone, immediately find the true head noun before the first of.

questions.stemHtml:
Calibrating the laser interferometer to isolate mirror displacements smaller than one-thousandth the diameter of a proton, ______

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.raw: gravitational waves from a distant binary black hole merger were detected by the observatory's physics team.
choices.html: gravitational waves from a distant binary black hole merger were detected by the observatory's physics team.

choices.raw: a distant binary black hole merger generated gravitational waves that the observatory's physics team recorded.
choices.html: a distant binary black hole merger generated gravitational waves that the observatory's physics team recorded.

choices.raw: the observatory's physics team detected gravitational waves from a distant binary black hole merger.
choices.html: the observatory's physics team detected gravitational waves from a distant binary black hole merger.

choices.raw: subtle ripples in spacetime from a distant binary black hole merger appeared on the physics team's sensors.
choices.html: subtle ripples in spacetime from a distant binary black hole merger appeared on the physics team's sensors.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Opening participial modifier = "Calibrating the laser interferometer..." Ask: Who calibrated the laser? Only the observatory's physics team! Therefore, the observatory's physics team must stand immediately after the comma.
  • Why others fail: A (gravitational waves), B (a distant binary black hole merger), and D (subtle ripples in spacetime) all create absurd dangling modifiers claiming waves, black holes, or ripples calibrated laboratory equipment!
  • Skill Assessed: SEC: Form, Structure, and Sense (Introductory Subject-Modifier Placement).
  • Next-Time Clue: Sentence starts with -ing / -ed phrase , ______? Read only the first word(s) of A–D and pick the actual doer in 10 seconds!

questions.stemHtml:
Because deep-sea glass sponges build intricate silica skeletons at exceedingly slow metabolic rates, marine biologists long predicted that Antarctic sponge populations would take centuries to colonize seafloor newly exposed by collapsing ice shelves. ______ submersible surveys conducted just four years after the Larsen A ice shelf disintegrated revealed glass sponge biomass had more than tripled across the sunlit basin.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.html: Instead,
Consequently,
Similarly,
For example,

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why A works: Sentence 1 states an unrealized scientific prediction (would take centuries to colonize). Sentence 2 reports what happened in place of that prediction (more than tripled in four years). Instead, signals "contrary to that expected outcome, here is what actually occurred."
  • Why others fail: *B (Consequently,)* = cause/result (slow metabolism did not cause rapid tripling!); *C (Similarly,)* = parallel similarity; *D (For example,)* = supporting example of slow growth.
  • Skill Assessed: Transitions (Expectation vs. Counter-Expectation).
  • Next-Time Clue: "long predicted X. ______, surveys showed opposite Y" → Instead, / However, / Nevertheless,.

questions.stemHtml:
Fourteenth-century Ragusan maritime statutes sought to halt imported epidemic disease without bankrupting the Adriatic port's merchant fleet. ______ incoming vessels from plague-affected harbors were required to anchor off uninhabited islands for forty days of observation, whereas non-perishable spice and metal cargoes were unloaded onto ventilated stone piers rather than destroyed.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.html: Nevertheless,
Specifically,
Conversely,
Afterwards,

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: Sentence 1 states a general policy goal (halt epidemic disease without bankrupting merchants). Sentence 2 details the exact concrete rules that achieved both halves (40-day island quarantine for disease + airing rather than burning cargo for solvency). Specifically, bridges a general claim to its concrete operational details.
  • Why others fail: *A (Nevertheless,)* & *C (Conversely,)* signal contradiction where none exists between Sentence 1 and Sentence 2; *D (Afterwards,)* falsely implies chronological sequence after the statutes ended.
  • Skill Assessed: Transitions (General Principle → Specific Implementation).
  • Next-Time Clue: Don't get tricked by whereas inside Sentence 2! The transition at the start of Sentence 2 connects Sentence 2 as a whole back to Sentence 1.

questions.stemHtml:
While researching passive climate architecture, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Burkinabè architect Diébédo Francis Kéré designed the Gando Primary School in Burkina Faso (completed in 2001).
  • Local residents constructed the classroom walls and perforated ceiling from compressed clay blocks made with on-site soil.
  • Above the clay ceiling sits a wide, elevated corrugated-metal roof supported on an open steel truss.
  • Rising warm air escapes through perforations in the clay ceiling, while cool cross-breezes pass through the open truss space beneath the metal roof to carry heat away.
  • This passive ventilation design keeps classrooms 6°C to 8°C cooler than outdoor shade temperatures without electric air-conditioning, and Kéré received the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2022.

The student wants to explain how two structural elements of the Gando Primary School interact to cool classrooms passively. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.raw: Designed by 2022 Pritzker Prize laureate Diébédo Francis Kéré, the Gando Primary School was built by local residents using compressed on-site clay blocks.
choices.html: Designed by 2022 Pritzker Prize laureate Diébédo Francis Kéré, the Gando Primary School was built by local residents using compressed on-site clay blocks.

choices.raw: Without relying on electric air-conditioning, the Gando Primary School maintains indoor classroom temperatures 6°C to 8°C below outdoor shade temperatures.
choices.html: Without relying on electric air-conditioning, the Gando Primary School maintains indoor classroom temperatures 6°C to 8°C below outdoor shade temperatures.

choices.raw: In Kéré's Gando Primary School, warm indoor air rises out through perforations in the clay ceiling while cross-breezes moving beneath an elevated corrugated-metal roof sweep the heat away.
choices.html: In Kéré's Gando Primary School, warm indoor air rises out through perforations in the clay ceiling while cross-breezes moving beneath an elevated corrugated-metal roof sweep the heat away.

choices.raw: Whereas the Gando Primary School's walls are made from compressed local clay blocks, its upper roof uses corrugated metal supported by a steel truss.
choices.html: Whereas the Gando Primary School's walls are made from compressed local clay blocks, its upper roof uses corrugated metal supported by a steel truss.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Check the prompt's three constraints: (1) explain how, (2) two structural elements interact, (3) to cool classrooms passively. Choice C names both elements (perforated clay ceiling + elevated corrugated-metal roof) and explains their joint airflow mechanism (warm air rises out while cross-breezes sweep heat away).
  • Why others fail: A discusses the prize and construction labor (zero cooling); B states the temperature result (6°C–8°C) without naming or explaining how the two structural elements work; D contrasts wall and roof materials without mentioning cooling at all!
  • Skill Assessed: Rhetorical Synthesis (Mechanism/Interaction goal vs. Outcome-only trap).
  • Next-Time Clue: "explain HOW X and Y interact to do Z" eliminates any option that merely states outcome Z or merely lists X and Y!

lessons.title: Lesson 1.4: Digital SAT Math 4-Domain Blueprint & Essential Formulas Not on the Reference Sheet
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 1.4: Digital SAT Math 4-Domain Blueprint & Essential Formulas Not on the Reference Sheet
lessons.html:
Bluebook provides a built-in Geometry Reference Sheet (circle area/circumference, rectangle/triangle area, Pythagorean theorem, special right triangles, basic volumes). However, ~80% of Digital SAT Math depends on algebraic, functional, statistical, and coordinate formulas NOT printed on that sheet! Memorize and apply these four domain pillars:

Pillar 1: Algebra (~35% of SAT Math)

  • Slope & Linear Interpretation: For y=mx+b:
    • m=x2​−x1​y2​−y1​​ = rate of change per 1-unit increase in x ("for every additional...", "each hour...").
    • b = initial / starting fixed value when x=0.
    • For standard form Ax+By=C: slope=−BA​, y-intercept=BC​.
  • Number of Solutions in a Linear System ({a1​x+b1​y=c1​a2​x+b2​y=c2​​):
    • Exactly One Solution: Different slopes (a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​).
    • No Solution (Parallel Distinct Lines): Same slope, different intercepts:
      a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​=c2​c1​​
    • Infinitely Many Solutions (Identical Line): Every coefficient is proportional:
      a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​=c2​c1​​

Pillar 2: Advanced Math (~35% of SAT Math)

  • Three Quadratic Forms — Each Displays One Feature Instantly:
    1. Standard Form: f(x)=ax2+bx+c → displays y-intercept (0,c); axis of symmetry / vertex x-coordinate is h=−2ab​; sum of solutions =−ab​; product of solutions =ac​.
    2. Factored Form: f(x)=a(x−r1​)(x−r2​) → displays x-intercepts / roots (r1​,0) and (r2​,0); vertex x-coordinate sits halfway between roots: h=2r1​+r2​​.
    3. Vertex Form: f(x)=a(x−h)2+k → displays vertex (h,k), where k (not h!) is the minimum (a>0) or maximum (a<0) value of the function.
  • The Discriminant (D=b2−4ac for ax2+bx+c=0):
    • b2−4ac>0⟹ 2 distinct real solutions
    • b2−4ac=0⟹ Exactly 1 real solution (graph is tangent to x-axis)
    • b2−4ac<0⟹ No real solutions
  • Exponential Growth & Decay Over Interval k:
    f(t)=a(1±r)t/k
    where a = initial value at t=0, r = decimal percent change, and k = time required for ONE change cycle ("every 6 hours" ⟹t/6, never 6t!).

Pillar 3: Problem-Solving and Data Analysis (~15% of SAT Math)

  • Successive Percent Multipliers: Never add successive percentages! Increasing by 15% then 20% multiplies by 1.15×1.20=1.38 (38% net increase, not 35%!).
  • Mean vs. Median: Adding a large high outlier pulls the mean up sharply while barely moving (or leaving unchanged) the median. Remember: Sum=(Count)×(Mean).
  • Statistical Generalization & Causation:
    • Random sampling from Population P⟹ results generalize only to Population P (never a wider population!).
    • Random assignment to treatment/control groups ⟹ supports cause-and-effect claims; observational surveys without random assignment show association/correlation only.

Pillar 4: Geometry and Trigonometry (~15% of SAT Math)

  • Circle Equation in the xy-Plane: (x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2 has center (h,k) and radius r. Given expanded form x2+bx+y2+cy=d, complete the square by adding (2b​)2+(2c​)2 to both sides!
  • Complementary Right-Triangle Identity: Whenever ∠A+∠B=90∘ (or 2π​ radians):
    sin(A)=cos(B)andcos(A)=sin(B)

Worked Example 1.4 (Quadratic Minimum + x vs. f(x) Trap)

Problem: For f(x)=3x2−12x+19, at what value of x does f reach its minimum, and what is that minimum value?

  • Solution: h=−2(3)−12​=612​=2. That is the x-value where the minimum occurs. The minimum value of f(x) itself is k=f(2)=3(4)−12(2)+19=12−24+19=7. Always read the final words carefully: "at what value of x" =2; "what is the minimum value of f(x)" =7!

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 1.4

  • CC-M-1: Under what coefficient ratio does the system 4x−6y=9 and px+9y=−12 have no solution? Solve for p.
  • CC-M-2: A bacterial culture starts with 500 cells and triples in population every 4 hours. Write P(t) after t hours.
  • CC-M-3: What is the center and radius of x2+y2+8x−4y−5=0?
  • CC-M-4: In right △PQR with right angle R, if cos(P)=135​, what is sin(Q)?

outline.text: Pillar 1: Algebra (~35% of SAT Math)
Pillar 2: Advanced Math (~35% of SAT Math)
Pillar 3: Problem-Solving and Data Analysis (~15% of SAT Math)
Pillar 4: Geometry and Trigonometry (~15% of SAT Math)
Worked Example 1.4 (Quadratic Minimum + x vs. f(x) Trap)
Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 1.4

checks.promptHtml: Under what coefficient ratio does the system 4x−6y=9 and px+9y=−12 have no solution? Solve for p.
checks.answerHtml: Set p4​=9−6​=−32​⟹−2p=12⟹p=−6. (Check constant ratio: −129​=−43​=−32​, confirming parallel distinct lines with zero solutions.)

checks.promptHtml: A bacterial culture starts with 500 cells and triples in population every 4 hours. Write P(t) after t hours.
checks.answerHtml: P(t)=500(3)t/4. (Check t=4: 500(3)1=1,500, tripled once after 4 hours.)

checks.promptHtml: What is the center and radius of x2+y2+8x−4y−5=0?
checks.answerHtml: (x2+8x+16)+(y2−4y+4)=5+16+4=25⟹(x+4)2+(y−2)2=25. Center: (−4,2); Radius: r=25​=5.

checks.promptHtml: In right △PQR with right angle R, if cos(P)=135​, what is sin(Q)?
checks.answerHtml: Since ∠P+∠Q=90∘, sin(Q)=cos(P)=135​.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.5: The 5-Second Desmos Decision Protocol & Careless-Error Firewall
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 1.5: The 5-Second Desmos Decision Protocol & Careless-Error Firewall
lessons.html:
A. The 5-Second Decision Matrix (Run Before Writing Any Equation!)

Problem Signature Fastest Method Exact Execution
Single linear isolation (4(x−2)=x+7) or isolating r in terms of P,t Manual Algebra (15–25 sec) Distribute cleanly; Desmos cannot output symbolic formulas in multiple variables directly.
System of 2 equations (linear OR quadratic-linear) asking for x,y, or number of intersections Desmos Graphing (15 sec) Type both equations on Lines 1 & 2; click gray intersection dots! (Zoom out once to verify no second curve intersection hides off-screen!)
Constant/Parameter slider (kx+6y=−8 has no solution; f(x)=ax2+4x+3 touches x-axis once) Algebraic Ratio/Discriminant OR Desmos Slider (20 sec) Type equation with k, click "add slider k," or apply b2−4ac=0 directly.
Function through 2–3 given points or data table Desmos Regression (20 sec) Click + → Table, enter (x1​,y1​) pairs, then type y_1 ~ m x_1 + b (linear), y_1 ~ a x_1^2 + b x_1 + c (quadratic), or y_1 ~ a * 2^(x_1) + b (exponential)!
Equivalent single-variable expressions (4 algebraic choices) Desmos Graph Match (25 sec) Graph original expression on Line 1; graph choices A–D and toggle visibility to see which curve overlaps 100% identically!

B. Four-Point Careless-Error Firewall (Mandatory on Every Math Question)

  1. Box the Final Target Phrase: Circle whether the prompt asks for x, y, x+y, 4x−5, diameter vs. radius, or minimum value (y) vs. value of x at minimum.
  2. Parentheses Around Negative Substitutions: In both scratch work and calculators, (−3)2=9, whereas typing -3^2 evaluates −(32)=−9!
  3. Unit & Axis-Scale Check: Check whether t is in minutes or hours, and whether graph axes start at (0,0) or (10,50) with step size 2 or 5.
  4. 90-Second Bailout Rule: Never spend 3.5 minutes fighting one problem while four solvable problems wait ahead. At 90 seconds without progress, flag it, pick your cleanest estimate, and advance.

Worked Example 1.5 (Desmos Regression Shortcut)

Problem: Quadratic function h(x)=ax2+bx+c passes through (−1,9), (0,4), and (2,6). What is h(4)?

  • Desmos 20-Second Solution: Add Table (+ → Table) with x1​=[−1,0,2] and y1​=[9,4,6]. On Line 2 type y_1 ~ a x_1^2 + b x_1 + c (Desmos gives a=2,b=−3,c=4). On Line 3 type f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 4, then f(4) → 24!

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 1.5

  • CC-M-5: You need the positive solution to x2−3x−1=2x+5. Is Manual Factoring or Desmos Graphing faster/safer first, and how do you avoid missing an intersection in Desmos?
  • CC-M-6: How do you convert a decimal output like 1.375 into an exact reduced fraction inside the Bluebook Desmos calculator?

outline.text: A. The 5-Second Decision Matrix (Run Before Writing Any Equation!)
B. Four-Point Careless-Error Firewall (Mandatory on Every Math Question)
Worked Example 1.5 (Desmos Regression Shortcut)
Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 1.5

checks.promptHtml: You need the positive solution to x2−3x−1=2x+5. Is Manual Factoring or Desmos Graphing faster/safer first, and how do you avoid missing an intersection in Desmos?
checks.answerHtml: Desmos Graphing (y = x^2 - 3x - 1 and y = 2x + 5) is faster and less error-prone because x2−5x−6=0 is easy to mis-factor with signs ((x-6)(x+1) vs (x-3)(x-2)). Zoom out slightly in Desmos so both intersections of the parabola and line are visible (x = -1 and x = 6 ⟹ positive solution 6).

checks.promptHtml: How do you convert a decimal output like 1.375 into an exact reduced fraction inside the Bluebook Desmos calculator?
checks.answerHtml: Click the small circle-with-fraction icon (a/b) on the left side of the Desmos expression box: 1.375 immediately converts to 11/8.

mathPractice.introHtml:
Explicit Origin Notice: All 15 problems below (MATH-D1-Q1 through MATH-D1-Q15) are original SAT-style practice questions covering Algebra, Advanced Math, Problem-Solving & Data Analysis, and Geometry & Trigonometry across Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulty, including 10 Multiple-Choice and 5 Student-Produced Response (SPR) questions.
Timed Calibration Option: Set a strict countdown timer for 24 minutes (~96 seconds/question). Open desmos.com/calculator alongside this document. Do not check Section 8 until finished!

questions.stemHtml:
C(m)=42+0.35m
The function C models a cloud-server customer's total monthly bill, in dollars, when transferring m gigabytes of data beyond the base allowance. If a customer's monthly bill was , how many gigabytes beyond the base allowance did the customer transfer?

choices.html: 42
60
120
180

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Set C(m)=63:
    42+0.35m=63⟹0.35m=21⟹m=0.3521​=352100​=60
  • Desmos Method: Type 42 + 0.35x = 63 on Line 1 → click vertical line at x = 60.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: Plug back in: 42+0.35(60)=42+21=63 ✓. Trap D (180): Dividing 63 by 0.35 without subtracting fixed base cost first!

questions.stemHtml:
5(2x−3)=3x+13
If x satisfies the given equation, what is the value of 4x−5?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    10x−15=3x+13⟹7x=28⟹x=4
    Boxed target expression: 4x−5=4(4)−5=11.
  • Desmos Method: Line 1: 5(2x - 3) = 3x + 13 (shows x=4). Line 2: 4(4) - 5 → 11.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: LHS =5(8−3)=25; RHS =3(4)+13=25 ✓. #1 SAT SPR Trap (E4): Entering 4 (x) instead of 11 (4x−5)!

questions.stemHtml: A university archive digitized 2,400 historical maps in 2024. In 2025, the number of maps digitized increased by 15% compared to 2024. In 2026, the number of maps digitized increased by 20% compared to 2025. How many historical maps did the archive digitize in 2026?

choices.html: 3,204
3,240
3,312
3,360

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Apply successive multipliers sequentially:
    2025 total=2,400×1.15=2,760
    2026 total=2,760×1.20=3,312
  • Alternative Fast Expression: Type 2400 * 1.15 * 1.20 directly in Desmos → 3312.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: Trap B (3,240): Adding 15%+20%=35% (2,400×1.35=3,240), ignoring the 20% gain applied to the new 360 maps added in 2025 (0.20×360=72; 3,240+72=3,312)!

questions.stemHtml:
6x−9ykx+6y​=14=−8​
In the given system of equations, k is a constant. If the system has no solution, what is the value of k?

choices.html: −9
−4
4
9

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: For no solution, slopes must match while y-intercepts differ (a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​=c2​c1​​):
    k6​=6−9​⟹−9k=36⟹k=−4
  • Desmos Slider Method: Type 6x - 9y = 14 on Line 1 and kx + 6y = -8 on Line 2; click add slider k and test choices -9, -4, 4, 9—at k = -4 the two lines become strictly parallel!
  • Verification & Trap Alert: Check constant ratio: −46​=−1.5, 6−9​=−1.5, and −814​=−1.75=−1.5 ✓ (parallel, not identical). Trap C (4): Dropping the negative sign!

questions.stemHtml: Which expression is equivalent to x+52x2+7x−15​ for all x>0?

choices.html: 2x−5
2x−3
2x+3
2x2+7x−3

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Algebraic Factoring: Find factors of 2(−15)=−30 summing to +7 (+10 and −3):
    2x2+10x−3x−15=2x(x+5)−3(x+5)=(2x−3)(x+5)
    Divide by (x+5) (valid for x>0 since x+5=0): 2x−3.
  • Desmos / Plug-In 10-Second Method: Graph y = (2x^2 + 7x - 15)/(x + 5) and y = 2x - 3 (identical line for x>0!), OR test x=1: 1+52+7−15​=6−6​=−1. Plug x=1 into choices: A gives −3, B gives 2(1)−3=−1, C gives 5, D gives 6.
  • Trap Alert: Trap D cancels 15/5=3 illegally across addition/subtraction!

questions.stemHtml: A laboratory sample of a medical tracer starts with a mass of 320 milligrams and loses 25% of its remaining mass every 6 hours. Which function M models the mass, in milligrams, of the tracer remaining t hours after observation begins?

choices.html: M(t)=320(0.25)t/6
M(t)=320(0.75)6t
M(t)=320(0.75)t/6
M(t)=320(1.25)t/6

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    • Initial mass at t=0: a=320.
    • Losing 25% leaves 100%−25%=75%=0.75 remaining per cycle.
    • One decay cycle occurs every 6 hours, so after t hours there have been t/6 cycles ⟹M(t)=320(0.75)t/6.
  • Plug-In Verification: At t=6 hours, mass must drop by 25% of 320 (80 mg) to 240 mg. Check C: 320(0.75)6/6=320(0.75)1=240 ✓.
  • Trap Alert: Trap A uses 0.25 (amount lost instead of amount remaining); Trap B uses 6t (36 decay cycles in 6 hours instead of 1!).

questions.stemHtml: Dataset A consists of the five integers 12,15,18,21, and 29. Dataset B is created by appending a sixth integer, x, to Dataset A. If the mean of Dataset B is 4 greater than the mean of Dataset A, what is the value of x?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    • Sum of Dataset A (5 integers) =12+15+18+21+29=95.
    • Mean of Dataset A =595​=19.
    • Mean of Dataset B (6 integers) =19+4=23.
    • Sum of Dataset B =6×23=138.
    • x=138−95=43.
  • Desmos Check: Type mean(12, 15, 18, 21, 29) → 19; then mean(12, 15, 18, 21, 29, 43) → 23 (23 - 19 = 4 ✓)!
  • Trap Alert: Multiplying 23×5 instead of 23×6 after adding the sixth element.

questions.stemHtml: In right triangle ABC, angle C is a right angle and sin(A)=178​. If the length of side BC (opposite angle A) is 24, what is the length of side AC?

choices.html: 34
40
45
51

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    • In right △ABC (∠C=90∘), sin(A)=HypotenuseOpposite​=ABBC​=178​.
    • Since BC=24=3×8, the scale factor is 3, so hypotenuse AB=3×17=51.
    • Recognize the 8-15-17 Pythagorean triple (or compute 512−242​=2,601−576​=2,025​=45): adjacent side AC=3×15=45.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: 242+452=576+2,025=2,601=512 ✓. Trap D (51) solves for hypotenuse AB instead of leg AC!

questions.skill: Linear Inequalities in One or Two Variables
questions.stemHtml: An environmental monitoring drone can carry a maximum payload of 35 kilograms per flight. It carries soil-moisture sensors weighing 1.5 kilograms each and water-sampling canisters weighing 2.4 kilograms each. If mission protocol requires carrying at least 8 soil-moisture sensors on a flight, what is the maximum whole number of water-sampling canisters the drone can carry on that flight?

choices.html: 9
10
14
15

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Let s = sensors and w = canisters:
    1.5s+2.4w≤35ands≥8
    To maximize w, make s as small as permitted (s=8):
    1.5(8)+2.4w≤35⟹12+2.4w≤35⟹2.4w≤23⟹w≤2.423​≈9.583
    Because w must be a whole number of canisters and cannot exceed the 35 kg payload limit, round down to 9.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: At w=9: 12+2.4(9)=12+21.6=33.6≤35 ✓. At Trap B (w=10): 12+24=36>35 (exceeds max payload—rounding 9.58 up to 10 is a classic real-world inequality mistake!).

questions.stemHtml:
f(x)=2x2−16x+39
The given function f models the electrical power consumption, in watts, of a laboratory cooling module operating at airflow setting x (where 1≤x≤8). According to the model, what is the minimum electrical power consumption, in watts, of the module?

choices.html: 4
7
23
39

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Since a=2>0, f(x) opens upward and reaches its minimum at vertex x-coordinate:
    h=−2ab​=−2(2)−16​=4
    Note 1≤4≤8 lies inside the domain. Minimum power consumption is f(4):
    f(4)=2(4)2−16(4)+39=32−64+39=7
  • Desmos 8-Second Method: Graph f(x) = 2x^2 - 16x + 39 → click bottom vertex dot (4, 7) → read y-coordinate 7.
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (4) gives the airflow setting x instead of minimum watts f(x); Trap D (39) gives the y-intercept f(0).

questions.stemHtml: To estimate shuttle-bus usage, a university transportation office selected a random sample of 250 undergraduate students currently living in on-campus dormitories. In the sample, 68% reported riding campus shuttles at least three days per week, with an associated margin of error of 4%. To which of the following populations can this survey result most appropriately be generalized?

choices.raw: All undergraduate and graduate students enrolled at the university
choices.html: All undergraduate and graduate students enrolled at the university

choices.raw: All undergraduate students currently living in on-campus dormitories at the university
choices.html: All undergraduate students currently living in on-campus dormitories at the university

choices.raw: Only the $250$ students surveyed, because the margin of error exceeds $3\%$
choices.html: Only the 250 students surveyed, because the margin of error exceeds 3%

choices.raw: All undergraduate students living in on-campus dormitories at public universities in the state
choices.html: All undergraduate students living in on-campus dormitories at public universities in the state

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Statistical inference rule: a random sample generalizes strictly to the sampling frame from which it was randomly drawn—here, undergraduate students currently living in on-campus dormitories at that university.
  • Why others fail: A improperly adds commuter undergraduates and graduate students (who likely use shuttles very differently!); C misunderstands margin of error (68%±4% is completely valid for generalizing to the sampled population); D improperly extrapolates to other universities statewide.

questions.stemHtml:
yy​=x2−5x+7=2x−3​
If (x1​,y1​) and (x2​,y2​) are the two distinct solutions to the system of equations above, what is the value of y1​+y2​?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Desmos 12-Second Method (Fastest!):
    • Line 1: y = x^2 - 5x + 7
    • Line 2: y = 2x - 3
    • Click the two intersection dots: (2, 1) and (5, 7).
    • Boxed target is y1​+y2​ (not x1​+x2​!): 1+7=8.
  • Algebraic Solution:
    x2−5x+7=2x−3⟹x2−7x+10=0⟹(x−2)(x−5)=0⟹x1​=2,x2​=5
    y1​=2(2)−3=1,y2​=2(5)−3=7⟹y1​+y2​=1+7=8
  • Trap Alert: Entering x1​+x2​=2+5=7 (E4 target misread)!

questions.stemHtml:
x2+y2−10x+6y−15=0
The equation above represents a circle in the xy-plane. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Algebraic Completing the Square:
    (x2−10x+25)+(y2+6y+9)=15+25+9
    (x−5)2+(y+3)2=49⟹r2=49⟹r=7
  • Desmos Visual Method: Type x^2 + y^2 - 10x + 6y - 15 = 0. Click the leftmost and rightmost points of the circle (or graph horizontal center line y = -3 to click (-2, -3) and (12, -3)): diameter =12−(−2)=14⟹ radius =14/2=7!
  • Trap Alert: Entering r2=49 instead of r=7!

questions.stemHtml:
3x2+bx+12=0
In the given equation, b is a negative constant. If the equation has exactly one real solution, what is the value of b?

choices.html: −36
−12
−6
12

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Exactly one real solution means discriminant D=b2−4ac=0:
    b2−4(3)(12)=0⟹b2−144=0⟹b2=144⟹b=±12
    Because the prompt specifies b is a negative constant, b=−12.
  • Desmos Check: Graph y = 3x^2 - 12x + 12: parabola touches the x-axis at a single vertex point (2, 0) ✓.
  • Trap Alert: Trap D (12) overlooks the word "negative" in the stem!

questions.stemHtml:
g(x)=a⋅2x+b
In the function g above, a and b are constants. In the xy-plane, the graph of y=g(x) has a y-intercept at (0,−5) and passes through (3,16). What is the value of g(2)?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Algebraic Solution:
    • Substitute (0,−5): a⋅20+b=−5⟹a+b=−5 (Caution: 20=1, NOT 0!)
    • Substitute (3,16): a⋅23+b=16⟹8a+b=16
    • Subtract Eq. 1 from Eq. 2: 7a=21⟹a=3, so 3+b=−5⟹b=−8.
    • Evaluate g(2): g(2)=3⋅22−8=3(4)−8=12−8=4.
  • Desmos Regression Method (20 Seconds): Add Table (+ → Table) with (0,−5) and (3,16). Type y_1 ~ a * 2^(x_1) + b → reads a=3,b=−8. Evaluate 3 * 2^2 - 8 → 4.
  • Trap Alert: Thinking 20=0, which wrongly gives b=−5 instead of a+b=−5!
