subSections.title: A. Lesson Short Comprehension Checks — Answer Key
subSections.titleHtml: A. Lesson Short Comprehension Checks — Answer Key
subSections.html:
Reading & Writing Checks (CC-RW-1 to CC-RW-8)

  • CC-RW-1: Questions 15–27 (Standard English Conventions, Transitions, and Rhetorical Synthesis) follow mechanical, high-speed rules (~35–50 sec/Q) that do not require deep reading of dense literature or science arguments. Banking those 12–13 points first in 10–11 minutes guarantees you never lose easy grammar/transition points to clock pressure and leaves 20+ minutes for Q1–Q14.
  • CC-RW-2: Main claim: Epiphytic orchids are not parasitic (they get water/nutrients from rain and air dust). The opening participial modifier "Widely regarded by early botanists as parasitic organisms," signals an outdated belief that "actually... rather than" immediately overturns.
  • CC-RW-3: Core 7-word skeleton: Microbial communities synthesize organic compounds through chemosynthesis. (Bracketed out: [thriving near hydrothermal vents] and [—environments devoid of sunlight and subjected to crushing hydrostatic pressure—].)
  • CC-RW-4: Simple prediction: "purely decorative / useless / random / impractical." "Far from being [impractical/decorative], the stone served three practical functions: ..."
  • CC-RW-5: It is a comma splice (IC , however , IC — however is a conjunctive adverb, NOT a FANBOYS conjunction). Two valid fixes: (1) ...methane; however, researchers... or (2) ...methane. However, researchers... (or ...methane, but researchers...).
  • CC-RW-6: Eliminate A (Furthermore) and B (Moreover) immediately because both are exact additive transitions (+ addition); on the Digital SAT, two functionally identical transitions cannot have one right and one wrong.
  • CC-RW-7: (b) geochemists concluded... — Only human geochemists can "have analyzed sediment cores." Placing "evidence" right after the comma creates an illogical dangling modifier claiming evidence analyzed the cores!
  • CC-RW-8: Read only the final question stem first and underline every rhetorical goal constraint (e.g., similarity vs. difference, cause vs. result, familiar vs. unfamiliar audience), because 2–3 choices will be factually true according to the notes yet violate the specific goal.

Math Checks (CC-M-1 to CC-M-6)

  • CC-M-1: Set p4​=9−6​=−32​⟹−2p=12⟹p=−6. (Check constant ratio: −129​=−43​=−32​, confirming parallel distinct lines with zero solutions.)
  • CC-M-2: P(t)=500(3)t/4. (Check t=4: 500(3)1=1,500, tripled once after 4 hours.)
  • CC-M-3: (x2+8x+16)+(y2−4y+4)=5+16+4=25⟹(x+4)2+(y−2)2=25. Center: (−4,2); Radius: r=25​=5.
  • CC-M-4: Since ∠P+∠Q=90∘, sin(Q)=cos(P)=135​.
  • CC-M-5: Desmos Graphing (y = x^2 - 3x - 1 and y = 2x + 5) is faster and less error-prone because x2−5x−6=0 is easy to mis-factor with signs ((x-6)(x+1) vs (x-3)(x-2)). Zoom out slightly in Desmos so both intersections of the parabola and line are visible (x = -1 and x = 6 ⟹ positive solution 6).
  • CC-M-6: Click the small circle-with-fraction icon (a/b) on the left side of the Desmos expression box: 1.375 immediately converts to 11/8.

subSections.title: B. Vocabulary Exercises (4A–4F) — Answer Key & Explanations
subSections.titleHtml: B. Vocabulary Exercises (4A–4F) — Answer Key & Explanations
subSections.html:
Exercise 4A (Words in Context MCQs)

  • VOC-Q1 → Correct: B (undermine)
    • Why B works: yet signals contrast between early ethnographers' claim (isolated) and new isotopic data (regular metal exchange across three zones). New data weakens (undermines) the isolation claim.
    • Why others fail: A (corroborate) and C (substantiate) mean confirm/prove (opposite polarity); D (infer) is an action a person performs from evidence—data itself does not "infer a view."
  • VOC-Q2 → Correct: A (tentative)
    • Why A works: Lack of apprentice names means any attribution without chemical/letter proof is provisional and unconfirmed (tentative).
    • Why others fail: B (nuanced) praises subtle balance rather than describing unconfirmed evidence; C (unambiguous) means 100% clear (contradicted by unless... provide proof); D (mandatory) means required.
  • VOC-Q3 → Correct: C (reconcile)
    • Why C works: Notice the pattern reconcile [Dataset A: steady sea surface] with [Dataset B: rapid local sinking], confirmed by "did the two datasets align."
    • Why others fail: A (undermine), B (infer), and D (assert) neither fit _____ X with Y grammar nor express making two conflicting datasets fit together.
  • VOC-Q4 → Correct: D (nuanced)
    • Why D works: The colon defines the blank: rejecting two one-sided extremes (purely prosperity vs. purely alienation) to show simultaneous benefits and losses = subtle, balanced (nuanced).
    • Why others fail: A (ambiguous) implies unclear/confusing writing rather than deliberate analytical subtlety; B (tentative) means provisional; C (plausible) means merely believable.

Exercise 4B (Signal & Polarity)

  • VOC-Q5: Signal = Although + failed to; Function of substantiate = Confirming/Proving (+), negated by failed to so overall clause shows negative outcome.
  • VOC-Q6: Signal = Colon (:) + both sources pointed to; Function of corroborated = Confirming (+).
  • VOC-Q7: Signal = Post-positioned notwithstanding; Function = Concession/Contrast (despite - obstacle → + outcome).
  • VOC-Q8: Signal = Because... weathered away + remain divided; Function of ambiguous = Unclear / Multiple Interpretations (?).
  • VOC-Q9: Signal = Given that [moths navigated without magnetic field]; Function of implausible = Unbelievable / Weakened (-).

Exercise 4C (Sentence Completion)

  • VOC-Q10: infer (deduce migration routes logically from chemical clues)
  • VOC-Q11: undermine (weaken/erode public trust)
  • VOC-Q12: notwithstanding (post-positioned = "Despite harsh subzero winds")
  • VOC-Q13: plausible (reasonable/believable, though drainage is another possible cause)
  • VOC-Q14: corroborated (or corroborate — independent European orbiter data confirmed NASA lander data)

Exercise 4D (Close-Synonym Discrimination)

  • VOC-Q15: ambiguous — The contract allows two competing interpretations, whereas tentative means temporary/cautious.
  • VOC-Q16: corroborate — Inanimate 16th-century ship logs confirm a claim with evidence; they cannot collaborate (work together socially like people).
  • VOC-Q17: underscore — "Far from weakening" requires the opposite of weaken: emphasize (underscore), never undermine (weaken)!
  • VOC-Q18: First blank = substantial (large in number); Second blank = substantiate (prove with hard evidence).

Exercise 4E (Academic Passage Synthesis)

  • VOC-Q19: Core meaning: Despite historians' skepticism, real raft voyages proved fresh balsa wood stays afloat long enough to cross oceans.
  • VOC-Q20: Showing a raft could float makes transoceanic contact plausible (physically possible/believable), but possibility alone does not substantiate (prove with hard evidence) that regular ancient trade actually happened.
  • VOC-Q21: Because rafts can float (not implausible), yet archaeological proof is still incomplete, any trade map is provisional and awaiting firmer data (tentative), rather than ambiguous (double-meaning wording).

Exercise 4F (Closed-Notes Retrieval Key — Score 1 point per accurate plain-English meaning)

  • VOC-Q22 (corroborate): Confirm with independent evidence.
  • VOC-Q23 (notwithstanding): Despite; in spite of; nevertheless.
  • VOC-Q24 (tentative): Provisional, cautious, not yet final.
  • VOC-Q25 (undermine): Weaken gradually or erode credibility.
  • VOC-Q26 (reconcile): Make two conflicting facts/ideas fit together.
  • VOC-Q27 (nuanced): Showing subtle, balanced distinctions (not simplistic).
  • VOC-Q28 (plausible): Reasonable and believable enough to be possible.
  • VOC-Q29 (ambiguous): Open to two or more meanings; unclear.
  • VOC-Q30 (substantiate): Prove or back up a claim with solid evidence.
  • VOC-Q31 (infer): Conclude logically from clues/evidence.

subSections.title: C. Reading & Writing Practice Set (RW-D1-Q1 to RW-D1-Q18) — Complete Explanations
subSections.titleHtml: C. Reading & Writing Practice Set (RW-D1-Q1 to RW-D1-Q18) — Complete Explanations
subSections.html:
RW-D1-Q1 → Correct Answer: A (conserve)

  • Why A works: Opening pores only at night prevents water from evaporating "in midday heat," meaning the plants save/preserve (conserve) internal water.
  • Why others fail: B (disperse) = scatter away; C (fabricate) = invent/manufacture from scratch; D (exhaust) = use up completely (the exact fate the plant avoids!).
  • Skill Assessed: Contextual vocabulary + otherwise contrast logic.
  • Next-Time Clue: "that would otherwise [be lost]" proves the blank must mean keep/protect.

RW-D1-Q2 → Correct Answer: B (ambiguous)

  • Why B works: Look right after the colon (:): the underdrawing "could plausibly date either to... 1528 or to... 1542." Two equally plausible interpretations = ambiguous.
  • Why others fail: A (definitive) = 100% settled (opposite); C (corroborated) = confirmed; D (overt) = obvious/openly visible.
  • Skill Assessed: Academic vocabulary + colon definition structure.
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever a colon is followed by "either X or Y," predict unclear / ambiguous / inconclusive.

RW-D1-Q3 → Correct Answer: B (qualified)

  • Why B works: In 2019 she made an absolute claim ("uniformly stifled"); after finding rural counter-evidence (however), she narrowed/limited (qualified) her claim "restricting it to capital-city luxury trades."
  • Why others fail: A (substantiated) & D (vindicated) mean proved her original sweeping 2019 claim completely right (ignoring however and restricting it); C (amplified) means expanded/made louder, opposite of restricting scope.
  • Skill Assessed: Secondary academic meaning (polysemy) of qualify (= moderate or limit an absolute statement).
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever a scholar shifts from "all/uniformly" to "only in certain cases," the SAT's favorite verb is qualify!

RW-D1-Q4 → Correct Answer: B

  • Why B works: Sentence 1 states a common assumption ("Municipal planners have long assumed..."); Sentence 2 overturns it with evidence ("Yet time-lapse... reveals..."); Sentence 3 identifies what actually drives lingering ("shopfronts, movable seating, and continuous tree canopies").
  • Why others fail: A reverses Sentence 3; C elevates a research tool (time-lapse mapping) into the main purpose and invents "replaced resident surveys"; D is an extreme fabrication ("forested suburban parks").
  • Skill Assessed: Text Structure and Purpose (Assumption → Empirical Refutation → Alternative Explanation).
  • Next-Time Clue: "have long assumed... Yet..." almost always maps to "question/challenge a common assumption."

RW-D1-Q5 → Correct Answer: C

  • Why C works: Text 2 opens with a polite concession ("Carbonate chemistry undoubtedly stressed tropical... corals") and pivots via Nevertheless to show northern sponge reefs died earlier due to sea-level drop—meaning acidification hurt some reefs but cannot explain the timing and full breadth of collapse.
  • Why others fail: A & B falsely claim total disagreement (contradicting "undoubtedly stressed"); D scrambles cause and effect between sponges and pH.
  • Skill Assessed: Cross-Text Connections — partial concession + scope limitation (±).
  • Next-Time Clue: When Text 2 starts with "Undoubtedly / Granted / Certainly... Nevertheless," look for an answer starting with "Acknowledge X, but contend/question Y."

RW-D1-Q6 → Correct Answer: A

  • Why A works: Captures both halves of the contrast (visitors marvel at rare orchids vs. however... her uncle privately sits beside childhood rosemary).
  • Why others fail: B (sell orchids / costly pipes), C (visitors prefer herbs), and D (Clara disapproves) all invent unsupported narrative claims.
  • Skill Assessed: Central Ideas and Details in literary prose.
  • Next-Time Clue: In fiction passages, track the contrast between public appearance and private character action.

RW-D1-Q7 → Correct Answer: D

  • Why D works: Matches the final sentence directly: humic acids "bind tightly to dissolved iron ions, locking them into chemical complexes that methane-consuming bacteria cannot access," reducing bacterial breakdown of methane.
  • Why others fail: A says oxygen (passage says oxygen-poor and limits bacteria); B confuses humic-iron binding with atmospheric methane forming solid iron; C invents stopping permafrost thaw.
  • Skill Assessed: Central Ideas and Details + dense clause tracking in biogeochemistry.
  • Next-Time Clue: Trace the 3-link causal chain on scratch paper: Humic acid binds Iron → Bacteria lose Iron → Less Methane broken down.

RW-D1-Q8 → Correct Answer: B

  • Why B works: Lindqvist's claim has two required parts: (1) memory is not passive preservation, and (2) memory actively reshapes the past for present feelings. Choice B's metaphor—"What we call yesterday is hammered new each dusk / upon the restless anvil of tonight's desire"—expresses both active remaking (hammered new) and present emotion (tonight's desire).
  • Why others fail: A depicts intact preservation (winter apples keeping October scent—the exact view Vane rejects!); C describes a harbor clock in the present; D discusses historical anonymity vs. enduring stone arches.
  • Skill Assessed: Command of Evidence (Textual) in poetry/literature.
  • Next-Time Clue: Check both halves of the critic's "not X, but Y" thesis; SAT traps often illustrate X instead of Y!

RW-D1-Q9 → Correct Answer: C

  • Why C works: To prove clover–rye "resolves this trade-off," the data must prove both (1) low nitrate leaching comparable to winter rye (16 vs. 14 kg/ha, far below 48) and (2) no corn-yield penalty (9.7 t/ha vs. 8.4 for rye and 8.9 for bare soil). Choice C cites both metrics accurately.
  • Why others fail: A & D omit the clover–rye mixture entirely! B proves the problem with winter rye alone, not the solution (clover–rye mixture).
  • Skill Assessed: Command of Evidence (Quantitative) (True-to-Table, Incomplete-for-Claim distractor elimination).
  • Next-Time Clue: When an argument claims Solution S fixes a trade-off between Metric 1 and Metric 2, eliminate any choice that mentions only one metric or omits Solution S!

RW-D1-Q10 → Correct Answer: A

  • Why A works: Even in a 100% Spanish session with zero German spoken, conflicting German gender slowed Spanish naming by 42 ms—logically demonstrating that the unspoken language's grammar stays partially active in the background.
  • Why others fail: B invents language-learning speed between native groups; C is too extreme ("consciously translate every noun"—42 milliseconds is subconscious co-activation, not full conscious translation); D invents concrete vs. abstract difficulty (abstract nouns were never tested).
  • Skill Assessed: Inferences — disciplined empirical deduction vs. extreme overreach.
  • Next-Time Clue: Prefer hedged, mechanism-accurate wording ("partially active") over sweeping psychological claims ("consciously translate every noun").

RW-D1-Q11 → Correct Answer: D

  • Why D works: Pure disjunctive deduction (A or B or C):
    • Flat spectrum = (1) UV haze OR (2) high gravity OR (3) no volatile atmosphere.
    • Data rules out (2) (low surface gravity like Titan) and rules out (1) (negligible UV radiation).
    • Necessary conclusion: (3) lacks a substantial volatile atmosphere (D)!
  • Why others fail: A & C invent unstated historical changes that contradict the passage's measurements; B overgeneralizes to all red-dwarf planets.
  • Skill Assessed: Inferences (Hard deductive elimination).
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever a science passage lists "one of three conditions: X, Y, or Z" and then disproves two of them, the answer must affirm the remaining one!

RW-D1-Q12 → Correct Answer: C (innovations:)

  • Why C works: Left of the blank is a complete independent clause (...the theater at Epidaurus projected whispered dialogue to fourteen thousand spectators through two acoustic innovations). Right of the blank is a two-item noun-phrase explanation (stepped limestone seating rows... and a steeply raked stage basin...). Complete IC : Noun-Phrase Explanation requires a colon (:).
  • Why others fail: A (, ) loosely attaches a heavy compound explanation where a formal colon is needed to signal "namely"; B (;) is grammatically illegal because the right side has no main verb for rows or basin (filtered and channeled sit inside subordinate that-clauses, making the right side a fragment!); D (innovations and) falsely treats "two acoustic innovations" as a parallel list item alongside the two innovations themselves.
  • Skill Assessed: SEC: Boundaries (Colon IC : Fragment/List vs. Semicolon IC ; IC).
  • Next-Time Clue: "two [noun]s: [Item 1] and [Item 2]" is a classic SAT colon pattern—just verify the clause before the colon is complete!

RW-D1-Q13 → Correct Answer: B (operation; nevertheless,)

  • Why B works: Left side = complete IC (The first... cable... suffered catastrophic insulation breakdown after just three weeks of operation). Right side = complete IC (commercial syndicates... remained convinced...). Because nevertheless is a conjunctive adverb (not FANBOYS), you must separate the two ICs with a semicolon (or period) before nevertheless, followed by a comma: operation; nevertheless,.
  • Why others fail: A and C are comma splices (IC , IC); D is a fused run-on sentence.
  • Skill Assessed: SEC: Boundaries (Conjunctive adverb comma-splice trap).
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever choices differ only by , word, vs. ; word,, check if both sides are complete ICs. If yes, , word, is an automatic comma splice!

RW-D1-Q14 → Correct Answer: D (requires)

  • Why D works: Strip the prepositional chain: Non-invasive legibility analysis [of carbonized papyrus scrolls and fragile wax tablets recovered from volcanic ash at Herculaneum] _____. The true grammatical subject is singular analysis, which takes singular requires!
  • Why others fail: A (require), B (have required), and C (are requiring) are all plural verbs lured by plural scrolls and tablets!
  • Skill Assessed: SEC: Form, Structure, and Sense (Subject-Verb Agreement across intervening prepositional phrases).
  • Next-Time Clue: Notice the 3-plural (A, B, C) vs. 1-singular (D) split! Whenever 3 verb options share number and 1 stands alone, immediately find the true head noun before the first of.

RW-D1-Q15 → Correct Answer: C

  • Why C works: Opening participial modifier = "Calibrating the laser interferometer..." Ask: Who calibrated the laser? Only the observatory's physics team! Therefore, the observatory's physics team must stand immediately after the comma.
  • Why others fail: A (gravitational waves), B (a distant binary black hole merger), and D (subtle ripples in spacetime) all create absurd dangling modifiers claiming waves, black holes, or ripples calibrated laboratory equipment!
  • Skill Assessed: SEC: Form, Structure, and Sense (Introductory Subject-Modifier Placement).
  • Next-Time Clue: Sentence starts with -ing / -ed phrase , ______? Read only the first word(s) of A–D and pick the actual doer in 10 seconds!

RW-D1-Q16 → Correct Answer: A (Instead,)

  • Why A works: Sentence 1 states an unrealized scientific prediction (would take centuries to colonize). Sentence 2 reports what happened in place of that prediction (more than tripled in four years). Instead, signals "contrary to that expected outcome, here is what actually occurred."
  • Why others fail: *B (Consequently,)* = cause/result (slow metabolism did not cause rapid tripling!); *C (Similarly,)* = parallel similarity; *D (For example,)* = supporting example of slow growth.
  • Skill Assessed: Transitions (Expectation vs. Counter-Expectation).
  • Next-Time Clue: "long predicted X. ______, surveys showed opposite Y" → Instead, / However, / Nevertheless,.

RW-D1-Q17 → Correct Answer: B (Specifically,)

  • Why B works: Sentence 1 states a general policy goal (halt epidemic disease without bankrupting merchants). Sentence 2 details the exact concrete rules that achieved both halves (40-day island quarantine for disease + airing rather than burning cargo for solvency). Specifically, bridges a general claim to its concrete operational details.
  • Why others fail: *A (Nevertheless,)* & *C (Conversely,)* signal contradiction where none exists between Sentence 1 and Sentence 2; *D (Afterwards,)* falsely implies chronological sequence after the statutes ended.
  • Skill Assessed: Transitions (General Principle → Specific Implementation).
  • Next-Time Clue: Don't get tricked by whereas inside Sentence 2! The transition at the start of Sentence 2 connects Sentence 2 as a whole back to Sentence 1.

RW-D1-Q18 → Correct Answer: C

  • Why C works: Check the prompt's three constraints: (1) explain how, (2) two structural elements interact, (3) to cool classrooms passively. Choice C names both elements (perforated clay ceiling + elevated corrugated-metal roof) and explains their joint airflow mechanism (warm air rises out while cross-breezes sweep heat away).
  • Why others fail: A discusses the prize and construction labor (zero cooling); B states the temperature result (6°C–8°C) without naming or explaining how the two structural elements work; D contrasts wall and roof materials without mentioning cooling at all!
  • Skill Assessed: Rhetorical Synthesis (Mechanism/Interaction goal vs. Outcome-only trap).
  • Next-Time Clue: "explain HOW X and Y interact to do Z" eliminates any option that merely states outcome Z or merely lists X and Y!

subSections.titleHtml: D. Math Practice Set (MATH-D1-Q1 to MATH-D1-Q15) — Complete Solutions & Desmos Methods
subSections.html:
MATH-D1-Q1 → Correct Answer: B (60)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Set C(m)=63:
    42+0.35m=63⟹0.35m=21⟹m=0.3521​=352100​=60
  • Desmos Method: Type 42 + 0.35x = 63 on Line 1 → click vertical line at x = 60.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: Plug back in: 42+0.35(60)=42+21=63 ✓. Trap D (180): Dividing 63 by 0.35 without subtracting fixed base cost first!

MATH-D1-Q2 → Correct Answer (SPR): 11

  • Step-by-Step Solution:
    10x−15=3x+13⟹7x=28⟹x=4
    Boxed target expression: 4x−5=4(4)−5=11.
  • Desmos Method: Line 1: 5(2x - 3) = 3x + 13 (shows x=4). Line 2: 4(4) - 5 → 11.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: LHS =5(8−3)=25; RHS =3(4)+13=25 ✓. #1 SAT SPR Trap (E4): Entering 4 (x) instead of 11 (4x−5)!

MATH-D1-Q3 → Correct Answer: C (3,312)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Apply successive multipliers sequentially:
    2025 total=2,400×1.15=2,760
    2026 total=2,760×1.20=3,312
  • Alternative Fast Expression: Type 2400 * 1.15 * 1.20 directly in Desmos → 3312.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: Trap B (3,240): Adding 15%+20%=35% (2,400×1.35=3,240), ignoring the 20% gain applied to the new 360 maps added in 2025 (0.20×360=72; 3,240+72=3,312)!

MATH-D1-Q4 → Correct Answer: B (-4)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: For no solution, slopes must match while y-intercepts differ (a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​=c2​c1​​):
    k6​=6−9​⟹−9k=36⟹k=−4
  • Desmos Slider Method: Type 6x - 9y = 14 on Line 1 and kx + 6y = -8 on Line 2; click add slider k and test choices -9, -4, 4, 9—at k = -4 the two lines become strictly parallel!
  • Verification & Trap Alert: Check constant ratio: −46​=−1.5, 6−9​=−1.5, and −814​=−1.75=−1.5 ✓ (parallel, not identical). Trap C (4): Dropping the negative sign!

MATH-D1-Q5 → Correct Answer: B (2x - 3)

  • Step-by-Step Algebraic Factoring: Find factors of 2(−15)=−30 summing to +7 (+10 and −3):
    2x2+10x−3x−15=2x(x+5)−3(x+5)=(2x−3)(x+5)
    Divide by (x+5) (valid for x>0 since x+5=0): 2x−3.
  • Desmos / Plug-In 10-Second Method: Graph y = (2x^2 + 7x - 15)/(x + 5) and y = 2x - 3 (identical line for x>0!), OR test x=1: 1+52+7−15​=6−6​=−1. Plug x=1 into choices: A gives −3, B gives 2(1)−3=−1, C gives 5, D gives 6.
  • Trap Alert: Trap D cancels 15/5=3 illegally across addition/subtraction!

MATH-D1-Q6 → Correct Answer: C (M(t) = 320(0.75)^(t/6))

  • Step-by-Step Solution:
    • Initial mass at t=0: a=320.
    • Losing 25% leaves 100%−25%=75%=0.75 remaining per cycle.
    • One decay cycle occurs every 6 hours, so after t hours there have been t/6 cycles ⟹M(t)=320(0.75)t/6.
  • Plug-In Verification: At t=6 hours, mass must drop by 25% of 320 (80 mg) to 240 mg. Check C: 320(0.75)6/6=320(0.75)1=240 ✓.
  • Trap Alert: Trap A uses 0.25 (amount lost instead of amount remaining); Trap B uses 6t (36 decay cycles in 6 hours instead of 1!).

MATH-D1-Q7 → Correct Answer (SPR): 43

  • Step-by-Step Solution:
    • Sum of Dataset A (5 integers) =12+15+18+21+29=95.
    • Mean of Dataset A =595​=19.
    • Mean of Dataset B (6 integers) =19+4=23.
    • Sum of Dataset B =6×23=138.
    • x=138−95=43.
  • Desmos Check: Type mean(12, 15, 18, 21, 29) → 19; then mean(12, 15, 18, 21, 29, 43) → 23 (23 - 19 = 4 ✓)!
  • Trap Alert: Multiplying 23×5 instead of 23×6 after adding the sixth element.

MATH-D1-Q8 → Correct Answer: C (45)

  • Step-by-Step Solution:
    • In right △ABC (∠C=90∘), sin(A)=HypotenuseOpposite​=ABBC​=178​.
    • Since BC=24=3×8, the scale factor is 3, so hypotenuse AB=3×17=51.
    • Recognize the 8-15-17 Pythagorean triple (or compute 512−242​=2,601−576​=2,025​=45): adjacent side AC=3×15=45.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: 242+452=576+2,025=2,601=512 ✓. Trap D (51) solves for hypotenuse AB instead of leg AC!

MATH-D1-Q9 → Correct Answer: A (9)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Let s = sensors and w = canisters:
    1.5s+2.4w≤35ands≥8
    To maximize w, make s as small as permitted (s=8):
    1.5(8)+2.4w≤35⟹12+2.4w≤35⟹2.4w≤23⟹w≤2.423​≈9.583
    Because w must be a whole number of canisters and cannot exceed the 35 kg payload limit, round down to 9.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: At w=9: 12+2.4(9)=12+21.6=33.6≤35 ✓. At Trap B (w=10): 12+24=36>35 (exceeds max payload—rounding 9.58 up to 10 is a classic real-world inequality mistake!).

MATH-D1-Q10 → Correct Answer: B (7)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Since a=2>0, f(x) opens upward and reaches its minimum at vertex x-coordinate:
    h=−2ab​=−2(2)−16​=4
    Note 1≤4≤8 lies inside the domain. Minimum power consumption is f(4):
    f(4)=2(4)2−16(4)+39=32−64+39=7
  • Desmos 8-Second Method: Graph f(x) = 2x^2 - 16x + 39 → click bottom vertex dot (4, 7) → read y-coordinate 7.
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (4) gives the airflow setting x instead of minimum watts f(x); Trap D (39) gives the y-intercept f(0).

MATH-D1-Q11 → Correct Answer: B

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Statistical inference rule: a random sample generalizes strictly to the sampling frame from which it was randomly drawn—here, undergraduate students currently living in on-campus dormitories at that university.
  • Why others fail: A improperly adds commuter undergraduates and graduate students (who likely use shuttles very differently!); C misunderstands margin of error (68%±4% is completely valid for generalizing to the sampled population); D improperly extrapolates to other universities statewide.

MATH-D1-Q12 → Correct Answer (SPR): 8

  • Desmos 12-Second Method (Fastest!):
    • Line 1: y = x^2 - 5x + 7
    • Line 2: y = 2x - 3
    • Click the two intersection dots: (2, 1) and (5, 7).
    • Boxed target is y1​+y2​ (not x1​+x2​!): 1+7=8.
  • Algebraic Solution:
    x2−5x+7=2x−3⟹x2−7x+10=0⟹(x−2)(x−5)=0⟹x1​=2,x2​=5
    y1​=2(2)−3=1,y2​=2(5)−3=7⟹y1​+y2​=1+7=8
  • Trap Alert: Entering x1​+x2​=2+5=7 (E4 target misread)!

MATH-D1-Q13 → Correct Answer (SPR): 7

  • Algebraic Completing the Square:
    (x2−10x+25)+(y2+6y+9)=15+25+9
    (x−5)2+(y+3)2=49⟹r2=49⟹r=7
  • Desmos Visual Method: Type x^2 + y^2 - 10x + 6y - 15 = 0. Click the leftmost and rightmost points of the circle (or graph horizontal center line y = -3 to click (-2, -3) and (12, -3)): diameter =12−(−2)=14⟹ radius =14/2=7!
  • Trap Alert: Entering r2=49 instead of r=7!

MATH-D1-Q14 → Correct Answer: B (-12)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Exactly one real solution means discriminant D=b2−4ac=0:
    b2−4(3)(12)=0⟹b2−144=0⟹b2=144⟹b=±12
    Because the prompt specifies b is a negative constant, b=−12.
  • Desmos Check: Graph y = 3x^2 - 12x + 12: parabola touches the x-axis at a single vertex point (2, 0) ✓.
  • Trap Alert: Trap D (12) overlooks the word "negative" in the stem!

MATH-D1-Q15 → Correct Answer (SPR): 4

  • Algebraic Solution:
    • Substitute (0,−5): a⋅20+b=−5⟹a+b=−5 (Caution: 20=1, NOT 0!)
    • Substitute (3,16): a⋅23+b=16⟹8a+b=16
    • Subtract Eq. 1 from Eq. 2: 7a=21⟹a=3, so 3+b=−5⟹b=−8.
    • Evaluate g(2): g(2)=3⋅22−8=3(4)−8=12−8=4.
  • Desmos Regression Method (20 Seconds): Add Table (+ → Table) with (0,−5) and (3,16). Type y_1 ~ a * 2^(x_1) + b → reads a=3,b=−8. Evaluate 3 * 2^2 - 8 → 4.
  • Trap Alert: Thinking 20=0, which wrongly gives b=−5 instead of a+b=−5!

errorLab.beforeKeyHtml:
Part A: Classify Five Authentic International-Student Mistakes

Before logging your own mistakes, train your diagnostic eye! Assign each student case (EL-CASE-1 to EL-CASE-5) its exact Primary Error Code (E1–E10) and (for R&W) exact Vocabulary/Language Sub-Label (V1–V7) from SAT-Error-Log-and-Daily-Reflections.md, plus a 1-sentence Next-Time Rule:
errorLab.caseKeyHtml:
• EL-CASE-1: E2 (Vocabulary gap) + V2 (Knew word but selected the wrong meaning) and V4 (Missed contrast clue "however... restricting") — Next-Time Rule: Never eliminate a familiar word before checking secondary academic meanings (qualify = limit scope), and never pick a choice (substantiated) that violates a however contrast!
  • EL-CASE-2: E5 / V7 — V7 (Failed to connect evidence to the claim) — Next-Time Rule: Underline every part of the researchers' thesis (resolves the trade-off via clover–rye) before checking data accuracy.
  • EL-CASE-3: E4 (Misread question) — Next-Time Rule: Physically box the final target expression (y1​+y2​) before typing any SPR answer.
  • EL-CASE-4: E6 (Grammar rule forgotten) — Next-Time Rule: On punctuation questions, test IC vs. Fragment on both sides before judging transition meaning; , nevertheless, between two ICs is always a comma splice.
  • EL-CASE-5: E8 (Timing problem) + E9 (Wrong strategy) — Next-Time Rule: Run the 5-Second Desmos Check first and enforce the strict 90-Second Bailout Rule so one stubborn item never destroys three solvable ones.
errorLab.afterKeyHtml:
Part B: Personal Day 1 Error-Log Entry Task (Complete Now — 10 Minutes)

Open SAT-Error-Log-and-Daily-Reflections.md and log every missed or guessed item from today's diagnostic work (Bluebook Practice Test 4 and/or RW-D1-Q1..18 + MATH-D1-Q1..15). Confirm that:

  • Every logged R&W miss carries a specific E + V code (never "didn't know").
  • Every logged Math miss notes whether a faster Desmos path existed.
  • Your Top 5 Personal Weaknesses are written at the bottom of Day 1's notes to steer Day 2!

cases.promptHtml: On RW-D1-Q3, Tariq knew the everyday word qualify ("pass an exam to enter a competition"), decided it made no sense in an economic history passage, crossed out qualified, and picked substantiated even though the sentence contained "however... restricting it to capital-city luxury trades."
cases.answerHtml: E2 (Vocabulary gap) + V2 (Knew word but selected the wrong meaning) and V4 (Missed contrast clue "however... restricting") — Next-Time Rule: Never eliminate a familiar word before checking secondary academic meanings (qualify = limit scope), and never pick a choice (substantiated) that violates a however contrast!

cases.promptHtml: On RW-D1-Q9, Mei checked the cover-crop table carefully, confirmed that Winter Rye Only really had 8.4 vs. 8.9 for Bare Soil, and selected Choice B—missing that Choice B only proved the problem rather than proving the clover–rye solution.
cases.answerHtml: E5 / V7 — V7 (Failed to connect evidence to the claim) — Next-Time Rule: Underline every part of the researchers' thesis (resolves the trade-off via clover–rye) before checking data accuracy.

cases.promptHtml: On MATH-D1-Q12, Lukas factored x2−7x+10=0 cleanly into (x−2)(x−5)=0, smiled, added 2+5=7, and typed 7 into the SPR box when the question asked for y1​+y2​.
cases.answerHtml: E4 (Misread question) — Next-Time Rule: Physically box the final target expression (y1​+y2​) before typing any SPR answer.

cases.promptHtml: On RW-D1-Q13, Sofia translated the whole sentence accurately into her native language, saw that nevertheless fit the meaning perfectly, and immediately clicked Choice A (operation, nevertheless,) without testing whether both sides were complete independent clauses.
cases.answerHtml: E6 (Grammar rule forgotten) — Next-Time Rule: On punctuation questions, test IC vs. Fragment on both sides before judging transition meaning; , nevertheless, between two ICs is always a comma splice.

cases.promptHtml: During a timed set, Kenji spent 4 minutes 10 seconds expanding algebraic fractions by hand on Question 11, ran out of time, and guessed randomly on Questions 13, 14, and 15 (two of which were 20-second Desmos problems).
cases.answerHtml: E8 (Timing problem) + E9 (Wrong strategy) — Next-Time Rule: Run the 5-Second Desmos Check first and enforce the strict 90-Second Bailout Rule so one stubborn item never destroys three solvable ones.

mastery.introHtml: Complete all 8 synthesis questions below closed-notes in 8 minutes to verify Day 1 concepts locked into long-term memory:

masteryItems.promptHtml: Fill the blank with one Day 1 word: "Preliminary ice-penetrating radar offered a ______ map of the subglacial lake, though glaciologists emphasized that seismic drilling would be required for definitive confirmation."
masteryItems.answerHtml: tentative (paired directly with "Preliminary" and contrasted against "definitive confirmation")

masteryItems.promptHtml: In academic SAT passages, what does the verb qualify mean when an author "qualifies an earlier hypothesis"?
masteryItems.answerHtml: To limit, narrow, or add conditions to the hypothesis so it is less sweeping/absolute.

masteryItems.promptHtml: Rewrite "Its steep construction cost notwithstanding, the tidal turbine generated profitable clean electricity within three years" in simple English without using notwithstanding.
masteryItems.answerHtml: "Despite its high construction cost, the tidal turbine generated profitable clean electricity within three years."

masteryItems.promptHtml: Fix the punctuation error in: "The ceramic glaze contained cobalt imported from Persia, consequently, archaeologists revised their trade-route timeline."
masteryItems.answerHtml: Replace the first comma with a semicolon (or period): ...imported from Persia; consequently, archaeologists...

masteryItems.promptHtml: Choose was or were: "The calibration of pressure sensors mounted along deep-ocean tsunami buoys (was / were) verified weekly."
masteryItems.answerHtml: was (true singular head noun = calibration, NOT plural sensors or buoys!)

masteryItems.promptHtml: For what value of c does 8x−12y=5 and cx+6y=7 have no solution?
masteryItems.answerHtml: c8​=6−12​=−2⟹c=−4 (and 75​=−2, confirming parallel lines with zero solutions).

masteryItems.promptHtml: What is the minimum value of g(x)=(x−6)2+11, and at what value of x does it occur?
masteryItems.answerHtml: Minimum value =11, occurring at x=6.

masteryItems.promptHtml: A phytoplankton colony of 1,200 cells doubles every 9 hours. Write function N(t) for the cell count after t hours.
masteryItems.answerHtml: N(t)=1,200(2)t/9.

mastery.keyHtml:
1. tentative (paired directly with "Preliminary" and contrasted against "definitive confirmation")
  2. To limit, narrow, or add conditions to the hypothesis so it is less sweeping/absolute.
  3. "Despite its high construction cost, the tidal turbine generated profitable clean electricity within three years."
  4. Replace the first comma with a semicolon (or period): ...imported from Persia; consequently, archaeologists...
  5. was (true singular head noun = calibration, NOT plural sensors or buoys!)
  6. c8​=6−12​=−2⟹c=−4 (and 75​=−2, confirming parallel lines with zero solutions).
  7. Minimum value =11, occurring at x=6.
  8. N(t)=1,200(2)t/9.

objectives.html:
By 14:55 today, you will demonstrate:

  1. Mechanical Punctuation Speed & Certainty (>=85% on Boundaries): Test whether clauses are independent (IC) or dependent/fragmentary (DC / Frag) in under 15 seconds—even when technical scientific nouns are unfamiliar.
  2. Finite Verb & Modifier Precision (>=85% on Form, Structure, and Sense): Distinguish true finite verbs (analyzes, were discovered) from non-finite verbals (analyzing, to analyze, having analyzed), match subjects across inverted syntax, and enforce parallel comparisons (those of / that of).
  3. 24-Hour Spaced Vocabulary Retention (>=8/10 on Day 1 Retrieval SR-D2-Q1..10): Recall and apply Day 1's 10 academic words from memory without consulting definitions.
  4. Expanded Academic Word Network (>=80% on Day 2 Words #11–#20): Master bolster, scrutinize, compelling, assert, conventional, disparate, concede, mitigate, ubiquitous, and conversely—linking them directly to Day 1's synonym/contrast web.
  5. High-Frequency Algebra Reliability (>=80% on MATH-D2-Q1..16): Solve linear equations/systems with constants (no solution vs. infinitely many solutions), perpendicular-line equations, unit-conversion rate problems, and strict vs. non-strict integer inequalities cleanly by hand and in Desmos.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Standard English Conventions I — Mastering Sentence Boundaries
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 2.1: Standard English Conventions I — Mastering Sentence Boundaries
lessons.html:
Why do we dedicate Day 2 morning to Standard English Conventions? Because on a 560 R&W score, grammar questions are the fastest 60–90 scaled points available on the entire Digital SAT. Better still, English punctuation obeys structural architecture, not vocabulary size: even if you do not know what calcified foraminifera or mercantilist tariffs mean, you can still score 100% on the punctuation between them!

A. Step 1 on Every Boundary Question: The Independent Clause (IC) Test

An Independent Clause (IC) has three mandatory ingredients:

  1. A grammatical subject (not trapped inside a prepositional phrase like In the museum).
  2. A finite main verb that shows tense (is, was, has evolved, illuminated) — CRITICAL INTERNATIONAL-STUDENT RULE: An -ing word by itself (illuminating, having illuminated) or an infinitive (to illuminate) is NEVER a finite main verb! The telescope orbiting Earth is a noun phrase fragment, NOT a sentence!
  3. No subordinating starter (Although, Because, Whereas, While, Since, Unless, If, When turn an IC into a Dependent Clause [DC] that cannot stand alone!).

B. The Complete Digital SAT Punctuation Matrix

Punctuation Structure Legal or Illegal? Exact SAT Usage Rule & Trap Alert
IC . IC (Period) LEGAL Clean hard stop between two complete thoughts.
IC ; IC (Semicolon) LEGAL Exact grammatical twin of a period! Shortcut: If one choice has word. Capital and another has word; lowercase with zero other wording differences, eliminate BOTH immediately—they are grammatically identical!
IC ; conjunctive adverb , IC (e.g., ; however, / ; moreover, / ; consequently,) LEGAL Words like however, nevertheless, therefore, consequently, furthermore, instead, thus are adverbs, NOT conjunctions. Joining two ICs with , however, is an automatic comma splice!
IC , FANBOYS IC (, for / , and / , nor / , but / , or / , yet / , so) LEGAL Comma + FANBOYS requires a complete IC on BOTH sides! Trap: The rover collected rock samples, and transmitted spectra has NO second subject after and—so no comma before and (collected... and transmitted...)!
IC : [Explanation / List / Single Word / IC] (Colon) LEGAL Left of : MUST be a complete IC! Right of : can be a full IC, a list, or a single noun phrase answering "What specifically?" #1 Colon Trap: NEVER put a colon right after a verb or preposition such as such as:, including:, consists of:, or are:—because the left side is incomplete!
Single Em-Dash (IC — Explanation) LEGAL Works just like a colon (Complete IC on the left; dramatic restatement/explanation on the right).
Paired Commas / Paired Dashes (, phrase , or — phrase —) LEGAL (Must Match!) Encloses a non-essential interrupting phrase. #1 Symmetry Trap: You can use , ... , OR — ... —, NEVER , ... — or — ... ,! Test by deleting the middle phrase: the remaining outer sentence must read smoothly and grammatically.
Super-Semicolon in Complex Lists (Item A, detail; Item B, detail; and Item C, detail) LEGAL The ONLY exception where a semicolon does not separate two ICs: when list items already contain internal commas (such as Lima, Peru; Quito, Ecuador; and Bogotá, Colombia), semicolons act as "super-commas" separating the main items!

C. Essential (No Commas!) vs. Non-Essential (Commas!) Names & Titles

International students miss this high-frequency SAT question constantly because spoken rhythm misleads them! Memorize the Specificity Test:

  • Title/Label + Specific Name (Essential Identifier → ZERO COMMAS!):
    Biochemist Katalin Karikó investigated mRNA modifications.
    (Why no commas around Katalin Karikó? Because "Biochemist" without "a" or "the" is a title phrase, OR in "The biochemist Katalin Karikó investigated..." deleting the name leaves "The biochemist investigated..."—which biochemist out of thousands?! Because the name restricts/specifies WHICH biochemist, zero commas surround the name!)
  • Unique Noun + Extra Description (Non-Essential Appositive → PAIRED COMMAS!):
    Katalin Karikó, a Hungarian-born biochemist, investigated mRNA modifications.
    (Why paired commas? "Katalin Karikó" already uniquely identifies one person; "a Hungarian-born biochemist" is bonus info you can lift right out!)

Worked Example 2.1 (Essential Title + Name Trap)

Original SAT-Style Example:
In 1977, Kenyan environmentalist ______ founded the Green Belt Movement, mobilizing rural women to plant tens of millions of native trees across eroded watersheds.

A) Wangari Maathai,
B) Wangari Maathai
C) Wangari Maathai—
D) , Wangari Maathai,

  • Step-by-Step Analysis: Delete "Wangari Maathai" to test D: "In 1977, Kenyan environmentalist founded..." — Ungrammatical! Missing an article (a), "Kenyan environmentalist" functions as a title directly attached to her name (Kenyan environmentalist Wangari Maathai = complete subject). Putting a single comma in A separates the subject from its own verb (founded)—illegal! C opens a dash with no closing dash. Correct: B (zero punctuation).

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 2.1 (Check answers in Section 8)

  • CC-D2-RW1: Why is "The exhibition features artifacts made of several durable materials: including bronze, obsidian, and fired stoneware" wrong, and how do you fix it?
  • CC-D2-RW2: Choice A reads ...in 1928. This discovery... and Choice B reads ...in 1928; this discovery... (with Choices C and D using commas). What can you conclude immediately about Choices A and B?
  • CC-D2-RW3: Punctuate (commas or no commas?): "Architectural historian [ Spiro Kostof ] argued that city skylines reflect civic power."
  • CC-D2-RW4: When is a semicolon grammatically correct on the Digital SAT even though the words after it do NOT form an independent clause?

checks.promptHtml: Why is "The exhibition features artifacts made of several durable materials: including bronze, obsidian, and fired stoneware" wrong, and how do you fix it?
checks.answerHtml: Placing a colon before including creates redundancy and violates colon mechanics (materials: including... treats including... as if materials weren't already introducing a list, or puts both a colon AND including doing the exact same job!). Two clean fixes: (1) ...several durable materials, including bronze, obsidian, and fired stoneware. OR (2) ...several durable materials: bronze, obsidian, and fired stoneware. (Never combine : + including!)

checks.promptHtml: Choice A reads ...in 1928. This discovery... and Choice B reads ...in 1928; this discovery... (with Choices C and D using commas). What can you conclude immediately about Choices A and B?
checks.answerHtml: Eliminate BOTH A and B immediately! Because IC . IC and IC ; IC are 100% grammatically interchangeable when all words match, College Board cannot make one right and the other wrong.

checks.promptHtml: Punctuate (commas or no commas?): "Architectural historian [ Spiro Kostof ] argued that city skylines reflect civic power."
checks.answerHtml: Zero commas! Architectural historian Spiro Kostof argued... (Architectural historian has no article An, acting as an essential title phrase naming which historian; adding commas would leave "Architectural historian argued..."—ungrammatical!).

checks.promptHtml: When is a semicolon grammatically correct on the Digital SAT even though the words after it do NOT form an independent clause?
checks.answerHtml: Inside a complex serial list of three or more items where at least one list item already contains internal commas (City A, Country A; City B, Country B; and City C, Country C).

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Standard English Conventions II — Form, Structure, and Sense
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 2.2: Standard English Conventions II — Form, Structure, and Sense
lessons.html:
Look at choices A–D first to spot which of the five grammar mechanisms is being tested:

1. Finite Main Verb vs. Non-Finite Verbal Fragment (Tested on Nearly Every SAT!)

Every sentence needs at least one finite tense verb (is, are, was, were, investigates, investigated, has investigated). If you strip out relative clauses (which..., that..., who...) and participial modifiers (...discovered in 1994), does the main subject have a real verb?

  • Fragment Trap: The porcelain kilns in Jingdezhen, which supplied imperial courts for five centuries, [producing] translucent white vessels. → which supplied... belongs to which; producing is an -ing participle, leaving The porcelain kilns with NO MAIN VERB!
  • Fix: The porcelain kilns in Jingdezhen, which supplied imperial courts for five centuries, **produced** translucent white vessels.

2. Subject-Verb Agreement Traps (3 Disguises)

  • Disguise A — Prepositional & Participial Chains: The alignment [of the limestone pillars carved by Neolithic builders] **corresponds** (singular alignment, not pillars or builders).
  • Disguise B — Inverted Sentences (Prepositional Phrase + Verb + Subject): When a sentence starts with a location phrase (In the deepest trench of the Mariana Arc **thrive** [specialized amphipods]), flip it backward in your head: [Specialized amphipods] **thrive** in the deepest trench!
  • Disguise C — Gerund (-ing) or Clause Subjects (Always Singular!): **Cataloging** four thousand medieval manuscripts **requires** (the single activity cataloging is singular, even though manuscripts is plural!).

3. Verb Tense & Timeline Anchors

Never pick a verb tense by "how it sounds" in isolation—find the time anchor in the surrounding text:

  • Historical Past (In 1889, during the Tang dynasty): Simple past (constructed, revealed).
  • Past-Before-Past (By the time X happened [past], Y _____): Past perfect (**had already occurred**).
  • Ongoing Since Past (Since 2010, over the past three decades): Present perfect (**has transformed** / **have documented**).
  • General Scientific/Literary Fact: Simple present (photosynthesis **converts**, in the novel, the protagonist **confronts**).

4. Pronouns, Determiners & Apostrophes (s vs. 's vs. s')

  • Match Antecedent Number Strictly: An institution, species, company, or guild (the guild, each orchestra, a coral polyp) is singular (it / its); plural nouns (guilds, orchestras, coral polyps) take they / them / their.
  • Contraction vs. Possessive: it's = it is; its = possessive (its surface). they're = they are; their = possessive (their surfaces).
  • Fast Apostrophe Decision Tree:
    1. Does the noun possess the next noun (can you flip "the [Noun 1]'s [Noun 2]" into "the [Noun 2] of the [Noun 1]"? If a preposition like of, in, or a verb follows immediately, NO apostrophe—just plural -s!).
    2. If it is possessive: Singular owner (one comet's tail) → 's; Plural owners ending in -s (two comets' tails) → s'.

5. Dangling Modifiers & Parallel Comparisons (that of / those of)

  • Introductory Modifier Rule: [Modifier Phrase], [True Doer Subject]... (covered in Lesson 1.3—verify every time!).
  • Apples-to-Apples Comparison Rule: Never compare an attribute directly to a person or object!
    • Wrong: The tensile strength of spider silk exceeds **steel** of equal thickness. (Compares "strength" to "steel"!)
    • Right: The tensile strength of spider silk exceeds **that of** steel of equal thickness. (Singular "that of" stands for "the tensile strength of"; use plural "those of" for plural nouns like "The vocalizations of humpback whales are more varied than **those of** minke whales.")

Worked Example 2.2 (Apostrophe + Number Precision)

Original SAT-Style Example:
Whereas Earth's magnetic field is generated by convection currents in a liquid iron core, ______ originate in shallower layers of electrically conducting slush composed of water, ammonia, and methane.

A) Uranus's and Neptune's magnetic fields
B) Uranuss and Neptunes magnetic fields'
C) Uranus's and Neptune's magnetic field's
D) Uranus and Neptune's magnetic fields'

  • Analysis: Does magnetic fields own anything after it? Next word is the verb originate—so fields is a plain plural subject (no apostrophe on fields, eliminating B, C, and D immediately!). Both planets individually possess magnetic fields (Uranus's and Neptune's magnetic fields). Correct: A.

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 2.2

  • CC-D2-RW5: Is this a complete sentence or a fragment? "Algae living symbiotically inside giant clam mantles, supplying up to seventy percent of the host mollusk's metabolic carbon." Fix it in one word!
  • CC-D2-RW6: Choose was or were: "Nestled beneath the volcanic tuff layers of Akrotiri (was / were) dozens of intact frescoed storage jars."
  • CC-D2-RW7: Choose the right tense: "By the time explorers reached the plateau in 1911, seasonal glaciers (carved / had already carved) deep striations across the granite bedrock."
  • CC-D2-RW8: Fix the illogical comparison: "Unlike traditional copper cables, glass optical fibers' data transmission rates surpass coaxial wires."

checks.promptHtml: Is this a complete sentence or a fragment? "Algae living symbiotically inside giant clam mantles, supplying up to seventy percent of the host mollusk's metabolic carbon." Fix it in one word!
checks.answerHtml: Fragment! living... and supplying... are both -ing participles—Algae has no finite main verb! One-word fix: change supplying to supply (and remove the comma: Algae living symbiotically inside giant clam mantles **supply** up to seventy percent...).

checks.promptHtml: Choose was or were: "Nestled beneath the volcanic tuff layers of Akrotiri (was / were) dozens of intact frescoed storage jars."
checks.answerHtml: were — Inverted location sentence! Flip backward: [Dozens of intact frescoed storage jars] **were** nestled beneath the volcanic tuff layers of Akrotiri.

checks.promptHtml: Choose the right tense: "By the time explorers reached the plateau in 1911, seasonal glaciers (carved / had already carved) deep striations across the granite bedrock."
checks.answerHtml: had already carved — "By the time explorers reached [past event, 1911]" requires past perfect (had + participle) for the earlier glacial action.

checks.promptHtml: Fix the illogical comparison: "Unlike traditional copper cables, glass optical fibers' data transmission rates surpass coaxial wires."
checks.answerHtml: Compare rates to rates, not rates to wires! Fix: ...glass optical fibers' data transmission rates surpass **those of** coaxial wires. (Plural those of = the data transmission rates of.)

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Words in Context Foundations — Academic Synonym/Contrast Networks & Avoiding the "Familiarity Trap"
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 2.3: Words in Context Foundations — Academic Synonym/Contrast Networks & Avoiding the "Familiarity Trap"
lessons.html:
International students at 560 frequently fall into two predictable traps on Words in Context:

  1. The Comfort Blanket Trap: Picking Choice B because it is the only word you recognize from everyday conversation, even though it has neutral or positive polarity where the sentence demands criticism.
  2. The Complexity Halo Trap: Picking Choice D solely because it looks long and academic, without checking whether two other choices already contradict or satisfy your prediction.

Building Synonym & Contrast Clusters (Not Isolated Flashcards!)

Instead of memorizing single words in a vacuum, store SAT vocabulary in 3-way polarity clusters:

Semantic Domain Confirm / Strengthen (+) Cautious / Partial / Neutral (±) Weaken / Doubt / Reject (-)
Evidence & Claims substantiate, corroborate, bolster, validate, vindicate assert, posit, qualify, concede, reconcile undermine, refute, contradict, discredit, repudiate
Certainty & Strength compelling, definitive, unambiguous, conclusive plausible, tentative, preliminary, nuanced implausible, ambiguous, dubious, tenuous, reductive
Harm & Change amplify, foster, proliferate modulate, adapt, conventional mitigate (reduce harm), curtail, check (restrain), erode

Worked Example 2.3 (Defeating the Familiarity Trap)

Original SAT-Style Example:
Proponents of vertical indoor farming often ______ that stacked hydroponic towers will soon replace outdoor grain agriculture worldwide; agricultural physicists note, however, that the electricity required to simulate sunlight for calorie-dense staple crops like wheat remains prohibitively expensive.

A) corroborate
B) assert
C) concede
D) mitigate

  • Context Clue Analysis: Look at the second clause: "agricultural physicists note, however, that the electricity... remains prohibitively expensive." That proves the proponents' bold claim does NOT have solid physical/economic proof!
  • Trap Elimination:
    • A (corroborate) means confirm with solid independent proof—if proponents proved it, physicists wouldn't refute its cost right after however!
    • B (assert) means state firmly/confidently as a claim (without necessarily proving it) → fits "Proponents... assert that..., physicists note, however..." like a glove!
    • C (concede) means reluctantly admit a weakness—replacing all outdoor agriculture is the proponents' optimistic boast, not a reluctant admission!
    • D (mitigate) means make a problem less severe (ungrammatical before a that-clause).
    • Correct: B (assert).

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 2.3

  • CC-D2-RW9: Explain in one simple sentence the crucial SAT difference between asserting a hypothesis and substantiating a hypothesis.
  • CC-D2-RW10: If a passage states that wetland mangroves mitigate storm-surge flooding along coastal towns, does mitigate mean mangroves stop 100% of all floodwater, or make the flood damage less severe?

checks.promptHtml: Explain in one simple sentence the crucial SAT difference between asserting a hypothesis and substantiating a hypothesis.
checks.answerHtml: Asserting means stating a claim confidently (even with zero evidence), whereas substantiating means proving that claim with concrete facts or data.

checks.promptHtml: If a passage states that wetland mangroves mitigate storm-surge flooding along coastal towns, does mitigate mean mangroves stop 100% of all floodwater, or make the flood damage less severe?
checks.answerHtml: Make flood damage less severe / milder—mitigate reduces harm rather than eliminating 100% of floodwater.

subSections.html:
STOP — Do NOT open yesterday's notes! Test your memory of Day 1's 10 core words (#1–#10: substantiate, undermine, corroborate, plausible, ambiguous, infer, reconcile, nuanced, tentative, notwithstanding) by answering SR-D2-Q1 to SR-D2-Q10 in 6 minutes:

  • SR-D2-Q1: Which Day 1 verb means "to make two conflicting facts or datasets fit together without contradiction"?
  • SR-D2-Q2: Which Day 1 word means "despite / in spite of" and can appear after the noun phrase it modifies ("Its high cost ______...")?
  • SR-D2-Q3: Fill the blank with a Day 1 word: "Because only nine ceramic shards were recovered from the trench, the archaeologist's reconstruction of the vessel's trade origin remains strictly ______."
  • SR-D2-Q4: Fill the blank with a Day 1 word: "Undisclosed thermometer calibration drift can ______ the reliability of an entire thirty-year temperature record."
  • SR-D2-Q5: Which Day 1 adjective describes an analysis that captures subtle, balanced distinctions rather than a crude black-and-white view?
  • SR-D2-Q6: Distinguish in 6–10 words: corroborate vs. collaborate.
  • SR-D2-Q7: Fill the blank with a Day 1 word: "Because the phrasing of Article 4 was ______, rival shipping guilds interpreted the harbor tax in two opposing ways."
  • SR-D2-Q8: Distinguish in 6–10 words: substantiate vs. substantial.
  • SR-D2-Q9: Which Day 1 adjective means "reasonable and believable enough that it could be true (though not 100% proven)"?
  • SR-D2-Q10: Which Day 1 verb means "to deduce a logical conclusion from evidence rather than from a direct statement"?

(Grade SR-D2-Q1..10 in Section 8 later; target is >=8/10!)

subSections.title: B. Day 2 Core Academic Vocabulary (Words #11–#20)
subSections.titleHtml: B. Day 2 Core Academic Vocabulary (Words #11–#20)
subSections.html:
Study all 8 dimensions of each word below, then review the pre-loaded model rows #11–#20 in Vocabulary-Notebook-and-Spaced-Review.md and write your own personal sentence for each.

11. bolster (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To strengthen, support, or reinforce an argument, institution, or confidence.
  • Alternative Meanings: (noun) A long firm cushion/structural support beam—which gives rise to the academic verb ("prop up / strengthen")!
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: reinforce, strengthen, buttress · Ant: undermine (Day 1 #2!), weaken, erode.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Newly translated customs registries from Aden bolstered the historian's argument that small family partnerships—not royal monopolies—financed twelfth-century Indian Ocean pepper voyages."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Fresh archival tax records directly reinforced and strengthened her thesis about family merchants.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing bolster ("strengthen with real support") with boast ("brag arrogantly").
  • Short Application Activity: Pair Day 1 & Day 2 opposites: If counter-evidence undermines a claim, supporting evidence ______ it. (bolsters).

12. scrutinize (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To examine or inspect something very closely, critically, and thoroughly to check every detail or flaw.
  • Related Word Family: scrutiny (n. — close critical inspection, e.g., "withstand scientific scrutiny").
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: inspect, audit, dissect, probe · Ant: skim, overlook, glance over.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Before accepting the medieval charter as genuine, paleographers scrutinized its parchment fibers, iron-gall ink chemistry, and seal impressions under ultraviolet magnification."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: UV magnification of fibers, ink, and wax seals shows intense, detail-by-detail critical inspection—not casual reading.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Assuming scrutinize always means "attack unfairly." Scientists scrutinize data neutrally to test accuracy; an honest study survives scrutiny!
  • Short Application Activity: Replace the bracketed words: "Peer reviewers [closely examined] every statistical assumption in the trial." (scrutinized).

13. compelling (adjective)

  • Simple English Definition: Powerfully convincing and persuasive because the evidence or reasoning is remarkably strong; also gripping/absorbing.
  • Alternative Meanings: From verb compel ("force someone to act," e.g., "compelled by law"), but as an SAT adjective modifying evidence, case, explanation, or portrait, compelling means strongly convincing (+)!
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: persuasive, cogent, forceful, convincing · Ant: unconvincing, weak, tenuous, implausible.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "By matching volcanic glass shards in Greenland ice cores directly to chemical fingerprints from an Alaskan caldera, geologists presented compelling evidence for the eruption's exact year."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Exact chemical fingerprinting across ice cores and volcano rock makes the case hard to doubt (compelling).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Translating compelling evidence literally as "violent/coercive evidence that forces people against their will" instead of "highly persuasive evidence."
  • Short Application Activity: Rank persuasion strength from cautious (1) to strong (2): plausible vs. compelling. (1 = plausible, 2 = compelling).

14. assert (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To state a belief, claim, or right firmly and confidently as true.
  • Related Word Family: assertion (n. — a confident claim, often still needing proof: "an unsubstantiated assertion"), assertive (adj.).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: contend, maintain, declare, claim · Ant: deny, retract, concede.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Although nineteenth-century phrenologists confidently asserted that cranial bumps revealed moral character, controlled anatomical studies soon exposed their claims as baseless."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Notice how phrenologists asserted something false! Assert describes confidence of statement, NOT truth or proof.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Treating assert as a synonym of prove / substantiate. On the SAT, authors often contrast what people assert with what data actually substantiates!
  • Short Application Activity: Spot the combination: What does "an unsubstantiated assertion" mean in plain English? (A confident claim with zero solid proof behind it.)

15. conventional (adjective)

  • Simple English Definition: Following standard, traditional, widely accepted methods, practices, or beliefs.
  • Alternative Nuance: Not necessarily an insult (conventional radiography = standard X-ray technology), though SAT passages frequently contrast conventional wisdom/methods with a novel (new/innovative) approach!
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: orthodox, traditional, standard, customary · Ant: unconventional, novel, unorthodox, innovative.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Whereas conventional desalination plants rely on energy-intensive high-pressure pumps, the experimental membrane filters brackish water using passive solar evaporation."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Whereas contrasts standard existing plants (conventional) with the new experimental solar design.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing conventional ("standard/traditional") with convenient ("easy/handy")! Look at the ending: convenient = easy; conventional = traditional/standard.
  • Short Application Activity: Pick the right word: "Traditional oil paints were too slow-drying for her outdoor murals, so she rejected [convenient / conventional] pigments." (conventional).

16. disparate (adjective)

  • Simple English Definition: Essentially different in kind; markedly distinct or unrelated, making comparison or combination striking.
  • Related Word Family: disparity (n. — a significant gap or inequality, e.g., income disparity).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: distinct, divergent, dissimilar, heterogeneous · Ant: homogeneous, uniform, analogous, identical.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "To reconstruct monsoon variability across a millennium, the paleoclimate team synthesized data from disparate archives: cave stalagmites, shipwreck timbers, and imperial grain-price decrees."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Cave rocks, wooden ship hulls, and government tax laws are completely different kinds of sources (disparate archives) brought together for one study.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: #1 Lookalike Trap: Confusing disparate (DIS-puh-rit = fundamentally different) with desperate (DES-puh-rit = hopeless / frantic)! Check the second letter: d-i-s-p-a-r-a-t-e = different (like disparity).
  • Short Application Activity: Why are cave stalagmites and grain-price decrees called disparate sources? (One is geological/natural; the other is written/economic—completely different types of evidence.)

17. concede (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To admit—often reluctantly—that an opposing fact, limitation, or point is true before presenting your main argument.
  • Alternative Meanings: In elections/sports, "admit defeat"; in SAT reading/rhetoric, make a strategic partial admission (±)!
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: acknowledge, grant, admit · Ant: dispute, deny, reject outright.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Critics of high-speed rail concede that electrified trains cut per-passenger carbon emissions between dense cities, yet they contend that tunnel construction costs outweigh those gains on low-ridership routes."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Even though the speakers are critics of high-speed rail, they fairly admit (concede) one real benefit before pivoting via yet to their main objection.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Assuming that if Author X concedes Point P, then Point P is Author X's main thesis! Quite the opposite: on the SAT, what an author concedes is the other side's valid point, right before however / yet introduces the author's true thesis!
  • Short Application Activity: In "While Dr. Patel concedes X, she argues Y," is Dr. Patel's main conclusion X or Y? (Y!).

18. mitigate (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To make a harmful, painful, or severe problem milder or less damaging (without necessarily curing it 100%).
  • Related Word Family: mitigation (n. — harm reduction, e.g., flood mitigation).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: alleviate, lessen, moderate, cushion · Ant: exacerbate, aggravate, intensify.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Planting deep-rooted native sedges along urban retention basins cannot prevent extreme cloudbursts, but it substantially mitigates downstream riverbank erosion."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Notice the contrast between "cannot prevent" (0% rain control) and "substantially mitigates" (reduces the severity of erosion damage).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing mitigate ("reduce harm") with migrate ("move/travel seasonally") or thinking mitigate means "completely eradicate/abolish."
  • Short Application Activity: Which action mitigates earthquake damage rather than preventing earthquakes: predicting tectonic motion or installing flexible rubber base isolators under hospital columns? (Installing flexible base isolators—earthquakes still happen, but structural damage is reduced.)

19. ubiquitous (adjective)

  • Simple English Definition: Present, appearing, or encountered seemingly everywhere at the same time; pervasive.
  • Related Word Family: ubiquity (n. — widespread presence everywhere).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: pervasive, omnipresent, universal, commonplace · Ant: rare, scarce, isolated, localized.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Once a rare laboratory curiosity costing more than gold per gram, aluminum became ubiquitous in household cookware and aircraft frames after the Hall–Héroult smelting process slashed production costs in 1886."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: "Once a rare laboratory curiosity" sets up a direct historical contrast with becoming found everywhere in daily life (ubiquitous).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing ubiquitous ("found everywhere") with ambiguous ("having two unclear meanings") because both end in -iguous / -iquitous!
  • Short Application Activity: Contrast check: ambiguous = unclear meaning; ubiquitous = __________. (found everywhere).

20. conversely (adverb — logical transition)

  • Simple English Definition: Introducing a statement or idea that reverses the relationship, direction, or condition just stated ("in the opposite direction / on the flip side").
  • Precision Nuance for SAT Transitions: Unlike nevertheless / notwithstanding (which mean "despite X, unexpected Y still happened"), conversely presents a symmetrical mirror-image flip (When A rises, B falls; conversely, when A falls, B rises).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: on the other hand, in contrast, inversely · Ant: similarly, likewise, correspondingly.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "During El Niño years, warm surface waters shift eastward and suppress upwelling off Peru; conversely, La Niña strengthens trade winds and intensifies cold, nutrient-rich coastal upwelling."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: El Niño weakens cold upwelling; La Niña does the exact mirror-image opposite (conversely), strengthening cold upwelling.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Using conversely whenever any surprise happens (confusing it with nevertheless). Remember: nevertheless = concession ("despite obstacle X"); conversely = opposite case ("meanwhile, in the reverse case").
  • Short Application Activity: Choose Nevertheless or Conversely: "High-salt marshes stunt inland willow seedlings; ______, halophytic cordgrass thrives in those same saline tides." (Conversely — opposite response of two species to the same condition).
