subSections.html:
Exercise 4C-1: Original SAT-Style Words in Context Multiple Choice (Blending Day 1 & Day 2 Words)

VOC-D2-Q1 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Easy]
Once restricted to specialized oceanographic vessels, autonomous acoustic gliders have become nearly ______ in coastal monitoring programs as miniature lithium batteries and open-source navigation sensors have lowered unit costs tenfold.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) ambiguous
B) ubiquitous
C) tentative
D) disparate

VOC-D2-Q2 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Medium]
To test whether ancient Roman marine concrete owed its remarkable durability to volcanic ash reactions, materials scientists ______ thin mineral slices from two-thousand-year-old harbor pilings using synchrotron X-ray diffraction to map every microscopic crystal boundary.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) mitigated
B) conceded
C) scrutinized
D) asserted

VOC-D2-Q3 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Medium]
Advocates of congestion pricing ______ that tolling downtown arterial roads can burden night-shift hospital workers who lack late-hour rail options, but they note that dedicating ten percent of toll revenue to twenty-four-hour express buses offsets that inequity.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) concede
B) bolster
C) substantiate
D) undermine

VOC-D2-Q4 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Hard]
What makes the ethnomusicologist's monograph so ______ is her synthesis of seemingly ______ forms of evidence: she pairs spectrographic pitch measurements of bamboo flutes with seventeenth-century court tax ledgers and oral harvest ballads to trace one coherent migration history. (Select the pair that best completes BOTH blanks in order!)
A) tentative ... conventional
B) compelling ... disparate
C) ambiguous ... ubiquitous
D) conventional ... nuanced

VOC-D2-Q5 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Hard]
While permeable street pavements cannot eliminate flash flooding when a tropical cyclone stalls over a coastal basin, civil engineers have found that porous asphalt layers significantly ______ peak storm-sewer overflow during routine summer thunderstorms.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) corroborate
B) assert
C) reconcile
D) mitigate

Exercise 4C-2: Context-Clue Signal & Polarity/Function Mapping

For each sentence (VOC-D2-Q6 to VOC-D2-Q10), identify (i) the exact structural clue word/punctuation, and (ii) how the bracketed word functions (Strengthens [+], Admits Opposite Point [±], Reduces Harm [-], Flips Case [↔], or Traditional Baseline [0]):

  • VOC-D2-Q6: "Whereas [conventional] seismic sensors require dedicated burial vaults, existing undersea fiber-optic telecom cables can detect seafloor tremors using laser interferometry."
  • VOC-D2-Q7: "Independent pollen cores from three crater lakes [bolstered] the archaeologist's timeline: each core showed maize pollen appearing centuries before stone terraces were built."
  • VOC-D2-Q8: *"In high-latitude boreal forests, darker tree canopies absorb winter sunlight over snow and warm local air; [conversely], tropical forests cool the land surface year-round via intense evapotranspiration."*
  • VOC-D2-Q9: "Although the defense attorney [asserted] that the ledger entry was forged later, forensic ink dating matched every surrounding page from 1894."
  • VOC-D2-Q10: "Reflective white roof coatings [mitigate] indoor heat stress in top-floor apartments during July heatwaves, even if they cannot replace full wall insulation."

Exercise 4C-3: Academic Sentence Completion

Complete each sentence (VOC-D2-Q11 to VOC-D2-Q15) using one word from Day 2's list (bolster, scrutinize, compelling, assert, conventional, disparate, concede, mitigate, ubiquitous, conversely — adjust verb tense if needed):

  • VOC-D2-Q11: Because smartphone cameras are now ______ among hikers, citizen-science apps receive thousands of timestamped wildflower photographs every spring.
  • VOC-D2-Q12: Auditors were hired to ______ every invoice exceeding ten thousand dollars after discrepancies surfaced in the construction budget.
  • VOC-D2-Q13: Merging two ______ fields—quantum optics and avian neurobiology—enabled researchers to test how migratory robins sense weak magnetic fields.
  • VOC-D2-Q14: Even skeptics of the asteroid-impact hypothesis found the global iridium spike at the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary a ______ piece of physical evidence.
  • VOC-D2-Q15: Newly discovered shipyard payrolls ______ Dr. Sato's thesis that skilled women caulkers worked alongside men in seventeenth-century Venetian arsenals.

Exercise 4C-4: Lookalike & Close-Synonym Trap Discrimination

Choose the exact word (VOC-D2-Q16 to VOC-D2-Q19) and explain in 5–10 words why the trap choice fails:

  • VOC-D2-Q16 (disparate vs. desperate): "The anthology brings together ______ literary forms—epistolary fragments, shipping manifests, and classical ghazals—under a single theme of maritime exile."
  • VOC-D2-Q17 (conventional vs. convenient): "Rejecting ______ linear chronology, the novelist narrates the family's history backward from 1998 to 1921."
  • VOC-D2-Q18 (assert vs. substantiate): "Anyone can ______ that a supplement improves memory, but controlled double-blind trials are required to prove the effect."
  • VOC-D2-Q19 (conversely vs. notwithstanding): "Severe drought conditions ______, deep-taproot alfalfa plots maintained eighty percent of their normal summer biomass."

Exercise 4C-5: Short Academic Synthesis Passage (Recycling Day 1 + Day 2 Vocabulary)

Read the 120-word passage below without translating, then answer VOC-D2-Q20 to VOC-D2-Q22:

Conventional accounts of medieval European book production portray monastic scriptoria as self-contained workshops isolated from urban commerce. Archival guild contracts from fourteenth-century Bologna and Paris undermine that portrait, offering compelling evidence that secular stationers coordinated disparate craft specialists—parchment makers, quill cutters, illuminators, and bookbinders—across busy university districts. Even historians who concede that rural monasteries copied liturgical texts independently now recognize that urban scholarly publishing relied on commercial division of labor. The survival of only fragmentary workshop ledgers notwithstanding, surviving tax rolls corroborate university statutes regulating piecework copying fees, allowing economic historians to reconcile rapid textbook proliferation before movable type with Europe's still-handwritten book technology.

  • VOC-D2-Q20: Map the contrast between conventional accounts (Sentence 1) and what 14th-century guild contracts show (Sentence 2). Why are the craft specialists called disparate?
  • VOC-D2-Q21: In Sentence 3, what point do historians concede, and why does that concession make their main conclusion about urban publishing nuanced rather than extreme?
  • VOC-D2-Q22: In the final sentence, explain how notwithstanding, corroborate, and reconcile interact logically.

Exercise 4C-6: Closed-Notes Rapid Retrieval Quiz on Day 2 Words

Cover Section 4B completely! Write a 3–6 word simple English meaning for each Day 2 item (VOC-D2-Q23 to VOC-D2-Q32):

  • VOC-D2-Q23: bolster → __________________
  • VOC-D2-Q24: disparate → __________________
  • VOC-D2-Q25: concede → __________________
  • VOC-D2-Q26: mitigate → __________________
  • VOC-D2-Q27: scrutinize → __________________
  • VOC-D2-Q28: ubiquitous → __________________
  • VOC-D2-Q29: assert → __________________
  • VOC-D2-Q30: conventional → __________________
  • VOC-D2-Q31: compelling → __________________
  • VOC-D2-Q32: conversely → __________________

vocabulary.answerKeyHtml:
Section 4A: Day 1 Spaced Retrieval Warm-Up (SR-D2-Q1 to SR-D2-Q10)

  • SR-D2-Q1: reconcile
  • SR-D2-Q2: notwithstanding
  • SR-D2-Q3: tentative (tiny 9-shard sample = provisional/cautious)
  • SR-D2-Q4: undermine (weaken reliability)
  • SR-D2-Q5: nuanced
  • SR-D2-Q6: Corroborate = confirm with independent evidence; collaborate = work together as partners.
  • SR-D2-Q7: ambiguous (open to two opposing interpretations)
  • SR-D2-Q8: Substantiate = prove with evidence (verb); substantial = large in size/amount (adjective).
  • SR-D2-Q9: plausible
  • SR-D2-Q10: infer

Section 4C: Day 2 Vocabulary Exercises (VOC-D2-Q1 to VOC-D2-Q32)

  • VOC-D2-Q1 → Correct: B (ubiquitous)

    • Why B works: "Once restricted to specialized... vessels" contrasts with tenfold cost drops making gliders found nearly everywhere (ubiquitous).
    • Why others fail: A (ambiguous) = unclear; C (tentative) = provisional; D (disparate) = fundamentally different in kind.

  • VOC-D2-Q2 → Correct: C (scrutinized)

    • Why C works: Mapping "every microscopic crystal boundary" with synchrotron X-ray diffraction describes close, thorough critical examination (scrutinized).
    • Why others fail: A (mitigated) = reduced harm; B (conceded) = reluctantly admitted; D (asserted) = claimed (you cannot "assert mineral slices"!).

  • VOC-D2-Q3 → Correct: A (concede)

    • Why A works: Advocates of congestion pricing fairly admit (concede) a valid criticism (tolls burden night-shift workers) before but introduces their policy fix (24-hour express buses).
    • Why others fail: B (bolster) & C (substantiate) = strengthen/prove (advocates wouldn't try to strengthen an argument against their own policy); D (undermine) = weaken (grammatically and logically wrong here).

  • VOC-D2-Q4 → Correct: B (compelling ... disparate)

    • Why B works: Blank 1 praises a unified migration history (compelling = powerfully convincing); Blank 2 after the colon describes flute acoustics, 17th-century tax ledgers, and oral ballads—three fundamentally different (disparate) types of evidence!
    • Why others fail: A calls strong synthesis tentative and unusual mixed sources conventional; C calls praise ambiguous; D calls praise conventional ("ordinary").

  • VOC-D2-Q5 → Correct: D (mitigate)

    • Why D works: While... cannot eliminate [100% cure] contrasts directly with significantly reducing the severity of (mitigate) routine sewer overflow.
    • Why others fail: A (corroborate) = confirm; B (assert) = claim; C (reconcile) = harmonize two conflicting things.

  • Exercise 4C-2 (VOC-D2-Q6–Q10):

    • VOC-D2-Q6: Signal = Whereas; Function = Traditional Baseline ([0]) contrasted against new fiber-optic method.
    • VOC-D2-Q7: Signal = Colon (:) + Independent... cores; Function = Strengthens ([+]).
    • VOC-D2-Q8: Signal = ; conversely, (warming in boreal vs. cooling in tropical); Function = Flips Case ([↔]).
    • VOC-D2-Q9: Signal = Although + forensic counter-proof; Function = Unproven Claim contrasted with evidence.
    • VOC-D2-Q10: Signal = even if they cannot replace...; Function = Reduces Harm ([-]).

  • Exercise 4C-3 (VOC-D2-Q11–Q15):

    • VOC-D2-Q11: ubiquitous
    • VOC-D2-Q12: scrutinize
    • VOC-D2-Q13: disparate
    • VOC-D2-Q14: compelling
    • VOC-D2-Q15: bolstered *(or bolster)*

  • Exercise 4C-4 (VOC-D2-Q16–Q19):

    • VOC-D2-Q16: disparate (distinct genres; desperate means hopeless/frantic).
    • VOC-D2-Q17: conventional (traditional linear order; convenient means easy/handy).
    • VOC-D2-Q18: assert (claim without proof; contrasted directly with "trials are required to prove").
    • VOC-D2-Q19: notwithstanding (post-positioned "Despite severe drought"; conversely cannot follow a noun phrase like a preposition!).

  • Exercise 4C-5 (VOC-D2-Q20–Q22):

    • VOC-D2-Q20: Conventional accounts claimed monasteries worked alone in isolation; guild contracts prove secular urban shops coordinated commercial book production. The specialists are disparate because animal-skin preparation, feather cutting, gold-leaf painting, and leather binding are distinct crafts.
    • VOC-D2-Q21: Historians concede that rural monasteries still copied religious texts on their own—making the thesis nuanced because it distinguishes urban university textbooks from rural religious copying instead of overclaiming that monasteries did zero copying.
    • VOC-D2-Q22: Notwithstanding signals that despite incomplete workshop ledgers, tax rolls corroborate (independently confirm) university fee statutes, enabling scholars to reconcile (resolve the apparent contradiction between) fast book growth and slow handwriting.

  • Exercise 4C-6 (VOC-D2-Q23–Q32 Rapid Retrieval Key):

    • VOC-D2-Q23 (bolster): Strengthen or reinforce with support.
    • VOC-D2-Q24 (disparate): Fundamentally different in kind.
    • VOC-D2-Q25 (concede): Admit reluctantly that an opposing point is true.
    • VOC-D2-Q26 (mitigate): Make a harmful problem less severe.
    • VOC-D2-Q27 (scrutinize): Examine closely and critically in detail.
    • VOC-D2-Q28 (ubiquitous): Present or found seemingly everywhere.
    • VOC-D2-Q29 (assert): State a claim firmly and confidently.
    • VOC-D2-Q30 (conventional): Standard, traditional, widely accepted.
    • VOC-D2-Q31 (compelling): Powerfully convincing and persuasive.
    • VOC-D2-Q32 (conversely): In the opposite direction / reverse case.

rwPractice.introHtml:
Explicit Origin Notice: All 20 questions below (RW-D2-Q1 through RW-D2-Q20) are original SAT-style practice questions (Q1–Q7: Boundaries; Q8–Q14: Form, Structure, and Sense; Q15–Q20: Words in Context).
Timed Mastery Target: Set a strict countdown timer for 18 minutes (~45 sec/Q on Q1–Q14 Grammar; ~65 sec/Q on Q15–Q20 Words in Context). Do not view Section 8 until all 20 answers are recorded.

questions.stemHtml:
To survive prolonged winter darkness above the Arctic Circle, Svalbard reindeer rely on two specialized physiological ______ tapetum lucidum eye tissue that shifts to deep blue to capture dim twilight and an expanded gut microbiome capable of digesting tough tundra moss.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: adaptations
adaptations;
adaptations:
adaptations, and

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Left of the blank is a complete IC (...Svalbard reindeer rely on two specialized physiological adaptations). Right of the blank is a noun-phrase pair specifying those two adaptations (tapetum lucidum eye tissue... and an expanded gut microbiome...). Complete IC : Specific Noun-Phrase List = Colon (:).
  • Why others fail: A fuses the list directly onto adaptations with zero boundary; B (;) fails because the right side lacks a main finite verb (shifts and capable sit inside modifiers); D (, and) turns "two... adaptations" into Item 1 of a nonsensical list.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Colon after complete IC.
  • Next-Time Clue: Spot "two [plural noun]: [Noun Phrase 1] and [Noun Phrase 2]" immediately!

questions.stemHtml:
Brass astrolabes fabricated in tenth-century Córdoba enabled astronomers and navigators to perform rapid celestial calculations, ______ determining local prayer times, measuring mountain elevations by shadow triangulation, and forecasting sunrise azimuths across latitudes.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: including:
including
including;
including—

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: The comma before the blank (calculations, ) already sets off the non-essential supplement including determining..., measuring..., and forecasting.... Adding zero punctuation after including preserves smooth syntax inside the preposition/participle phrase.
  • Why others fail: A (including:), C (including;), and D (including—) all illegally sever including from its own objects!
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — No colon/semicolon/dash after including / such as.
  • Next-Time Clue: Never put :, ;, or — immediately after including, such as, or for example!

questions.stemHtml:
In 2009, American political economist ______ became the first woman awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for demonstrating how local communities sustainably govern shared fisheries and irrigation canals without top-down privatization.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: Elinor Ostrom,
, Elinor Ostrom,
Elinor Ostrom—
Elinor Ostrom

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why D works: American political economist lacks an article (an or the), functioning as a restrictive title directly introducing Elinor Ostrom. Together they form one unified subject before became.
  • Why others fail: A places a single comma between subject and verb (Ostrom, became — always wrong!); B treats Elinor Ostrom as removable, leaving the broken fragment "In 2009, American political economist became..."; C opens an unpaired dash.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Essential/Restrictive Name Identifier (zero commas).
  • Next-Time Clue: Delete the name! If "In 2009, American political economist became..." sounds broken without an, use zero commas!

questions.stemHtml:
Mycorrhizal fungal networks—microscopic root filaments that exchange soil phosphorus for host-tree ______ connect dozens of individual Douglas firs across a single old-growth forest stand.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: sugars,
sugars—
sugars;
sugars

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: Look back at Mycorrhizal fungal networks—microscopic root filaments...: an interrupting non-essential definition opened with an em-dash (—), so it must close with a matching em-dash (sugars—) right before the main verb connect!
  • Why others fail: A (,) mismatches — ... , (always illegal on the SAT!); C (;) and D (no punctuation) fail to close the interrupting dash phrase, leaving networks stranded without its verb connect.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Paired Em-Dash Symmetry (— ... —).
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever choices include an em-dash (—), scan 10 words to the left to see if a first — already opened a pair!

questions.stemHtml:
Although synthetic indigo dye largely displaced plant-derived indigo across European textile mills by 1905, artisans in Tokushima, Japan, preserved natural sukumo fermentation ______ contemporary denim workshops still prize the botanical pigment for its subtle tonal depth.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: vats,
vats; and
vats;
vats

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Break the sentence into its three clauses:
    1. Although synthetic indigo dye... by 1905, (Dependent Clause — closed by the comma after 1905!)
    2. artisans in Tokushima, Japan, preserved natural sukumo fermentation vats (Independent Clause 1!)
    3. contemporary denim workshops still prize the botanical pigment... (Independent Clause 2!) Joining IC_1 and IC_2 with no FANBOYS conjunction requires a semicolon (vats;)!
  • Why others fail: A (vats,) is a comma splice tricked by the early Although; B (vats; and) misuses ; before coordinating and; D (vats) is a fused run-on.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — DC , IC_1 ; IC_2 structure.
  • Next-Time Clue: Don't let an opening Although fool you! Once you pass the comma + IC_1, a second IC_2 still needs a semicolon or period!

questions.stemHtml:
Economic historians tracing fourteenth-century Mediterranean silk tariffs consulted archival registries in Genoa, Italy, where private merchant banks recorded marine insurance; Ragusa, Croatia, where municipal scribes logged overland caravan ______ and Alexandria, Egypt, where Mamluk customs officials weighed imported spice bales.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: tolls,
tolls:
tolls;
tolls—

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Three complex city items each contain internal commas (Genoa, Italy, where...; | Ragusa, Croatia, where...; | and Alexandria, Egypt, where...). Notice the semicolon already printed after insurance;—parallel list boundaries demand tolls; before and Alexandria!
  • Why others fail: A (,) blurs main list items with internal City, Country commas; B (:) and D (—) break parallel semicolon structure.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Super-Semicolons in Complex Serial Lists.
  • Next-Time Clue: Spot an earlier semicolon inside a list (insurance; Ragusa, Croatia,) → match it with ; before and [Item 3]!

questions.stemHtml:
High-altitude Andean condors rarely flap their wings once morning thermal updrafts ______ gliding over one hundred miles along steep cordillera ridges while expending scarcely more metabolic energy than perching birds.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: form. Instead
form; instead
form, instead
form; and instead

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Left side = complete IC (High-altitude Andean condors rarely flap their wings once morning thermal updrafts form). Right side = instead gliding over one hundred miles... — gliding is an -ing participle, NOT a finite verb! Thus the right side is a supplemental modifier, attached with a comma (form, instead).
  • Why others fail: A (. Instead), B (; instead), and D (; and instead) all strand Instead gliding... as a sentence fragment after a hard stop! (Bonus: A and B are period/semicolon twins—instant double elimination!)
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Participial Modifier vs. Independent Clause.
  • Next-Time Clue: Check the verb after instead! instead glided = IC (needs ;); instead gliding = participle (needs ,)!

questions.stemHtml:
Constructed from interlocking hinoki-cypress beams without iron nails, the seventh-century five-story pagoda at Hōryū-ji Temple, which has withstood dozens of severe earthquakes over fourteen centuries, ______ how flexible timber joinery dissipates seismic wave energy.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: demonstrating
to demonstrate
having demonstrated
demonstrates

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why D works: Bracket modifiers: [Constructed from... nails,] the seventh-century five-story pagoda [at Hōryū-ji Temple,] [which has withstood... centuries,] _____. Singular subject pagoda needs finite main verb demonstrates.
  • Why others fail: A (demonstrating), B (to demonstrate), and C (having demonstrated) are all non-finite verbals that create a 38-word fragment with zero main verb!
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Finite Main Verb Requirement.
  • Next-Time Clue: Three non-finite forms (-ing, to + verb, having + participle) vs. one finite tense verb (demonstrates) almost always tests sentence completeness!

questions.stemHtml:
Cataloged inside the sunken Late Bronze Age merchant hull excavated off Uluburun ______ ten tons of Cypriot copper ingots, Baltic amber beads, and carved hippopotamus-ivory lute fragments.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: was
has been
is
were

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why D works: Inverted passive participle opening! Flip it into normal order: Ten tons of Cypriot copper ingots, Baltic amber beads, and carved hippopotamus-ivory lute fragments were cataloged inside the sunken... hull. Plural subject ten tons... takes plural were.
  • Why others fail: A (was), B (has been), and C (is) are all singular verbs lured by singular hull or Uluburun right before the blank!
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Inverted Subject-Verb Agreement.
  • Next-Time Clue: Sentence opens with -ed / prepositional phrase before the verb + 3 singular choices (was/has been/is) vs. 1 plural (were)? Look after the blank for the true plural subject!

questions.stemHtml:
When British crystallographer Dorothy Hodgkin published the complete three-dimensional atomic structure of vitamin B12​ in 1955, organic chemists ______ for nearly a decade to determine the molecule's intricate corrin-ring arrangement using classical chemical degradation alone.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: struggle
have struggled
will struggle
had been struggling

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why D works: Past time anchor = When... Hodgkin published... in 1955 + duration prior to that past moment = for nearly a decade. An ongoing struggle before a 1955 milestone requires past perfect progressive had been struggling.
  • Why others fail: A (struggle) = present; B (have struggled) links to today rather than ending in 1955; C (will struggle) = future.
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Past-Before-Past Tense Sequence.
  • Next-Time Clue: "When X happened in [past year], scientists _____ for a decade" → had + participle / had been -ing.

questions.stemHtml:
Synchronizing atomic clocks aboard twenty-four orbiting navigation satellites with terrestrial master stations ______ continuous relativistic adjustments because weaker gravitational pull in medium Earth orbit causes satellite clocks to tick microseconds faster per day than clocks at sea level.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: require
requires
have required
are requiring

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: Strip objects and prepositions: Synchronizing [atomic clocks aboard twenty-four orbiting navigation satellites with terrestrial master stations] requires... A gerund (-ing activity) subject is always singular!
  • Why others fail: A (require), C (have required), and D (are requiring) are all plural verbs fooled by clocks, satellites, and stations.
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Singular Gerund Subject Agreement.
  • Next-Time Clue: Sentence begins with [Verb]-ing [plural nouns] without a comma? That -ing word is your singular subject!

questions.stemHtml:
Unlike territorial songbirds that learn courtship melodies almost exclusively from conspecific males, female superb lyrebirds defend solo foraging territories and mimic dozens of neighboring ______ with astonishing acoustic accuracy.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: bird's alarm calls
birds' alarm calls
birds' alarm call's
birds alarm calls'

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works:
    1. "dozens of neighboring..." requires plural birds, and those birds possess the alarm calls ⟹ plural possessive birds'.
    2. "alarm calls" is followed immediately by preposition "with" (owns nothing!) ⟹ plain plural calls (zero apostrophe).
  • Why others fail: A (bird's) is singular after "dozens of"; C (call's) and D (calls') put illegal apostrophes before "with".
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Plural vs. Possessive Apostrophes.
  • Next-Time Clue: Preposition (with, of, in, for) right after the blank? The final word cannot have an apostrophe!

questions.stemHtml:
Synthesized from agricultural oat-hull cellulose rather than petrochemical feedstocks, ______

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.raw: materials engineers formulated the biodegradable barrier film to decompose rapidly in municipal compost facilities.
choices.html: materials engineers formulated the biodegradable barrier film to decompose rapidly in municipal compost facilities.

choices.raw: the biodegradable barrier film formulated by materials engineers decomposes rapidly in municipal compost facilities.
choices.html: the biodegradable barrier film formulated by materials engineers decomposes rapidly in municipal compost facilities.

choices.raw: municipal compost facilities break down the biodegradable barrier film within ten weeks.
choices.html: municipal compost facilities break down the biodegradable barrier film within ten weeks.

choices.raw: oxygen permeability in the biodegradable barrier film matched conventional polyethylene wraps.
choices.html: oxygen permeability in the biodegradable barrier film matched conventional polyethylene wraps.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: Ask: *What was "Synthesized from agricultural oat-hull cellulose"?* Only the biodegradable barrier film! Placing the biodegradable barrier film immediately after the comma makes the modifier logical and accurate.
  • Why others fail: A claims materials engineers were synthesized from oat-hull cellulose (!); C claims municipal compost facilities were synthesized from cellulose; D claims oxygen permeability (an abstract measurement) was synthesized from cellulose.
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Introductory Participial Modifier Placement.
  • Next-Time Clue: Don't blindly pick a human noun! Read the participle carefully: people calibrate lasers (Day 1 Q15), whereas films/compounds are synthesized from cellulose (Day 2 Q13)!

questions.stemHtml:
Acoustic measurements conducted inside sixteenth-century Ottoman mosques designed by Mimar Sinan reveal that the reverberation times of Sinan's domed prayer halls are significantly more uniform across human speech frequencies than ______ contemporary European stone cathedrals of comparable interior volume.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: contemporary European stone cathedrals

choices.raw: that of contemporary European stone cathedrals
choices.html: that of contemporary European stone cathedrals

choices.raw: those of contemporary European stone cathedrals
choices.html: those of contemporary European stone cathedrals
in contemporary European stone cathedrals'

questions.answerHeadlineHtml: Correct Answer: C (those of contemporary European stone cathedrals)
questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Subject of comparison = plural the reverberation times (of Sinan's prayer halls). You must compare reverberation times to reverberation times (those of contemporary European stone cathedrals), never directly to stone buildings!
  • Why others fail: A illogically compares reverberation times (seconds) to cathedrals (buildings); B (that of) is singular, clashing with plural times; D (in ... cathedrals') breaks parallel syntax and leaves a dangling possessive.
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Parallel Logical Comparisons (those of vs. that of).
  • Next-Time Clue: Spot more [adj] than or exceeds: check whether the subject noun before the verb is singular (that of) or plural (those of)!

questions.stemHtml:
By deploying curtains of rising air bubbles around offshore wind-turbine foundations during pile-driving operations, marine acoustic engineers can substantially ______ underwater sound pressure levels that would otherwise impair harbor porpoise echolocation.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: mitigate
bolster
scrutinize
assert

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why A works: Bubble curtains reduce the harmful intensity of (mitigate) underwater pile-driving noise so porpoise sonar isn't damaged.
  • Why others fail: B (bolster) = strengthen/increase noise (harms porpoises!); C (scrutinize) = inspect closely; D (assert) = state confidently.
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Harm-reduction verb.
  • Next-Time Clue: Protective engineering + "noise/damage that would otherwise impair..." → mitigate / attenuate / curtail.

questions.stemHtml:
Rather than dismissing ancient oral epics as purely mythical inventions, classical topographers ______ Linear B palace tablet inventories alongside Homeric geographic epithets, checking each bronze-age harbor description detail by detail against sediment core maps.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: conceded
mitigated
scrutinized
undermined

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: The participial phrase at the end defines the blank: "checking each bronze-age harbor description detail by detail against sediment core maps" = scrutinized.
  • Why others fail: A (conceded) = admitted reluctantly; B (mitigated) = lessened harm; D (undermined) = weakened (contradicts "Rather than dismissing...").
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Trailing participial definition clue.
  • Next-Time Clue: A comma + -ing explanation at the end of a sentence often restates the exact verb in the blank!

questions.stemHtml:
Mechanical vapor-compression refrigerators were still rare, expensive curiosities in 1915, yet within three decades electric cold storage had become ______ in urban apartments, transforming daily dairy distribution and household meal planning.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: tentative
ubiquitous
ambiguous
disparate

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why B works: yet contrasts "rare, expensive curiosities in 1915" with becoming commonplace everywhere (ubiquitous) across urban apartments within 30 years.
  • Why others fail: A (tentative) = provisional; C (ambiguous) = unclear; D (disparate) = essentially different.
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Historical rare → widespread contrast.
  • Next-Time Clue: "still rare in [Year 1], yet within decades became _____" → ubiquitous / commonplace / pervasive.

questions.stemHtml:
In healthy kelp forest ecosystems along the northern Pacific coast, predation by sea otters helps ______ purple sea urchin populations; in coastal zones where sea otters were extirpated, unchecked urchin grazing has stripped vast kelp beds down to bare rock.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: substantiate
amplify
check
foster

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why C works: Look at the second clause after the semicolon: where otters vanished, unchecked urchin grazing destroyed kelp! Here check carries its classic SAT secondary verb meaning: to restrain, hold back, or limit population growth.
  • Why others fail: A (substantiate) = prove; B (amplify) and D (foster) = increase/encourage urchin numbers (the exact opposite of predation!).
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Polysemy (V2) secondary meaning of check (= restrain/curb).
  • Next-Time Clue: Add check (v.) = restrain / hold back right alongside Day 1's qualify (v.) = limit a claim on your Top Polysemy Alert list!

questions.stemHtml:
Even biogeographers who ______ that cyclonic winds occasionally carry lightweight fern spores across the Tasman Sea contend that wind transport alone cannot account for the shared presence of flightless soil beetles and salt-intolerant southern beech trees on both landmasses.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: concede
refute
bolster
reconcile

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why A works: "Even biogeographers who [grant minor point X: wind carries light spores] contend that [main thesis Y: wind cannot carry flightless beetles or salt-sensitive trees]" is the textbook SAT concession (concede) pattern!
  • Why others fail: B (refute) breaks "Even... contend" logic (if they refuted wind dispersal of spores too, there would be no "Even" contrast!); C (bolster) = strengthen; D (reconcile) requires reconcile A with B.
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Academic concession syntax (Even scholars who concede X contend Y).
  • Next-Time Clue: "Even [experts] who _____ that [Point 1] maintain/contend that [Point 2]" → concede / acknowledge / grant!

questions.stemHtml:
Although mid-twentieth-century pioneers of machine translation hoped a single formal rulebook could map every human language onto one universal template, typological fieldwork soon demonstrated how ______ grammatical architectures—from polysynthetic Inuktitut verbs to tonal analytic Mandarin clauses—defied any uniform mechanical schema.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: plausible
conventional
corroborated
disparate

questions.explanationHtml:
• Why D works: Although contrasts early hopes for "one universal template / uniform mechanical schema" against radically different, structurally distinct (disparate) languages like polysynthetic Inuktitut and tonal analytic Mandarin.
  • Why others fail: A (plausible) = believable; B (conventional) = traditional (traditional architectures wouldn't inherently defy uniformity—their extreme difference did!); C (corroborated) = confirmed.
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Contrast with single / universal / uniform.
  • Next-Time Clue: Contrast against uniform, homogeneous, single template → disparate / divergent / heterogeneous.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.4: Priority Algebra Mastery I — Linear Equations, Functions, Parallel/Perpendicular Lines & Two-Variable Systems
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 2.4: Priority Algebra Mastery I — Linear Equations, Functions, Parallel/Perpendicular Lines & Two-Variable Systems
lessons.html:
Algebra accounts for ~35% of the entire Digital SAT Math section (13–15 questions per test). Moving from 640 to 700–750+ requires 100% precision on every linear disguise College Board uses:

A. Number of Solutions in a One-Variable Linear Equation (Ax+B=Cx+D)

Collect all x-terms on the left and constants on the right, or compare sides directly:

  1. Exactly One Solution: A=C (e.g., 5x−3=2x+9⟹x=4).
  2. No Solution: Same x-coefficient, DIFFERENT constant (A=C and B=D, e.g., 4x−6=4x+5⟹−6=5, impossible!).
  3. Infinitely Many Solutions: IDENTICAL x-coefficient AND IDENTICAL constant (A=C and B=D, e.g., 12x−20=12x−20, true for every real number x!).

B. Standard Form Term-by-Term Interpretation (Ax+By=C)

International students frequently confuse the rate (A) with the sub-total product (Ax)! Memorize this exact 3-layer anatomy for 0.8b+2.5p=60:

  • p = count of items of type 2 (e.g., number of large platters).
  • 2.5 = unit rate per 1 item of type 2 (e.g., kilograms of clay per one platter).
  • 2.5p = total amount contributed by all p items (e.g., total kilograms of clay used for all p platters).
  • 60 = combined grand total across both item types.

C. Linear Function Shortcuts, Translations & Perpendicular Slopes

  • Equal-Step Table Shortcut: If f(x) is linear and x jumps by equal steps (2→6→10, step +4), then f(x) must jump by equal steps too! You don't even need to find b: if f(2)=11 and f(6)=29 (Δy=+18), then f(10)=29+18=47 in 4 seconds!
  • Vertical & Horizontal Graph Shifts:
    • Translating y=f(x) up k units gives g(x)=f(x)+k (adds k to the y-intercept; changes the x-intercept!).
    • Translating y=f(x) right h units gives g(x)=f(x−h).
  • Parallel vs. Perpendicular Slopes:
    • Parallel lines (or no-solution systems): m2​=m1​.
    • Perpendicular lines (meet at 90∘): Negative reciprocal slope! Flip the fraction AND flip the sign:
      m1​=−43​⟹m⊥​=+34​
  • Stacked Combination Shortcut for Systems: Whenever an SAT system asks for x+y, x−y, or 3x+3y rather than x alone, add or subtract the two stacked equations for 3 seconds first before substituting!

Worked Example 2.4 (Perpendicular Line + Point-Slope Speed)

Problem: Line p has equation 2x−5y=10. Line q is perpendicular to line p and passes through (4,−3). What is the y-intercept of line q?

  • Step 1: Slope of 2x−5y=10 is mp​=−BA​=−−52​=52​.
  • Step 2: Perpendicular slope is mq​=−25​.
  • Step 3: Use point-slope with (4,−3): y−(−3)=−25​(x−4)⟹y+3=−25​x+10⟹y=−25​x+7. Thus the y-intercept is (0,7). (Verify in Desmos by graphing both lines and checking (4, -3)!)

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 2.4

  • CC-D2-M1: For what values of a and b does 3(2x−4)=ax+b have infinitely many solutions? What if it has no solution?
  • CC-D2-M2: In 12c+18t=540, representing 540 seats across c vans (12 seats each) and t buses (18 seats each), what does the term 18t represent?
  • CC-D2-M3: Line k is perpendicular to y=−4x+9. What is the slope of line k?
  • CC-D2-M4: Given 7x+2y=29 and 3x+8y=41, find x+y in one addition step without solving for x or y!

B. Standard Form Term-by-Term Interpretation (Ax+By=C)
C. Linear Function Shortcuts, Translations & Perpendicular Slopes
Worked Example 2.4 (Perpendicular Line + Point-Slope Speed)
Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 2.4

checks.promptHtml: For what values of a and b does 3(2x−4)=ax+b have infinitely many solutions? What if it has no solution?
checks.answerHtml: Expand LHS: 6x−12=ax+b. Infinitely many solutions: a=6 AND b=−12. No solution: a=6 AND b=−12 (any constant except −12).

checks.promptHtml: In 12c+18t=540, representing 540 seats across c vans (12 seats each) and t buses (18 seats each), what does the term 18t represent?
checks.answerHtml: The total number of seats across all t buses (NOT 18 seats per bus, and NOT t buses!).

checks.promptHtml: Line k is perpendicular to y=−4x+9. What is the slope of line k?
checks.answerHtml: Negative reciprocal of −4=−14​ is +41​ (0.25).

checks.promptHtml: Given 7x+2y=29 and 3x+8y=41, find x+y in one addition step without solving for x or y!
checks.answerHtml: Add the two equations vertically: (7x+3x)+(2y+8y)=29+41⟹10x+10y=70⟹x+y=7!

lessons.title: Lesson 2.5: Priority Algebra Mastery II — Linear Inequalities, Word Constraints & Desmos Shading
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 2.5: Priority Algebra Mastery II — Linear Inequalities, Word Constraints & Desmos Shading
lessons.html:
A. Translating English Inequality Phrases Without Traps (Crucial for International Students!)

English Phrase in SAT Word Problem Exact Symbol Watch the Boundary Case!
"at least k" / "no less than k" / "a minimum of k" ≥k k IS allowed (x=8 satisfies "at least 8").
"at most k" / "no more than k" / "cannot exceed k" ≤k k IS allowed (w≤9.58⟹maxinteger w=9).
"strictly less than k" / "fewer than k" / "cheaper than" <k k is NOT allowed! (c>76 means minimum integer is 77, NOT 76!).
"exceeds k" / "more than k" >k k is NOT allowed!

B. Two Algebraic Traps in Inequalities

  1. Negative Multiplier/Divisor Flip: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality direction (−6x≥−12⟹x≤2). Always test x=0 in the original inequality to confirm!
  2. Combining Inequalities to Maximize One Variable: If 3x+2y≤34 and x−y≥3, do not guess random pairs! Isolate x≥y+3, replace x with its minimum boundary y+3 inside 3(y+3)+2y≤34, and solve directly—or graph both inequalities in Desmos in 10 seconds!

C. Desmos Inequality Superpower

Type any system of inequalities directly into Desmos using <, >, <=, or >=:

  • Desmos automatically draws dashed boundary lines for <, > (points on the line are NOT solutions!) and solid boundary lines for <=, >= (points on the line ARE solutions!).
  • The overlapping dark-shaded region shows every valid (x,y) solution instantly—letting you see which Quadrants (I, II, III, IV) are touched and click exact corner vertices!

Worked Example 2.5 (Strict Break-Even Trap)

Problem: Plan X costs ; Plan Y costs . For what minimum whole number n is Plan Y cheaper than Plan X?

  • Solution: "Cheaper than" means strictly less (<): 160+3n<100+5n⟹60<2n⟹n>30. At n=30, both plans cost (a tie—not cheaper!). The smallest whole number >30 is 31.

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 2.5

  • CC-D2-M5: Solve 9−4(x+2)<13 for x, and verify using x=0.
  • CC-D2-M6: In Desmos, if (4,7) lies right at the intersection corner of y <= 2x - 1 (solid) and y > x + 3 (dashed), is (4,7) a valid solution to the system? Why or why not?

B. Two Algebraic Traps in Inequalities
C. Desmos Inequality Superpower
Worked Example 2.5 (Strict Break-Even Trap)
Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 2.5

checks.promptHtml: Solve 9−4(x+2)<13 for x, and verify using x=0.
checks.answerHtml: 9−4x−8<13⟹1−4x<13⟹−4x<12⟹x>−3 (flipped < to > when dividing by −4!). Test x=0: 9−4(2)=1<13 (True, confirming 0>−3 ✓).

checks.promptHtml: In Desmos, if (4,7) lies right at the intersection corner of y <= 2x - 1 (solid) and y > x + 3 (dashed), is (4,7) a valid solution to the system? Why or why not?
checks.answerHtml: NO! Even though 7≤2(4)−1=7 is true, (4,7) sits directly on the dashed line y=x+3 (7>4+3⟹7>7 is false!). A solution to a system must satisfy both inequalities.

mathPractice.introHtml:
Explicit Origin Notice: All 16 problems below (MATH-D2-Q1 through MATH-D2-Q16) are original SAT-style practice questions spanning all five Official SAT Algebra skills across Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulty (10 Multiple-Choice + 6 SPR).
Timed Mastery Target: Set a strict countdown timer for 24 minutes (~90 seconds/question). Open desmos.com/calculator alongside this workbook. Do not view Section 8 until finished!

questions.stemHtml:
43​x−7=11
What value of x satisfies the given equation?

choices.html: 6
13.5
24
32

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    43​x−7=11⟹43​x=18⟹x=18×34​=6×4=24
  • Desmos Check: Type (3/4)x - 7 = 11 → vertical line at x = 24.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: 43​(24)−7=18−7=11 ✓. Trap B (13.5) multiplies 18×43​ instead of multiplying by the reciprocal 34​; Trap A (6) subtracts 11−7=4 instead of adding 7.

questions.stemHtml: A botanical conservatory cistern holds 850 liters of collected rainwater at 6:00 AM and drains through misting nozzles at a constant rate of 18 liters per hour. Which function V models the volume of rainwater, in liters, remaining in the cistern t hours after 6:00 AM (for 0≤t≤40)?

choices.html: V(t)=18t−850
V(t)=850−18t
V(t)=850+18t
V(t)=(850−18)t

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Initial volume at t=0 is b=850 liters; "drains... at a constant rate of 18 liters per hour" means slope m=−18 L/hr ⟹V(t)=850−18t.
  • Verification & Trap Alert: Check t=1: 850−18=832 L ✓. Trap A gives negative volume at t=0; Trap C adds water instead of draining; Trap D multiplies 832t.

questions.stemHtml:
4(3x−5)=ax−20
In the given equation, a is a constant. If the equation has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of a?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Expand LHS:
    4(3x−5)=12x−20
    For 12x−20=ax−20 to have infinitely many solutions, both the x-coefficients and constants must match identically ⟹a=12.
  • Desmos Check: Graph y = 4(3x - 5) and y = ax - 20 with slider a → lines overlap completely at a = 12.

questions.stemHtml: A ceramics studio shapes small tea bowls that each require 0.8 kilograms of stoneware clay and wide serving platters that each require 2.5 kilograms of stoneware clay. The equation 0.8b+2.5p=60 represents a production batch of b tea bowls and p serving platters that uses a combined 60 kilograms of stoneware clay. Which is the best interpretation of 2.5p in this context?

choices.raw: The mass of clay, in kilograms, required to shape one serving platter
choices.html: The mass of clay, in kilograms, required to shape one serving platter

choices.raw: The total number of serving platters shaped in the batch
choices.html: The total number of serving platters shaped in the batch

choices.raw: The total mass of clay, in kilograms, used to shape all $p$ serving platters
choices.html: The total mass of clay, in kilograms, used to shape all p serving platters

choices.raw: The maximum number of serving platters that can be shaped from $60$ kilograms of clay
choices.html: The maximum number of serving platters that can be shaped from 60 kilograms of clay

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Break down 0.8b+2.5p=60:
    • 2.5 = kilograms of clay per one serving platter (Trap A).
    • p = number of serving platters (Trap B).
    • (2.5 kg/platter)×(p platters)=2.5p = total mass of clay, in kilograms, used to shape all p serving platters (C)!
  • Trap Alert: Trap D describes the p-intercept 2.560​=24 when b=0, not the expression 2.5p.

questions.stemHtml: For the linear function f, f(2)=11 and f(6)=29. What is the value of f(10)?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Equal-Step 5-Second Shortcut: Notice x steps up by +4 from 2 to 6, and then by the exact same +4 from 6 to 10! Since Δy=29−11=+18 on the first +4 step, add +18 again:
    f(10)=29+18=47
  • Standard Slope-Intercept Verification: m=6−229−11​=418​=4.5; f(x)=4.5x+b⟹11=4.5(2)+b⟹b=2⟹f(10)=4.5(10)+2=47 ✓.
  • Desmos Regression Check: Table (2, 11), (6, 29) → y_1 ~ m x_1 + b (m=4.5,b=2) → 4.5(10) + 2 = 47.

questions.stemHtml:
5x+3y2x+4y​=31=25​
If (x,y) satisfies the system of equations above, what is the value of x+y?

choices.html: 6
7
8
9

questions.explanationHtml:
• Stacked Addition 5-Second Shortcut: Add Equation 1 and Equation 2 directly:
    (5x+2x)+(3y+4y)=31+25⟹7x+7y=56⟹7(x+y)=56⟹x+y=8
  • Desmos Intersection Method: Graph 5x + 3y = 31 and 2x + 4y = 25 → click intersection (3.5, 4.5) → 3.5+4.5=8 ✓!
  • Strategic Takeaway: Manually isolating y=331−5x​ creates messy fractions (3.5, 4.5), whereas checking stacked addition OR Desmos solves it in seconds with zero fraction errors!

questions.stemHtml: In the xy-plane, line ℓ is defined by the equation 3x+4y=12. Line m is perpendicular to line ℓ and passes through the point (6,−1). Which equation defines line m?

choices.html: y=−34​x+7
y=−43​x+27​
y=34​x−9
y=34​x+7

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    1. Slope of ℓ (3x+4y=12): mℓ​=−43​.
    2. Perpendicular slope (negative reciprocal): mm​=+34​ (instantly eliminates A and B!).
    3. Plug in (6,−1): y−(−1)=34​(x−6)⟹y+1=34​x−8⟹y=34​x−9.
  • Desmos Visual Check: Graph 3x + 4y = 12, point (6, -1), and Choice C y = (4/3)x - 9: line passes straight through (6, -1) at a clean 90∘ angle to ℓ ✓.
  • Trap Alert: Trap A flips the fraction without flipping the negative sign; Trap D mis-applies signs when plugging in (6,−1).

questions.stemHtml: Which inequality represents all values of x that satisfy 14−3(2x−1)≥5?

choices.html: x≤34​
x≥34​
x≤2
x≥2

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Distribute −3 across (2x−1) carefully:
    14−6x+3≥5⟹17−6x≥5⟹−6x≥−12
    Divide both sides by −6 and flip ≥ to ≤:
    x≤2
  • Zero-Plug Verification: Test x=0: 14−3(−1)=17≥5 (True! Eliminates B and D). Test x=2: 14−3(3)=5≥5 (True boundary! Eliminates A).
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (x≤34​) distributes −3(−1) as −3 (11−6x≥5⟹x≤1, or mis-adds constants); Trap D (x≥2) forgets to flip the inequality sign when dividing by −6!

questions.stemHtml: A maritime history museum sold a total of 190 admission tickets on Tuesday, consisting entirely of student tickets priced at each and adult tickets priced at each. If total ticket revenue on Tuesday was , how many student tickets did the museum sell?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Desmos 10-Second Method:
    • Line 1: x + y = 190 (let x= student tickets, y= adult tickets)
    • Line 2: 9x + 15y = 2370
    • Zoom out and click intersection: (80, 110). Boxed target = student tickets =x=80!
  • Algebraic Elimination: Multiply s+a=190 by 15: 15s+15a=2,850. Subtract 9s+15a=2,370: 6s=480⟹s=80.
  • Trap Alert: Entering 110 (adult tickets instead of student tickets — E4 target misread)!

questions.stemHtml: In the xy-plane, the graph of the linear function f(x)=−25​x+15 is translated up 5 units to produce the graph of y=g(x). What are the coordinates of the x-intercept of the graph of y=g(x)?

choices.html: (4,0)
(8,0)
(11,0)
(20,0)

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    1. Translating f(x) up 5 units adds 5 to the output:
      g(x)=f(x)+5=−25​x+15+5=−25​x+20
    2. Find the x-intercept by setting g(x)=0:
      −25​x+20=0⟹25​x=20⟹x=20×52​=8⟹(8,0)
  • Desmos 8-Second Method: Type f(x) = -(5/2)x + 15 on Line 1, g(x) = f(x) + 5 on Line 2 → click x-axis dot of g(x) at (8, 0)!
  • Trap Alert: Trap C ((11, 0)) simply adds +5 to the old x-intercept (6,0); Trap D ((20, 0)) confuses the new y-intercept (0,20) with the x-intercept!

questions.stemHtml:
yy​>2x−6<−21​x−2​
In the xy-plane, if the point (a,b) is a solution to the system of inequalities above, which quadrant can never contain (a,b)?

choices.html: Quadrant I
Quadrant II
Quadrant III
Quadrant IV

questions.explanationHtml:
• Desmos 10-Second Visual Proof: Type y > 2x - 6 on Line 1 and y < -0.5x - 2 on Line 2. Look at the overlapping dark-shaded region: it spans Quadrants II, III, and IV, and stays completely below y=−2 whenever x>0—never entering Quadrant I!
  • Algebraic Proof: In Quadrant I, both x>0 and y>0. However, when x>0, −21​x<0⟹−21​x−2<−2. Since y<−21​x−2, y must be strictly less than −2 whenever x>0, so y>0 is impossible! (Check sample solutions in the other three quadrants: QII (-8, 1), QIII (-2, -5), QIV (1, -3) all satisfy both inequalities.)

questions.stemHtml:
32​(6x−9)−kx=21​(4x+10)
In the given equation, k is a constant. If the equation has no solution, what is the value of k?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Simplify both sides into Ax+B=Cx+D:
    • LHS: 32​(6x−9)−kx=4x−6−kx=(4−k)x−6.
    • RHS: 21​(4x+10)=2x+5.
    • Since constants −6=5 already differ, no solution occurs when the x-coefficients match:
      4−k=2⟹k=2
  • Verification: Plug k=2 back in: 4x−6−2x=2x−6; setting 2x−6=2x+5 yields −6=5 (no solution ✓).

questions.stemHtml:
53​x−54​yax−12y​=6=b​
In the system of equations above, a and b are constants. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of a+b?

choices.html: 27
81
99
105

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    1. Clear fifths in Equation 1 by multiplying every term by 5:
      3x−4y=30
    2. Compare 3x−4y=30 to ax−12y=b: to turn −4y into −12y, multiply every term of 3x−4y=30 by 3:
      9x−12y=90
    3. For infinitely many solutions, both equations must represent the exact same line ⟹a=9 and b=90.
    4. Boxed target: a+b=9+90=99.
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (27) multiplies 3x by 3 (a=9) and 6 by 3 (b=18) while forgetting the factor of 5 on the constant!

questions.stemHtml: Freshwater flows out of a reverse-osmosis desalination unit according to the linear model W(m)=140+4.5m, where W(m) is the total volume of freshwater in the storage tank, in liters, m minutes after the pump starts. At this constant rate, how many additional liters of freshwater enter the storage tank every 2 hours?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Watch two simultaneous wording traps:
    1. Unit Conversion: Model input m is in minutes, whereas the question asks about 2 hours =2×60=120 minutes!
    2. "Additional" = Change Only (ΔW): Do not include the initial 140 liters already in the tank!
      ΔW=(rate)×Δm=4.5 L/min×120 min=540
  • Verification: W(120)−W(0)=(140+540)−140=540 ✓; or W(240)−W(120)=1,220−680=540 ✓.
  • Trap Alert: Entering 9 (4.5×2, ignoring minutes-to-hours) OR entering 680 (W(120), ignoring "additional").

questions.stemHtml:
3x+2yx−y​≤34≥3​
If (x,y) satisfies the system of inequalities above and both x and y are positive integers, what is the maximum possible value of y?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Desmos 10-Second Method: Graph 3x + 2y <= 34 and x - y >= 3. Click the top corner vertex of the double-shaded region: (8, 5)! Since x=8 and y=5 are both positive integers and all shaded points lie at or below y=5, maximum y=5.
  • Algebraic Elimination/Substitution: From x−y≥3, x≥y+3. Since 3x+2y≤34 and 3>0, replacing x with its smallest possible value y+3 gives:
    3(y+3)+2y≤34⟹5y+9≤34⟹5y≤25⟹y≤5
    Verify (8,5): 3(8)+2(5)=34≤34 ✓ and 8−5=3≥3 ✓.

questions.stemHtml: An artisan glassblowing collective is comparing two monthly studio furnace contracts. Contract A charges a fixed monthly fee of plus per annealing cycle. Contract B charges a fixed monthly fee of plus per annealing cycle. What is the minimum whole number of annealing cycles in a month for which the total monthly cost of Contract B is strictly less than the total monthly cost of Contract A?

choices.html: 75
76
77
80

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Let c = monthly annealing cycles. Set Contract B strictly less (<) than Contract A:
    510+1.75c<320+4.25c⟹190<2.50c⟹c>2.50190​=76
    Because c must be strictly greater than 76, the minimum whole number of cycles is 77!
  • Direct Dollar Verification:
    • At Trap B (c=76): Contract A =320+4.25(76)=; Contract B =510+1.75(76)= (exact tie—NOT strictly less!).
    • At c=77: Contract A =; Contract B = ✓!

subSections.html:
Reading & Writing Checks (CC-D2-RW1 to CC-D2-RW10)

  • CC-D2-RW1: Placing a colon before including creates redundancy and violates colon mechanics (materials: including... treats including... as if materials weren't already introducing a list, or puts both a colon AND including doing the exact same job!). Two clean fixes: (1) ...several durable materials, including bronze, obsidian, and fired stoneware. OR (2) ...several durable materials: bronze, obsidian, and fired stoneware. (Never combine : + including!)
  • CC-D2-RW2: Eliminate BOTH A and B immediately! Because IC . IC and IC ; IC are 100% grammatically interchangeable when all words match, College Board cannot make one right and the other wrong.
  • CC-D2-RW3: Zero commas! Architectural historian Spiro Kostof argued... (Architectural historian has no article An, acting as an essential title phrase naming which historian; adding commas would leave "Architectural historian argued..."—ungrammatical!).
  • CC-D2-RW4: Inside a complex serial list of three or more items where at least one list item already contains internal commas (City A, Country A; City B, Country B; and City C, Country C).
  • CC-D2-RW5: Fragment! living... and supplying... are both -ing participles—Algae has no finite main verb! One-word fix: change supplying to supply (and remove the comma: Algae living symbiotically inside giant clam mantles **supply** up to seventy percent...).
  • CC-D2-RW6: were — Inverted location sentence! Flip backward: [Dozens of intact frescoed storage jars] **were** nestled beneath the volcanic tuff layers of Akrotiri.
  • CC-D2-RW7: had already carved — "By the time explorers reached [past event, 1911]" requires past perfect (had + participle) for the earlier glacial action.
  • CC-D2-RW8: Compare rates to rates, not rates to wires! Fix: ...glass optical fibers' data transmission rates surpass **those of** coaxial wires. (Plural those of = the data transmission rates of.)
  • CC-D2-RW9: Asserting means stating a claim confidently (even with zero evidence), whereas substantiating means proving that claim with concrete facts or data.
  • CC-D2-RW10: Make flood damage less severe / milder—mitigate reduces harm rather than eliminating 100% of floodwater.

Math Checks (CC-D2-M1 to CC-D2-M6)

  • CC-D2-M1: Expand LHS: 6x−12=ax+b. Infinitely many solutions: a=6 AND b=−12. No solution: a=6 AND b=−12 (any constant except −12).
  • CC-D2-M2: The total number of seats across all t buses (NOT 18 seats per bus, and NOT t buses!).
  • CC-D2-M3: Negative reciprocal of −4=−14​ is +41​ (0.25).
  • CC-D2-M4: Add the two equations vertically: (7x+3x)+(2y+8y)=29+41⟹10x+10y=70⟹x+y=7!
  • CC-D2-M5: 9−4x−8<13⟹1−4x<13⟹−4x<12⟹x>−3 (flipped < to > when dividing by −4!). Test x=0: 9−4(2)=1<13 (True, confirming 0>−3 ✓).
  • CC-D2-M6: NO! Even though 7≤2(4)−1=7 is true, (4,7) sits directly on the dashed line y=x+3 (7>4+3⟹7>7 is false!). A solution to a system must satisfy both inequalities.

subSections.html:
Section 4A: Day 1 Spaced Retrieval Warm-Up (SR-D2-Q1 to SR-D2-Q10)

  • SR-D2-Q1: reconcile
  • SR-D2-Q2: notwithstanding
  • SR-D2-Q3: tentative (tiny 9-shard sample = provisional/cautious)
  • SR-D2-Q4: undermine (weaken reliability)
  • SR-D2-Q5: nuanced
  • SR-D2-Q6: Corroborate = confirm with independent evidence; collaborate = work together as partners.
  • SR-D2-Q7: ambiguous (open to two opposing interpretations)
  • SR-D2-Q8: Substantiate = prove with evidence (verb); substantial = large in size/amount (adjective).
  • SR-D2-Q9: plausible
  • SR-D2-Q10: infer

Section 4C: Day 2 Vocabulary Exercises (VOC-D2-Q1 to VOC-D2-Q32)

  • VOC-D2-Q1 → Correct: B (ubiquitous)

    • Why B works: "Once restricted to specialized... vessels" contrasts with tenfold cost drops making gliders found nearly everywhere (ubiquitous).
    • Why others fail: A (ambiguous) = unclear; C (tentative) = provisional; D (disparate) = fundamentally different in kind.

  • VOC-D2-Q2 → Correct: C (scrutinized)

    • Why C works: Mapping "every microscopic crystal boundary" with synchrotron X-ray diffraction describes close, thorough critical examination (scrutinized).
    • Why others fail: A (mitigated) = reduced harm; B (conceded) = reluctantly admitted; D (asserted) = claimed (you cannot "assert mineral slices"!).

  • VOC-D2-Q3 → Correct: A (concede)

    • Why A works: Advocates of congestion pricing fairly admit (concede) a valid criticism (tolls burden night-shift workers) before but introduces their policy fix (24-hour express buses).
    • Why others fail: B (bolster) & C (substantiate) = strengthen/prove (advocates wouldn't try to strengthen an argument against their own policy); D (undermine) = weaken (grammatically and logically wrong here).

  • VOC-D2-Q4 → Correct: B (compelling ... disparate)

    • Why B works: Blank 1 praises a unified migration history (compelling = powerfully convincing); Blank 2 after the colon describes flute acoustics, 17th-century tax ledgers, and oral ballads—three fundamentally different (disparate) types of evidence!
    • Why others fail: A calls strong synthesis tentative and unusual mixed sources conventional; C calls praise ambiguous; D calls praise conventional ("ordinary").

  • VOC-D2-Q5 → Correct: D (mitigate)

    • Why D works: While... cannot eliminate [100% cure] contrasts directly with significantly reducing the severity of (mitigate) routine sewer overflow.
    • Why others fail: A (corroborate) = confirm; B (assert) = claim; C (reconcile) = harmonize two conflicting things.

  • Exercise 4C-2 (VOC-D2-Q6–Q10):

    • VOC-D2-Q6: Signal = Whereas; Function = Traditional Baseline ([0]) contrasted against new fiber-optic method.
    • VOC-D2-Q7: Signal = Colon (:) + Independent... cores; Function = Strengthens ([+]).
    • VOC-D2-Q8: Signal = ; conversely, (warming in boreal vs. cooling in tropical); Function = Flips Case ([↔]).
    • VOC-D2-Q9: Signal = Although + forensic counter-proof; Function = Unproven Claim contrasted with evidence.
    • VOC-D2-Q10: Signal = even if they cannot replace...; Function = Reduces Harm ([-]).

  • Exercise 4C-3 (VOC-D2-Q11–Q15):

    • VOC-D2-Q11: ubiquitous
    • VOC-D2-Q12: scrutinize
    • VOC-D2-Q13: disparate
    • VOC-D2-Q14: compelling
    • VOC-D2-Q15: bolstered *(or bolster)*

  • Exercise 4C-4 (VOC-D2-Q16–Q19):

    • VOC-D2-Q16: disparate (distinct genres; desperate means hopeless/frantic).
    • VOC-D2-Q17: conventional (traditional linear order; convenient means easy/handy).
    • VOC-D2-Q18: assert (claim without proof; contrasted directly with "trials are required to prove").
    • VOC-D2-Q19: notwithstanding (post-positioned "Despite severe drought"; conversely cannot follow a noun phrase like a preposition!).

  • Exercise 4C-5 (VOC-D2-Q20–Q22):

    • VOC-D2-Q20: Conventional accounts claimed monasteries worked alone in isolation; guild contracts prove secular urban shops coordinated commercial book production. The specialists are disparate because animal-skin preparation, feather cutting, gold-leaf painting, and leather binding are distinct crafts.
    • VOC-D2-Q21: Historians concede that rural monasteries still copied religious texts on their own—making the thesis nuanced because it distinguishes urban university textbooks from rural religious copying instead of overclaiming that monasteries did zero copying.
    • VOC-D2-Q22: Notwithstanding signals that despite incomplete workshop ledgers, tax rolls corroborate (independently confirm) university fee statutes, enabling scholars to reconcile (resolve the apparent contradiction between) fast book growth and slow handwriting.

  • Exercise 4C-6 (VOC-D2-Q23–Q32 Rapid Retrieval Key):

    • VOC-D2-Q23 (bolster): Strengthen or reinforce with support.
    • VOC-D2-Q24 (disparate): Fundamentally different in kind.
    • VOC-D2-Q25 (concede): Admit reluctantly that an opposing point is true.
    • VOC-D2-Q26 (mitigate): Make a harmful problem less severe.
    • VOC-D2-Q27 (scrutinize): Examine closely and critically in detail.
    • VOC-D2-Q28 (ubiquitous): Present or found seemingly everywhere.
    • VOC-D2-Q29 (assert): State a claim firmly and confidently.
    • VOC-D2-Q30 (conventional): Standard, traditional, widely accepted.
    • VOC-D2-Q31 (compelling): Powerfully convincing and persuasive.
    • VOC-D2-Q32 (conversely): In the opposite direction / reverse case.

subSections.title: C. Reading & Writing Practice Set (RW-D2-Q1 to RW-D2-Q20) — Complete Explanations
subSections.titleHtml: C. Reading & Writing Practice Set (RW-D2-Q1 to RW-D2-Q20) — Complete Explanations
subSections.html:
RW-D2-Q1 → Correct Answer: C (adaptations:)

  • Why C works: Left of the blank is a complete IC (...Svalbard reindeer rely on two specialized physiological adaptations). Right of the blank is a noun-phrase pair specifying those two adaptations (tapetum lucidum eye tissue... and an expanded gut microbiome...). Complete IC : Specific Noun-Phrase List = Colon (:).
  • Why others fail: A fuses the list directly onto adaptations with zero boundary; B (;) fails because the right side lacks a main finite verb (shifts and capable sit inside modifiers); D (, and) turns "two... adaptations" into Item 1 of a nonsensical list.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Colon after complete IC.
  • Next-Time Clue: Spot "two [plural noun]: [Noun Phrase 1] and [Noun Phrase 2]" immediately!

RW-D2-Q2 → Correct Answer: B (including)

  • Why B works: The comma before the blank (calculations, ) already sets off the non-essential supplement including determining..., measuring..., and forecasting.... Adding zero punctuation after including preserves smooth syntax inside the preposition/participle phrase.
  • Why others fail: A (including:), C (including;), and D (including—) all illegally sever including from its own objects!
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — No colon/semicolon/dash after including / such as.
  • Next-Time Clue: Never put :, ;, or — immediately after including, such as, or for example!

RW-D2-Q3 → Correct Answer: D (Elinor Ostrom)

  • Why D works: American political economist lacks an article (an or the), functioning as a restrictive title directly introducing Elinor Ostrom. Together they form one unified subject before became.
  • Why others fail: A places a single comma between subject and verb (Ostrom, became — always wrong!); B treats Elinor Ostrom as removable, leaving the broken fragment "In 2009, American political economist became..."; C opens an unpaired dash.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Essential/Restrictive Name Identifier (zero commas).
  • Next-Time Clue: Delete the name! If "In 2009, American political economist became..." sounds broken without an, use zero commas!

RW-D2-Q4 → Correct Answer: B (sugars—)

  • Why B works: Look back at Mycorrhizal fungal networks—microscopic root filaments...: an interrupting non-essential definition opened with an em-dash (—), so it must close with a matching em-dash (sugars—) right before the main verb connect!
  • Why others fail: A (,) mismatches — ... , (always illegal on the SAT!); C (;) and D (no punctuation) fail to close the interrupting dash phrase, leaving networks stranded without its verb connect.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Paired Em-Dash Symmetry (— ... —).
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever choices include an em-dash (—), scan 10 words to the left to see if a first — already opened a pair!

RW-D2-Q5 → Correct Answer: C (vats;)

  • Why C works: Break the sentence into its three clauses:
    1. Although synthetic indigo dye... by 1905, (Dependent Clause — closed by the comma after 1905!)
    2. artisans in Tokushima, Japan, preserved natural sukumo fermentation vats (Independent Clause 1!)
    3. contemporary denim workshops still prize the botanical pigment... (Independent Clause 2!) Joining IC_1 and IC_2 with no FANBOYS conjunction requires a semicolon (vats;)!
  • Why others fail: A (vats,) is a comma splice tricked by the early Although; B (vats; and) misuses ; before coordinating and; D (vats) is a fused run-on.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — DC , IC_1 ; IC_2 structure.
  • Next-Time Clue: Don't let an opening Although fool you! Once you pass the comma + IC_1, a second IC_2 still needs a semicolon or period!

RW-D2-Q6 → Correct Answer: C (tolls;)

  • Why C works: Three complex city items each contain internal commas (Genoa, Italy, where...; | Ragusa, Croatia, where...; | and Alexandria, Egypt, where...). Notice the semicolon already printed after insurance;—parallel list boundaries demand tolls; before and Alexandria!
  • Why others fail: A (,) blurs main list items with internal City, Country commas; B (:) and D (—) break parallel semicolon structure.
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Super-Semicolons in Complex Serial Lists.
  • Next-Time Clue: Spot an earlier semicolon inside a list (insurance; Ragusa, Croatia,) → match it with ; before and [Item 3]!

RW-D2-Q7 → Correct Answer: C (form, instead)

  • Why C works: Left side = complete IC (High-altitude Andean condors rarely flap their wings once morning thermal updrafts form). Right side = instead gliding over one hundred miles... — gliding is an -ing participle, NOT a finite verb! Thus the right side is a supplemental modifier, attached with a comma (form, instead).
  • Why others fail: A (. Instead), B (; instead), and D (; and instead) all strand Instead gliding... as a sentence fragment after a hard stop! (Bonus: A and B are period/semicolon twins—instant double elimination!)
  • Rule Assessed: Boundaries — Participial Modifier vs. Independent Clause.
  • Next-Time Clue: Check the verb after instead! instead glided = IC (needs ;); instead gliding = participle (needs ,)!

RW-D2-Q8 → Correct Answer: D (demonstrates)

  • Why D works: Bracket modifiers: [Constructed from... nails,] the seventh-century five-story pagoda [at Hōryū-ji Temple,] [which has withstood... centuries,] _____. Singular subject pagoda needs finite main verb demonstrates.
  • Why others fail: A (demonstrating), B (to demonstrate), and C (having demonstrated) are all non-finite verbals that create a 38-word fragment with zero main verb!
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Finite Main Verb Requirement.
  • Next-Time Clue: Three non-finite forms (-ing, to + verb, having + participle) vs. one finite tense verb (demonstrates) almost always tests sentence completeness!

RW-D2-Q9 → Correct Answer: D (were)

  • Why D works: Inverted passive participle opening! Flip it into normal order: Ten tons of Cypriot copper ingots, Baltic amber beads, and carved hippopotamus-ivory lute fragments were cataloged inside the sunken... hull. Plural subject ten tons... takes plural were.
  • Why others fail: A (was), B (has been), and C (is) are all singular verbs lured by singular hull or Uluburun right before the blank!
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Inverted Subject-Verb Agreement.
  • Next-Time Clue: Sentence opens with -ed / prepositional phrase before the verb + 3 singular choices (was/has been/is) vs. 1 plural (were)? Look after the blank for the true plural subject!

RW-D2-Q10 → Correct Answer: D (had been struggling)

  • Why D works: Past time anchor = When... Hodgkin published... in 1955 + duration prior to that past moment = for nearly a decade. An ongoing struggle before a 1955 milestone requires past perfect progressive had been struggling.
  • Why others fail: A (struggle) = present; B (have struggled) links to today rather than ending in 1955; C (will struggle) = future.
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Past-Before-Past Tense Sequence.
  • Next-Time Clue: "When X happened in [past year], scientists _____ for a decade" → had + participle / had been -ing.

RW-D2-Q11 → Correct Answer: B (requires)

  • Why B works: Strip objects and prepositions: Synchronizing [atomic clocks aboard twenty-four orbiting navigation satellites with terrestrial master stations] requires... A gerund (-ing activity) subject is always singular!
  • Why others fail: A (require), C (have required), and D (are requiring) are all plural verbs fooled by clocks, satellites, and stations.
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Singular Gerund Subject Agreement.
  • Next-Time Clue: Sentence begins with [Verb]-ing [plural nouns] without a comma? That -ing word is your singular subject!

RW-D2-Q12 → Correct Answer: B (birds' alarm calls)

  • Why B works:
    1. "dozens of neighboring..." requires plural birds, and those birds possess the alarm calls ⟹ plural possessive birds'.
    2. "alarm calls" is followed immediately by preposition "with" (owns nothing!) ⟹ plain plural calls (zero apostrophe).
  • Why others fail: A (bird's) is singular after "dozens of"; C (call's) and D (calls') put illegal apostrophes before "with".
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Plural vs. Possessive Apostrophes.
  • Next-Time Clue: Preposition (with, of, in, for) right after the blank? The final word cannot have an apostrophe!

RW-D2-Q13 → Correct Answer: B

  • Why B works: Ask: *What was "Synthesized from agricultural oat-hull cellulose"?* Only the biodegradable barrier film! Placing the biodegradable barrier film immediately after the comma makes the modifier logical and accurate.
  • Why others fail: A claims materials engineers were synthesized from oat-hull cellulose (!); C claims municipal compost facilities were synthesized from cellulose; D claims oxygen permeability (an abstract measurement) was synthesized from cellulose.
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Introductory Participial Modifier Placement.
  • Next-Time Clue: Don't blindly pick a human noun! Read the participle carefully: people calibrate lasers (Day 1 Q15), whereas films/compounds are synthesized from cellulose (Day 2 Q13)!

RW-D2-Q14 → Correct Answer: C (those of contemporary European stone cathedrals)

  • Why C works: Subject of comparison = plural the reverberation times (of Sinan's prayer halls). You must compare reverberation times to reverberation times (those of contemporary European stone cathedrals), never directly to stone buildings!
  • Why others fail: A illogically compares reverberation times (seconds) to cathedrals (buildings); B (that of) is singular, clashing with plural times; D (in ... cathedrals') breaks parallel syntax and leaves a dangling possessive.
  • Rule Assessed: Form, Structure, and Sense — Parallel Logical Comparisons (those of vs. that of).
  • Next-Time Clue: Spot more [adj] than or exceeds: check whether the subject noun before the verb is singular (that of) or plural (those of)!

RW-D2-Q15 → Correct Answer: A (mitigate)

  • Why A works: Bubble curtains reduce the harmful intensity of (mitigate) underwater pile-driving noise so porpoise sonar isn't damaged.
  • Why others fail: B (bolster) = strengthen/increase noise (harms porpoises!); C (scrutinize) = inspect closely; D (assert) = state confidently.
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Harm-reduction verb.
  • Next-Time Clue: Protective engineering + "noise/damage that would otherwise impair..." → mitigate / attenuate / curtail.

RW-D2-Q16 → Correct Answer: C (scrutinized)

  • Why C works: The participial phrase at the end defines the blank: "checking each bronze-age harbor description detail by detail against sediment core maps" = scrutinized.
  • Why others fail: A (conceded) = admitted reluctantly; B (mitigated) = lessened harm; D (undermined) = weakened (contradicts "Rather than dismissing...").
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Trailing participial definition clue.
  • Next-Time Clue: A comma + -ing explanation at the end of a sentence often restates the exact verb in the blank!

RW-D2-Q17 → Correct Answer: B (ubiquitous)

  • Why B works: yet contrasts "rare, expensive curiosities in 1915" with becoming commonplace everywhere (ubiquitous) across urban apartments within 30 years.
  • Why others fail: A (tentative) = provisional; C (ambiguous) = unclear; D (disparate) = essentially different.
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Historical rare → widespread contrast.
  • Next-Time Clue: "still rare in [Year 1], yet within decades became _____" → ubiquitous / commonplace / pervasive.

RW-D2-Q18 → Correct Answer: C (check)

  • Why C works: Look at the second clause after the semicolon: where otters vanished, unchecked urchin grazing destroyed kelp! Here check carries its classic SAT secondary verb meaning: to restrain, hold back, or limit population growth.
  • Why others fail: A (substantiate) = prove; B (amplify) and D (foster) = increase/encourage urchin numbers (the exact opposite of predation!).
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Polysemy (V2) secondary meaning of check (= restrain/curb).
  • Next-Time Clue: Add check (v.) = restrain / hold back right alongside Day 1's qualify (v.) = limit a claim on your Top Polysemy Alert list!

RW-D2-Q19 → Correct Answer: A (concede)

  • Why A works: "Even biogeographers who [grant minor point X: wind carries light spores] contend that [main thesis Y: wind cannot carry flightless beetles or salt-sensitive trees]" is the textbook SAT concession (concede) pattern!
  • Why others fail: B (refute) breaks "Even... contend" logic (if they refuted wind dispersal of spores too, there would be no "Even" contrast!); C (bolster) = strengthen; D (reconcile) requires reconcile A with B.
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Academic concession syntax (Even scholars who concede X contend Y).
  • Next-Time Clue: "Even [experts] who _____ that [Point 1] maintain/contend that [Point 2]" → concede / acknowledge / grant!

RW-D2-Q20 → Correct Answer: D (disparate)

  • Why D works: Although contrasts early hopes for "one universal template / uniform mechanical schema" against radically different, structurally distinct (disparate) languages like polysynthetic Inuktitut and tonal analytic Mandarin.
  • Why others fail: A (plausible) = believable; B (conventional) = traditional (traditional architectures wouldn't inherently defy uniformity—their extreme difference did!); C (corroborated) = confirmed.
  • Skill Assessed: Words in Context — Contrast with single / universal / uniform.
  • Next-Time Clue: Contrast against uniform, homogeneous, single template → disparate / divergent / heterogeneous.
