checks.promptHtml: Store X sold 90 bikes and Store Y sold 75 bikes. Store X sold what percent more bikes than Store Y?
checks.answerHtml: Noun after "than" is Store Y (75), so denominator =75: 7590−75​×100%=7515​×100%=20%.

checks.promptHtml: How many square centimeters (1 m=100 cm) are in 2.5 square meters?
checks.answerHtml: Square the linear conversion factor! 1 m=100 cm⟹1 m2=(100 cm)2=10,000 cm2. Thus 2.5 m2=2.5×10,000=25,000 cm2.

checks.promptHtml: In a table of 500 voters (200 Rural, 300 Urban), 110 Rural voters support Proposal K. If one Rural voter is chosen at random, what is the denominator of the probability fraction?
checks.answerHtml: Denominator =200 (Rural voters only, because the selection is restricted to "one Rural voter chosen at random", NOT all 500 voters; probability =200110​=2011​).

mathPractice.introHtml:
Explicit Origin Notice: All 16 problems below (MATH-D3-Q1 through MATH-D3-Q16) are original SAT-style practice questions (Q1–Q8: Advanced Math; Q9–Q16: Problem-Solving and Data Analysis; 10 Multiple-Choice + 6 SPR).
Timed Mastery Target: Set a strict countdown timer for 24 minutes (~90 seconds/question). Keep desmos.com/calculator open! Do not view Section 8 until finished.

questions.stemHtml: Which expression is equivalent to (3x2−4x+7)−2(x2−5x+3)?

choices.html: x2−14x+1
x2−9x+4
x2+6x+1
x2+6x+13

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Distribute −2 across every term inside the second parentheses:
    (3x2−4x+7)−2x2+10x−6=(3−2)x2+(−4+10)x+(7−6)=x2+6x+1
  • Quick Value Check (x=1): Original: (3−4+7)−2(1−5+3)=6−2(−1)=8. Test Choice C at x=1: 1+6+1=8 ✓ (A gives −12, B gives −4, D gives 20—all eliminated instantly!).
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (-14x) distributes −2(−5x) as −10x; Trap D (+13) distributes −2(+3) as +6.

questions.stemHtml:
(2x−7)(x+4)=0
What is the positive solution to the given equation?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: By the Zero-Product Property, either factor equals 0:
    • 2x−7=0⟹2x=7⟹x=3.5 (7/2)
    • x+4=0⟹x=−4
    • Boxed target asks for the positive solution ⟹3.5 (or 7/2).
  • Trap Alert: Entering -4 or adding the two roots!

questions.stemHtml: In the xy-plane, the graph of the quadratic function f(x)=(x+2)2−9 has its vertex at (−2,−9). If the function g is defined by g(x)=f(x−5)+4, what are the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of y=g(x)?

choices.html: (−7,−5)
(−7,−13)
(3,−5)
(3,−13)

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Apply Lesson 3.4's transformation rule to vertex (−2,−9):
    • Inside f(x−5) shifts RIGHT 5 units ⟹xnew​=−2+5=3.
    • Outside +4 shifts UP 4 units ⟹ynew​=−9+4=−5.
    • New vertex: (3,−5).
  • Desmos 8-Second Method: Type f(x) = (x + 2)^2 - 9 on Line 1 and g(x) = f(x - 5) + 4 on Line 2 → click the minimum point of g(x): (3, -5)!
  • Trap Alert: Trap A ((-7, -5)) moves left 5 instead of right 5 (the #1 sign-direction error on SAT functions!).

questions.stemHtml:
2x2−18x+29=0
What is the sum of the real solutions to the given equation?
questions.explanationHtml:
• 3-Second Vieta Shortcut: For 2x2−18x+29=0 (a=2,b=−18,c=29):
    1. Check real roots exist: D=(−18)2−4(2)(29)=324−232=92>0 ✓ (two distinct real roots).
    2. Sum of solutions =−ab​=−2−18​=9.
  • Desmos Verification: Graph y = 2x^2 - 18x + 29 and click both x-intercepts (2.102 and 6.898): 2.102+6.898=9!
  • Trap Alert: Forgetting to divide by a=2 (entering 18) or dropping the negative sign in −b/a (entering -9).

questions.stemHtml: For all x>3, which expression is equivalent to x−34​+x+35​?

choices.html: 2x9​
x2−99​
x2−99x−3​
x2−99x+27​

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Algebraic Solution: Common denominator is (x−3)(x+3)=x2−9:
    (x−3)(x+3)4(x+3)+5(x−3)​=x2−94x+12+5x−15​=x2−99x−3​
  • Desmos / Plug-In x=5 Check: At x=5, original =24​+85​=2+0.625=2.625 (21/8). Choice C gives 25−945−3​=1642​=821​=2.625 ✓!
  • Trap Alert: Trap A adds numerators AND denominators (x−3+x+34+5​); Trap D distributes +5(−3) as +15.

questions.stemHtml:
h(t)=−5t2+25t+30
An atmospheric research sonde is launched upward from an observation platform above a valley floor. The function h models the height, in meters, of the sonde above the valley floor t seconds after launch. How many seconds after launch does the sonde strike the valley floor (h(t)=0)?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Set height h(t)=0 and divide every term by −5:
    −5t2+25t+30=0⟹t2−5t−6=0⟹(t−6)(t+1)=0
    Since time after launch satisfies t≥0, discard t=−1 ⟹t=6 seconds.
  • Desmos 5-Second Method: Graph y = -5x^2 + 25x + 30 and click the positive x-intercept at (6, 0)!
  • Trap Alert: Entering 2.5 (the time of maximum height at the vertex (2.5, 61.25), rather than when the sonde strikes the valley floor!).

questions.stemHtml:
(ax+3)(2x−b)=10x2−29x−21
If the equation above holds true for all real values of x, where a and b are constants, what is the value of a+b?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Coefficient Matching: Expand (ax+3)(2x−b)=2ax2+(6−ab)x−3b and match coefficients to 10x2−29x−21:
    1. Match x2: 2a=10⟹a=5.
    2. Match constant: −3b=−21⟹b=7.
    3. Verify middle x term (never skip!): 6−(5)(7)=6−35=−29 ✓!
    4. Boxed target: a+b=5+7=12.
  • Desmos Regression Shortcut: Type (a*x_1 + 3)(2*x_1 - b) ~ 10*x_1^2 - 29*x_1 - 21 with list x_1 = [1, 2, 3] → Desmos outputs a = 5, b = 7 immediately!
  • Trap Alert: Matching −3b=−21 as b=−7 (sign slip → entering -2).

questions.stemHtml:
4x+21​=x
Which statement accurately describes the real solution(s) to the given equation?

choices.html: −3 only
7 only
Both −3 and 7
Both 3 and −7

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    1. Square both sides to generate candidates:
      4x+21=x2⟹x2−4x−21=0⟹(x−7)(x+3)=0⟹x=7 or x=−3
    2. Mandatory Un-Squared Substitution Check:
    • Test x=7: 4(7)+21​=49​=7=RHS ✓ (Valid!)
    • Test x=−3: 4(−3)+21​=9​=+3=−3 (Extraneous—Reject!)
  • Desmos Visual Guarantee: Graph y = sqrt(4x + 21) and y = x. Because x​≥0, the radical curve stays on or above the x-axis and intersects y = x ONLY once, at (7, 7)!
  • Trap Alert: Trap C (Both -3 and 7) is the #1 Advanced Math trap on the entire Digital SAT—never skip checking radical roots!

questions.stemHtml: An autonomous underwater glider travels horizontally at a constant speed of 1.8 kilometers per hour. What is this speed in meters per minute? (1 kilometer=1,000 meters)

choices.html: 0.03
18
30
108

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Dimensional Analysis: Write fraction units explicitly so unwanted units cancel diagonally:
    1 hr1.8 km​×1 km1,000 m​×60 min1 hr​=60 min1,800 m​=30 m/min
  • Trap Alert: Trap D (108) multiplies 1.8×60 without converting kilometers to meters (or multiplies by 60 instead of dividing!).

questions.stemHtml: During an agronomic trial, Experimental Plot A yielded 65 bushels of soybeans per acre, while Control Plot B yielded 50 bushels of soybeans per acre. Experimental Plot A's yield per acre was what percent greater than Control Plot B's yield per acre?

choices.html: 15%
23%
30%
130%

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Box the phrase percent greater than Control Plot B:
    • Difference =65−50=15 bushels/acre.
    • Reference denominator (after "than") =Control Plot B=50:
      5065−50​×100%=5015​×100%=30%
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (15%) confuses raw bushel difference (15) with percentage; Trap B (23%) divides by 65 (Plot A) instead of 50 (Plot B); Trap D (130%) answers "what percent OF Plot B" rather than "what percent GREATER THAN Plot B."

questions.stemHtml: In a physical chemistry study across mountain weather stations, a line of best fit y^​=100−3.3x models the predicted boiling point of pure water y^​, in degrees Celsius (∘C), at an elevation of x kilometers above sea level. At a high-altitude research camp located 2.5 kilometers above sea level, the actual measured boiling point of water was 92.1∘C. By how many degrees Celsius did the actual boiling point exceed the boiling point predicted by the line of best fit?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    1. Plug x=2.5 km into the line of best fit to get the predicted boiling point:
      y^​=100−3.3(2.5)=100−8.25=91.75∘C
    2. Subtract predicted from actual (92.1∘C):
      Residual=y−y^​=92.1−91.75=0.35
  • Trap Alert: Entering 91.75 (stopping at the predicted value without subtracting from 92.1).

questions.stemHtml:
Glaze Composition of 240 Archived Ceramic Vessels

Vessel Body Type Lead-Free Glaze Mineral-Flux Glaze Total
Porcelain 78 42 120
Stoneware 54 66 120
Total 132 108 240

The table above summarizes 240 ceramic vessels in a museum conservation catalog classified by clay body and glaze chemistry. If one vessel is selected at random from those with a lead-free glaze, what is the probability that the selected vessel is porcelain?

choices.html: 4013​
2213​
2013​
2011​

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution: Read the exact restriction after "selected at random from":
    • Subgroup denominator: those with a lead-free glaze ⟹ Column 1 Total =132 (ignore 240 and 120!).
    • Favorable numerator: porcelain AND lead-free glaze =78.
    • Simplify fraction (or type 78/132 in Desmos and click the fraction button!):
      13278​=132÷678÷6​=2213​
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (13/40) uses grand total 240 (24078​); Trap C (13/20) uses Porcelain row total 120 (12078​, answering "given porcelain, what is the probability of lead-free glaze?"—backwards condition!).

questions.stemHtml: During a distributor clearance event, a laboratory stereomicroscope's original catalog price was discounted by 20%. After a 5% insured freight fee was added to that discounted price, the total amount billed was . What was the stereomicroscope's original catalog price, in dollars?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Multiplier Equation: Let P = original catalog price.
    • 20% discount multiplies price by (1−0.20)=0.80.
    • 5% freight fee added to that discounted price multiplies by (1+0.05)=1.05:
      P×0.80×1.05=672⟹0.84P=672⟹P=0.84672​=800
  • Forward Check: ✓!
  • Trap Alert: Combining −20%+5%=−15% (672/0.85=790.59 — wrong, because +5% applies to the discounted 0.80P, not to P!), or multiplying .

questions.stemHtml: A coastal salt-marsh sanctuary covers an area of 4.5 square kilometers. If 1 kilometer=1,000 meters, into how many non-overlapping ecological monitoring quadrats, each having an area of 900 square meters, can the entire 4.5-square-kilometer sanctuary be divided?

choices.html: 5
50
500
5,000

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Squared-Unit Solution:
    1. Square the linear conversion 1 km=1,000 m:
      1 km2=(1,000 m)×(1,000 m)=1,000,000 m2
    2. Convert sanctuary area to square meters:
      4.5 km2=4.5×1,000,000 m2=4,500,000 m2
    3. Divide total area by area per quadrat (900 m2):
      900 m24,500,000 m2​=945,000​=5,000
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (5) uses 1 km2=1,000 m2 (9004,500​=5)—off by a factor of 1,000!

questions.stemHtml: Public-health researchers selected a random sample of 400 adult residents of Rotterdam and surveyed them about their weekly outdoor leisure habits. Analysis revealed that respondents who spent at least 4 hours per week tending community garden plots had significantly lower afternoon salivary cortisol levels than respondents who did not garden. Based on the design of this study, which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.raw: Spending at least $4$ hours per week gardening causes a reduction in afternoon cortisol levels for adults worldwide.
choices.html: Spending at least 4 hours per week gardening causes a reduction in afternoon cortisol levels for adults worldwide.

choices.raw: Spending at least $4$ hours per week gardening causes a reduction in afternoon cortisol levels for adult residents of Rotterdam, though not necessarily in other cities.
choices.html: Spending at least 4 hours per week gardening causes a reduction in afternoon cortisol levels for adult residents of Rotterdam, though not necessarily in other cities.

choices.raw: Among adult residents of Rotterdam, there is a negative association between gardening at least $4$ hours per week and afternoon cortisol levels, but the study cannot establish that gardening causes lower cortisol.
choices.html: Among adult residents of Rotterdam, there is a negative association between gardening at least 4 hours per week and afternoon cortisol levels, but the study cannot establish that gardening causes lower cortisol.

choices.raw: Because the $400$ adult residents were chosen at random, confounding lifestyle variables cannot account for the observed cortisol difference.
choices.html: Because the 400 adult residents were chosen at random, confounding lifestyle variables cannot account for the observed cortisol difference.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Study-Design Evaluation: Check the two SAT Statistical Inference Rules:
    1. Who was randomly sampled? Adult residents of Rotterdam ⟹ scope generalizes to Rotterdam adults (eliminates A "adults worldwide").
    2. Was gardening randomly assigned? No! It was an observational survey of existing habits (maybe retirees or low-stress workers have more free time to garden). Without random assignment to treatments, causation cannot be claimed (eliminates A, B, and D), leaving negative association (Choice C)!

questions.stemHtml: Forest entomologists inspected a random sample of 300 mature ash trees out of all 18,000 mature ash trees in a regional conservation district and found that 14% exhibited emerald ash borer gallery marks, with an associated margin of error of 3% at the 95% confidence level. Which of the following is the most plausible interval for the total number of mature ash trees in the district with emerald ash borer gallery marks?

choices.html: Between 33 and 51
Between 1,980 and 3,060
Between 2,220 and 2,820
Between 2,520 and 3,060

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step-by-Step Solution:
    1. Form the plausible percentage interval using sample estimate ± margin of error:
      14%−3%=11%to14%+3%=17%
    2. Scale to the entire district population of 18,000 mature ash trees:
    • Lower bound: 0.11×18,000=1,980
    • Upper bound: 0.17×18,000=3,060
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (33 to 51) multiplies [11%,17%] by sample size 300 instead of population 18,000; Trap D forgets to subtract the 3% margin of error on the lower bound!

answerVault.introHtml: Active-Learning Rule: Check answers only after completing each set independently. Whenever you miss an item, hide the explanation and re-solve the question cold on blank paper before moving forward.

subSections.title: A. Lesson Short Comprehension Checks — Answer Key
subSections.titleHtml: A. Lesson Short Comprehension Checks — Answer Key
subSections.html:
Reading & Writing Checks (CC-D3-RW1 to CC-D3-RW5)

  • CC-D3-RW1:
    • Empirical Evidence (Raw Measured Fact): "Glacier thickness declined by 11 meters between 2010 and 2024."
    • Theoretical Interpretation (Claim / Model): "Warm subsurface ocean currents—rather than summer air temperatures alone—are melting the ice shelf from below." (Signaled by the verb posit!)
  • CC-D3-RW2: Real scientific and historical studies examine finite samples under bounded conditions, so authors hedge their conclusions (often, primarily, at least in part, tends to). Words like solely, exclusively, never, and prove conclusively over-extrapolate beyond what finite evidence can license unless the passage itself explicitly states a 100% universal rule.
  • CC-D3-RW3: Comparing Biochar + Compost (9.5 kg) against Sandy Soil (4 kg) only proves that the combination boosts yield—it does not rule out the possibility that biochar works great all by itself! To prove "only when paired with compost," you must also cite Biochar Only = 4.1 kg (showing biochar alone barely differs from the 4 kg control) alongside Compost Only = 6 kg vs. Biochar + Compost = 9.5 kg.
  • CC-D3-RW4: Sentence 2 introduces an empirical counterexample (however) that challenges Sentence 1's broad generalization and sets up Sentence 3's alternative ecological mechanism (plankton blooms rather than day length).
  • CC-D3-RW5: Because "While Dr. Kim rightly notes that urban tree canopies lower sidewalk temperatures..." explicitly concedes / agrees that Dr. Kim's sidewalk-cooling observation is true! Any choice claiming Text 2 "rejects" that point is an instant polarity falsehood.

Math Checks (CC-D3-M1 to CC-D3-M6)

  • CC-D3-M1: For 3x2−21x+11=0 (a=3,b=−21,c=11; check D=(−21)2−4(3)(11)=441−132=309>0):
    • Sum of solutions: −ab​=−3−21​=7.
    • Product of solutions: ac​=311​.
  • CC-D3-M2: Inside p(x+6) shifts LEFT 6 units (4−6=−2); outside −2 shifts DOWN 2 units (−7−2=−9). New vertex: (−2,−9).
  • CC-D3-M3: Because the radical symbol x​ denotes the principal (non-negative) square root! Substituting x=−4 into the original un-squared equation gives LHS=5(−4)+36​=16​=+4, whereas RHS=−4. Since +4=−4, x=−4 is an extraneous solution created when squaring erased the negative sign.
  • CC-D3-M4: Noun after "than" is Store Y (75), so denominator =75: 7590−75​×100%=7515​×100%=20%.
  • CC-D3-M5: Square the linear conversion factor! 1 m=100 cm⟹1 m2=(100 cm)2=10,000 cm2. Thus 2.5 m2=2.5×10,000=25,000 cm2.
  • CC-D3-M6: Denominator =200 (Rural voters only, because the selection is restricted to "one Rural voter chosen at random", NOT all 500 voters; probability =200110​=2011​).

subSections.title: B. Vocabulary Retrieval & Exercises (4A & 4C) — Answer Key
subSections.titleHtml: B. Vocabulary Retrieval & Exercises (4A & 4C) — Answer Key
subSections.html:
Section 4A: Multi-Day Spaced Retrieval Warm-Up (SR-D3-Q1 to SR-D3-Q12)

  • SR-D3-Q1: notwithstanding (Postposed concession: "Harsh monsoon squalls notwithstanding" = Despite harsh monsoon squalls).
  • SR-D3-Q2: reconcile (Bring two conflicting expansion-rate measurements into harmony/agreement).
  • SR-D3-Q3: ambiguous (Open to two valid competing explanations—smelting vs. natural weathering).
  • SR-D3-Q4: nuanced (Subtle, balanced account avoiding crude all-good or all-bad extremes).
  • SR-D3-Q5: tentative (Provisional/unconfirmed because based on only a single flyby).
  • SR-D3-Q6: scrutinize (Day 2 #12).
  • SR-D3-Q7: disparate (Day 2 #16).
  • SR-D3-Q8: mitigate (Day 2 #18).
  • SR-D3-Q9: compelling (Day 2 #13).
  • SR-D3-Q10: concede (Day 2 #17).
  • SR-D3-Q11: ubiquitous (Day 2 #19).
  • SR-D3-Q12: Assert = state a claim confidently (often with zero proof yet); bolster = actively strengthen and reinforce a claim with real evidence.

Exercise 4C-1: Words in Context Multiple Choice (VOC-D3-Q1 to VOC-D3-Q4)

  • VOC-D3-Q1 → B (underscored): Survival of native perennials through five drought summers strongly highlighted / emphasized (underscored) the value of preserving native seed banks. Trap A (undermined) and Trap C (refuted) flip positive support into negative attack; D (mitigated) means "softened a harm" (you don't mitigate agronomic value!).
  • VOC-D3-Q2 → A (tenuous): Evaporative cooling in canvas buckets distorted raw deck readings, making their unadjusted link to true ocean temperatures weak / shaky (tenuous). B (compelling) means convincingly strong (opposite!); C (ubiquitous) means everywhere; D (conventional) means traditional.
  • VOC-D3-Q3 → C (posited): Whereas contrasts what theoretical ecologists had long proposed as a theoretical model (posited) against what empirical GPS tracking revealed in real life. A (refuted) reverses their belief; B (delineated) doesn't fit that-clause hypothesis framing; D (mitigated) is nonsensical here.
  • VOC-D3-Q4 → D (entails): The colon explains why thermal jackets are an unavoidable requirement (without buffers, molten cryolite would freeze solid)—switching to wind power necessarily requires (entails) potline redesign. A (attributes), B (concedes), and C (extrapolates) all fail the requirement logic after the colon.

Exercise 4C-2: Argument & Evidence Role Identification (VOC-D3-Q5 to VOC-D3-Q8)

  • VOC-D3-Q5: (c) Decisive Disproof (refuted = proved the first-century origin claim false using radiocarbon data).
  • VOC-D3-Q6: (d) Methodological Warning/Limit (caveat = caution that smartphone samples missed elderly riders).
  • VOC-D3-Q7: (b) Experimental Data (empirical = real physical ocean-bottom seismometer measurements).
  • VOC-D3-Q8: (a) Proposed Hypothesis (posited = put forward the lock-and-key model before direct imaging existed).

Exercise 4C-3: Academic Sentence Completion (VOC-D3-Q9 to VOC-D3-Q13)

  • VOC-D3-Q9: attribute (matches exact structure attribute [statuette] to [Mantuan workshop]).
  • VOC-D3-Q10: delineates (or delineated — draws clear legal boundaries between municipal vs. provincial powers).
  • VOC-D3-Q11: extrapolate (project long 50-year trends from a tiny, unrepresentative 3-year wet spell).
  • VOC-D3-Q12: tenuous (shaky, poorly supported link based on only two degraded fragments).
  • VOC-D3-Q13: underscored (or underscore — vividly highlighted the urgency of debris tracking).

Exercise 4C-4: High-Risk Lookalike & Precision Discrimination (VOC-D3-Q14 to VOC-D3-Q17)

  • VOC-D3-Q14: underscore — "Far from casting doubt" rules out undermine ("weaken"); the new records emphasize/reinforce her warning.
  • VOC-D3-Q15: empirical — Glaciology requires observational field measurements (empirical), not royal empire decrees (imperial).
  • VOC-D3-Q16: tenacious — Clinging to bare rock through hurricane winds is a stubbornly tight, persistent grip (tenacious), the exact opposite of weak/flimsy (tenuous)!
  • VOC-D3-Q17: refute — Synthesizing an organic molecule from inorganic salts disproved (refuted) vitalism's "living-tissue-only" claim rather than admitting (conceding) it was true.

Exercise 4C-5: Closed-Notes Rapid Retrieval Quiz (VOC-D3-Q18 to VOC-D3-Q27)

(Grade for accurate core meaning in your own simple English words)

  • VOC-D3-Q18 (posit): Put forward a hypothesis or model for reasoning.
  • VOC-D3-Q19 (entail): Necessarily require or involve as an unavoidable consequence.
  • VOC-D3-Q20 (empirical): Based on real-world observation, experiment, or measured data.
  • VOC-D3-Q21 (extrapolate): Project or estimate unknown values beyond existing data.
  • VOC-D3-Q22 (refute): Prove a claim or theory false using hard evidence.
  • VOC-D3-Q23 (underscore): Strongly emphasize or highlight an important point.
  • VOC-D3-Q24 (delineate): Outline, trace, or mark exact boundaries clearly.
  • VOC-D3-Q25 (tenuous): Very weak, flimsy, or poorly supported by evidence.
  • VOC-D3-Q26 (attribute): Regard an effect or work as caused or created by a source (attribute X to Y).
  • VOC-D3-Q27 (caveat): An important warning, caution, or limiting condition on a claim.

subSections.title: C. Reading & Writing Practice Questions (RW-D3-Q1 to RW-D3-Q18) — Detailed Explanations
subSections.titleHtml: C. Reading & Writing Practice Questions (RW-D3-Q1 to RW-D3-Q18) — Detailed Explanations
subSections.html:
RW-D3-Q1 → Correct Answer: B (posited)

  • Skill & Domain: Craft and Structure · Words in Context (Easy)
  • Why B is Correct: Observing out-of-place alpine granite boulders led Agassiz to propose the scientific hypothesis (posit) that ancient continental ice sheets had carried them there.
  • Why Distractors Fail: A (mitigated) = made less severe; C (refuted) = disproved (reverses Agassiz's own ice-age theory!); D (conceded) = reluctantly admitted an opponent's point.
  • Next-Time Clue: [Observation of puzzling natural clue] + [blank] + that [explanatory scientific model] = posited / hypothesized.

RW-D3-Q2 → Correct Answer: C (tenuous)

  • Skill & Domain: Craft and Structure · Words in Context (Medium)
  • Why C is Correct: After the colon, the passage explains why a single snail shell is terrible proof of industrial dye commerce (single shells were ornaments; dye vats needed tens of thousands). Thus the claim rests on weak, shaky (tenuous) footing.
  • Why Distractors Fail: A (compelling) means strongly convincing (opposite!); B (ubiquitous) means everywhere; D (conventional) means standard/traditional.
  • Next-Time Clue: Always treat a colon (:) in Words in Context as an = sign defining the blank!

RW-D3-Q3 → Correct Answer: A (attributed)

  • Skill & Domain: Craft and Structure · Words in Context (Hard)
  • Why A is Correct: Both logic and grammar lock in attributed: health boards regarded [Effect: the epidemic] as caused by to [Proposed Cause: noxious miasma vapors], contrasting (by contrast) with John Snow tracing the true cause to contaminated pump water.
  • Why Distractors Fail: B (extrapolated) = projected outside a dataset (extrapolated X from Y, not to vapors); C (delineated) = outlined boundaries; D (entailed) = necessarily required (does not take "to").
  • Next-Time Clue: Spot the syntactic frame _____ [Effect X] to [Cause Y] → test attributed / ascribed immediately.

RW-D3-Q4 → Correct Answer: B

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Central Ideas and Details (Easy/Medium — Literature)
  • Why B is Correct: Captures both halves of the paragraph balanced around Yet: Sentence 1 shows Don Esteban demands tenth-of-a-millimeter caliper precision when building new violins, while Sentence 2 (Yet) shows that judging how forty damp winters shaped an old violin's tone requires setting calipers aside and listening to bow on string.
  • Why Distractors Fail:
    • A (Too Extreme): Contradicts Sentence 1 (every morning he handed the narrator brass calipers and insisted geometry mattered!).
    • C (Alien Comparison + Distortion): "Mellowed a violin's voice" is positive/musical, not rapid deterioration, and Genoese vs. Buenos Aires durability is never compared.
    • D (Invented Narrator Preference): The narrator never states a personal preference between tasks.
  • Next-Time Clue: When a literary paragraph pivots with Yet, the main idea must honor the tension between Sentence 1 AND Sentence 2, never erasing Sentence 1.

RW-D3-Q5 → Correct Answer: C

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Central Ideas and Details (Medium — History)
  • Why C is Correct: Sentence 1 challenges "older maritime histories" that credited European demand alone, arguing the trade "depended just as fundamentally on fiscal transformation inside Ming China"; Sentence 2 explains how the Single Whip silver tax created massive Chinese silver demand.
  • Why Distractors Fail:
    • A (Fabrication): Ming China never abandoned silk or porcelain!
    • B (Absurd Distortion): Spanish merchants traded silver in Manila markets; they did not collect Chinese domestic land taxes.
    • D (Alien Comparison): Silver purity at Potosí vs. earlier Ming silver is never mentioned.
  • Next-Time Clue: Opening participial frames like "Long framed by older histories as X, Phenomenon P depended just as fundamentally on Y" hand you the central claim (Y mattered alongside X, revising X-only accounts) right in Sentence 1!

RW-D3-Q6 → Correct Answer: D

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Central Ideas and Details (Hard — Neuroscience)
  • Why D is Correct: Matches the exact experimental result in Sentence 2: "although the modified mice slept for the exact same total nightly duration as unmodified control mice, clearance of beta-amyloid metabolic proteins from cortical tissue slowed by sixty percent."
  • Why Distractors Fail:
    • A (Misplaced Number Swap): Transfers "sixty percent" from protein clearance onto sleep duration (which remained exact same!).
    • B (Invented Mechanism): Never stated that neurons took over clearance.
    • C (Confusing Clearance with Production + Extreme): Clearance slowed by 60% during sleep = production ceased completely during wakefulness!
  • Next-Time Clue: Watch out for SAT "Number-Swap Distractors" (Choice A) that attach a genuine passage number (60%) to the wrong noun (sleep duration instead of protein clearance)!

RW-D3-Q7 → Correct Answer: A

  • Skill & Domain: Craft and Structure · Text Structure and Purpose (Easy/Medium — Ecology)
  • Why A is Correct: Abstractly names the exact rhetorical job of the passage: Problem (wildfires strip shade -> lethal creek heat for juvenile coho salmon) → Observed Buffer + Physical Mechanism (beaver dams push water through gravel beds, returning cool groundwater where young salmon congregate). "One species' habitat modifications" = beaver dams; "buffer another species against post-wildfire heat stress" = keep water 4.5∘C cooler for coho salmon!
  • Why Distractors Fail:
    • B (Policy Advocacy Trap): Purely descriptive ecology—forestry policy priorities are never argued.
    • C (Off-Topic): Salmon diets are never mentioned.
    • D (Distortion): Gravel beds cool water via subsurface groundwater exchange, not by absorbing more solar radiation.
  • Next-Time Clue: Translate concrete nouns (beavers, dams, coho salmon) into abstract SAT Purpose categories (one species, habitat modification, another species)!

RW-D3-Q8 → Correct Answer: B

  • Skill & Domain: Craft and Structure · Text Structure and Purpose — Underlined Sentence Function (Medium/Hard)
  • Why B is Correct: Look BEFORE and AFTER:
    • Sentence 1: Prediction that physical proximity wouldn't matter anymore.
    • Sentence 2 (Underlined): Audit of 42,000 teams (empirical findings) + however (challenges opening prediction) + co-located = 2x breakthrough patents, whereas remote = replication & cataloging (distinguishes between two kinds of scientific output).
    • Sentence 3: Sociological explanation (hallway exchanges) for Sentence 2's pattern.
  • Why Distractors Fail:
    • A: Cloud/video technology was Sentence 1, not Sentence 2.
    • C: Sociological hallway explanation is Sentence 3 (and university vs. corporate labs is never compared!).
    • D: Direct opposite of "filed nearly twice as many breakthrough... patents" on-site!
  • Next-Time Clue: Never let an underlined-function trap steal the job of the sentence before it (Trap A) or after it (Trap C)!

RW-D3-Q9 → Correct Answer: C

  • Skill & Domain: Craft and Structure · Text Structure and Purpose — Overall Structure (Hard)
  • Why C is Correct: Maps the 3 sentences 1-to-1:
    1. Art-conservation puzzle: Matisse's vibrant cadmium yellows turning into chalky beige crusts.
    2. Initial causal hypothesis: Conservators blamed gallery UV light.
    3. Why incomplete + true chemical driver + improved preservation: Hidden frame-covered paint (zero UV!) formed the exact same crusts when humidity >65% with chlorides, leading museums to combine low-UV LEDs with dehumidification.
  • Why Distractors Fail: A invents scolding curators and banning oil yellows; B invents "two rival painters"; D invents a history of X-ray spectroscopy and a technology failure.
  • Next-Time Clue: Break Overall Structure choices into 3 clauses separated by commas and verify Clause 1 = Beginning, Clause 2 = Middle, Clause 3 = End!

RW-D3-Q10 → Correct Answer: D

  • Skill & Domain: Craft and Structure · Cross-Text Connections (Medium)
  • Why D is Correct: Notice why Day 3's strong verb refute IS justified here!
    • Text 1: Historical travelers claimed Silbo Gomero could transmit only 24–36 memorized herding commands (not open-ended language).
    • Text 2: Meyer proved experimentally that whistlers accurately transmitted newly coined sentences with unfamiliar proper names they had never heard before—directly disproving (refuting) the "fixed memorized command code" claim!
  • Why Distractors Fail: A reverses Text 2; B misreads experimental barriers as evolutionary origin; C exaggerates "exceeding three kilometers" into "ravines of any width."
  • Next-Time Clue: Check when refute IS earned: if Text 1 says "X can ONLY do memorized list L" and Text 2 proves experimentally "X effortlessly does brand-new unmemorized sentences," Text 1's restriction is falsified!

RW-D3-Q11 → Correct Answer: A

  • Skill & Domain: Craft and Structure · Cross-Text Connections — Shared Agreement (Hard)
  • Why A is Correct: Look at the opening sentence of both texts:
    • Text 1: "Carbon-offset programs that pay landowners strictly per tree seedling planted frequently backfire ecologically..."
    • Text 2: "Paying landowners by raw seedling headcount undeniably encourages single-species timber plantations over resilient native ecosystems."
    • Although they disagree sharply on the remedy (10-year delayed payout vs. annual stipends + free native nurseries), both authors explicitly agree that per-seedling headcount subsidies create perverse anti-ecological incentives!
  • Why Distractors Fail: B is rejected by Text 2 (excludes small family farms); C contradicts Text 1 (eucalyptus stores less stable carbon); D contradicts both authors' critique of headcount payments.
  • Next-Time Clue: On "both authors would agree" questions, hunt for Text 2's concession sentence ("undeniably," "rightly notes," "while it is true that")—that overlap is 95% of the time the exact correct answer!

RW-D3-Q12 → Correct Answer: C

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Command of Evidence — Textual (Medium)
  • Why C is Correct: Apply Lesson 3.2's Two-Half Checklist!
    • Hypothesis: Cuttlefish adjust camouflage (Half 1) not merely to seafloor texture (so hold seafloor constant!), (Half 2) to exploit specific visual limitations of whichever predator approaches.
    • Choice C holds seafloor texture constant ("identical uniform sand") AND shows cuttlefish switching between polarized stripes (invisible to groupers!) vs. non-polarized speckles (when polarization-seeing mantis shrimp approach!).
  • Why Distractors Fail: A only shows seafloor-texture matching without predators (the baseline "not merely..." part!); B tests tank brightness, not predator vision; D doesn't even test cuttlefish!
  • Next-Time Clue: When a hypothesis says "not merely Factor X, but also Factor Y," the winning experiment holds X constant and varies Y!

RW-D3-Q13 → Correct Answer: B

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Command of Evidence — Literary Quotation (Medium/Hard)
  • Why B is Correct: Check both halves of Park's literary claim:
    • Half 1 (Tidy predictability on charts): "every sunken reef kept its inked margin and every squall obeyed brass dividers—a quiet obedience..."
    • Half 2 (Refuge amid capricious household illness, NOT adventure yearning): "...that my sister's recurring winter fever stubbornly denied our parlor."
  • Why Distractors Fail: A suggests youthful seafaring adventure (what Park argues against!); C praises commercial accuracy only (misses household illness); D describes harbor fog only.
  • Next-Time Clue: Translate poetic contrast (obeyed brass dividers vs. recurring winter fever stubbornly denied) straight into the critic's two abstract nouns (tidy predictability vs. capricious household illness).

RW-D3-Q14 → Correct Answer: D

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Command of Evidence — Quantitative (Medium/Hard)
  • Why D is Correct: Box the engineers' full thesis: Although nanostructured TiO2​ cleans best in morning dew, hydrophobic silica is better overall for energy harvesting in dew-prone coastal deserts. Why would a solar panel that cleans slightly less dew dust (79% vs. 84%) harvest more solar energy? Because Clean-Panel Light Transmission for TiO2​ plunges to 82%, whereas hydrophobic silica transmits 93% of sunlight (even beating uncoated glass at 91%)! Choice D cites both exact pairs of numbers (84% vs. 79% dew cleaning AND 82% vs. 93% light transmission).
  • Why Distractors Fail: A argues against hydrophobic silica using dry-wind conditions (irrelevant/opposing to coastal dew conclusion); B ignores both target coatings; C cites dry wind (41% vs. 38%) rather than explaining why TiO2​'s 84% morning-dew lead loses out on energy harvesting.
  • Next-Time Clue: When an "although X beats Y on Metric 1, Y wins overall" claim appears above a 3-column table, look immediately at Column 3 to see where X collapses and Y excels!

RW-D3-Q15 → Correct Answer: A

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Command of Evidence — Quantitative Rate Normalization (Hard)
  • Why A is Correct: Box the claim: Raw valley-floor hearth counts appear to drop after 3500 BCE, but hearth density per surveyed km2 actually increased in Period II. Compute the valley-floor densities from Row 1:
    • Period I: 12 km242 hearths​=3.5 hearths/km2.
    • Period II: 4 km219 hearths​=4.75 hearths/km2. Choice A is both arithmetically true and logically proves every word of the claim!
  • Why Distractors Fail: B cites Mid-Slope instead of Valley Floor; C compares raw un-normalized Period II counts (repeating the exact fallacy the archaeologists warn against!); D cites Alpine Ridge area only.
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever a prompt says "when normalized for [area / population / hours]," divide Count ÷ Denominator before reading the choices!

RW-D3-Q16 → Correct Answer: B

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Inferences (Medium)
  • Why B is Correct: Combine the experimental premises:
    • P1: Both newcomers (Group A) and 5-year residents (Group B) owned cars, got identical free 30-day bus passes, lived ≤300 m from frequent stops, and rated reliability equally high.
    • P2: Yet newcomers boosted bus rides by +48%, whereas long-term residents boosted rides by only +6%!
    • Deduction: Since stop distance and perceived reliability were equal, established routine/habit among settled residents blunts temporary free-fare incentives (Choice B).
  • Why Distractors Fail: A invents commute distance to job centers; C uses extreme "permanently eliminate automobile ownership" from a 30-day trial; D invents a speculation about morning crowding.
  • Next-Time Clue: In controlled experiments where Variables X and Y are held equal (even though both groups lived within 300 m and rated reliability equally high), the inference must trace the outcome gap to the one variable that differed (recent move vs. 5-year settled routine)!

RW-D3-Q17 → Correct Answer: C

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Inferences (Hard — Chemical Ecology)
  • Why C is Correct: Combine the bioassay puzzle pieces carefully:
    • P1: Dodder grows toward tomato volatiles (α-pinene) and away from wheat volatiles ((Z)-3-hexenyl acetate).
    • P2: Dodder grows vigorously toward purified α-pinene alone (proving α-pinene suffices to attract it).
    • P3: When a real, healthy tomato stem (full of attractive α-pinene!) is dabbed with trace (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate, dodder stops growing toward the tomato completely!
    • Deduction: Wheat avoidance isn't just "wheat lacks α-pinene"—(Z)-3-hexenyl acetate actively repels / overrides attractive tomato signals (Choice C, hedged carefully with "at least in part").
  • Why Distractors Fail: A contradicts P1; B directly contradicts P2 (grew vigorously toward purified α-pinene alone!); D invents internal wheat biosynthesis shutdown.
  • Next-Time Clue: Notice how Choice B fails by contradicting a single clause (purified α-pinene alone)—checking premises one by one eliminates hard science traps cleanly.

RW-D3-Q18 → Correct Answer: B

  • Skill & Domain: Information and Ideas · Inferences (Hard — Quantitative History)
  • Why B is Correct: Combine the historical premises:
    • P1: Historians count marriage-register signatures to estimate how many villagers were literate (could read).
    • P2: Rural schools taught reading at ages 6–9, but taught quill writing/signing only after age 10!
    • P3: Most peasant daughters left school before age 10 for farm/textile work (after learning to read, BEFORE learning to sign their names!).
    • Deduction: Many villagers—and disproportionately rural women—could read printed text even though they marked a cross on marriage registers, so signature counts systematically underestimate reading literacy (Choice B)!
  • Why Distractors Fail: A reverses ages 6–9 (reading) vs. 10+ (quill writing); C introduces an Alien Comparison (urban French ports never mentioned!); D compares household book vs. paper rarity beyond the text.
  • Next-Time Clue: Whenever Historians use Proxy Metric M (signatures) to measure Trait T (reading) and archival facts show people acquired T without acquiring M, conclude: M underestimates T!

subSections.title: D. Math Practice Questions (MATH-D3-Q1 to MATH-D3-Q16) — Step-by-Step & Desmos Explanations
subSections.titleHtml: D. Math Practice Questions (MATH-D3-Q1 to MATH-D3-Q16) — Step-by-Step & Desmos Explanations
subSections.html:
MATH-D3-Q1 → Correct Answer: C (x^2 + 6x + 1)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Distribute −2 across every term inside the second parentheses:
    (3x2−4x+7)−2x2+10x−6=(3−2)x2+(−4+10)x+(7−6)=x2+6x+1
  • Quick Value Check (x=1): Original: (3−4+7)−2(1−5+3)=6−2(−1)=8. Test Choice C at x=1: 1+6+1=8 ✓ (A gives −12, B gives −4, D gives 20—all eliminated instantly!).
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (-14x) distributes −2(−5x) as −10x; Trap D (+13) distributes −2(+3) as +6.

MATH-D3-Q2 → Correct Answer (SPR): 3.5 (or 7/2)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: By the Zero-Product Property, either factor equals 0:
    • 2x−7=0⟹2x=7⟹x=3.5 (7/2)
    • x+4=0⟹x=−4
    • Boxed target asks for the positive solution ⟹3.5 (or 7/2).
  • Trap Alert: Entering -4 or adding the two roots!

MATH-D3-Q3 → Correct Answer: C ((3, -5))

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Apply Lesson 3.4's transformation rule to vertex (−2,−9):
    • Inside f(x−5) shifts RIGHT 5 units ⟹xnew​=−2+5=3.
    • Outside +4 shifts UP 4 units ⟹ynew​=−9+4=−5.
    • New vertex: (3,−5).
  • Desmos 8-Second Method: Type f(x) = (x + 2)^2 - 9 on Line 1 and g(x) = f(x - 5) + 4 on Line 2 → click the minimum point of g(x): (3, -5)!
  • Trap Alert: Trap A ((-7, -5)) moves left 5 instead of right 5 (the #1 sign-direction error on SAT functions!).

MATH-D3-Q4 → Correct Answer (SPR): 9

  • 3-Second Vieta Shortcut: For 2x2−18x+29=0 (a=2,b=−18,c=29):
    1. Check real roots exist: D=(−18)2−4(2)(29)=324−232=92>0 ✓ (two distinct real roots).
    2. Sum of solutions =−ab​=−2−18​=9.
  • Desmos Verification: Graph y = 2x^2 - 18x + 29 and click both x-intercepts (2.102 and 6.898): 2.102+6.898=9!
  • Trap Alert: Forgetting to divide by a=2 (entering 18) or dropping the negative sign in −b/a (entering -9).

MATH-D3-Q5 → Correct Answer: C ((9x - 3) / (x^2 - 9))

  • Step-by-Step Algebraic Solution: Common denominator is (x−3)(x+3)=x2−9:
    (x−3)(x+3)4(x+3)+5(x−3)​=x2−94x+12+5x−15​=x2−99x−3​
  • Desmos / Plug-In x=5 Check: At x=5, original =24​+85​=2+0.625=2.625 (21/8). Choice C gives 25−945−3​=1642​=821​=2.625 ✓!
  • Trap Alert: Trap A adds numerators AND denominators (x−3+x+34+5​); Trap D distributes +5(−3) as +15.

MATH-D3-Q6 → Correct Answer (SPR): 6

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Set height h(t)=0 and divide every term by −5:
    −5t2+25t+30=0⟹t2−5t−6=0⟹(t−6)(t+1)=0
    Since time after launch satisfies t≥0, discard t=−1 ⟹t=6 seconds.
  • Desmos 5-Second Method: Graph y = -5x^2 + 25x + 30 and click the positive x-intercept at (6, 0)!
  • Trap Alert: Entering 2.5 (the time of maximum height at the vertex (2.5, 61.25), rather than when the sonde strikes the valley floor!).

MATH-D3-Q7 → Correct Answer (SPR): 12

  • Step-by-Step Coefficient Matching: Expand (ax+3)(2x−b)=2ax2+(6−ab)x−3b and match coefficients to 10x2−29x−21:
    1. Match x2: 2a=10⟹a=5.
    2. Match constant: −3b=−21⟹b=7.
    3. Verify middle x term (never skip!): 6−(5)(7)=6−35=−29 ✓!
    4. Boxed target: a+b=5+7=12.
  • Desmos Regression Shortcut: Type (a*x_1 + 3)(2*x_1 - b) ~ 10*x_1^2 - 29*x_1 - 21 with list x_1 = [1, 2, 3] → Desmos outputs a = 5, b = 7 immediately!
  • Trap Alert: Matching −3b=−21 as b=−7 (sign slip → entering -2).

MATH-D3-Q8 → Correct Answer: B (7 only)

  • Step-by-Step Solution:
    1. Square both sides to generate candidates:
      4x+21=x2⟹x2−4x−21=0⟹(x−7)(x+3)=0⟹x=7 or x=−3
    2. Mandatory Un-Squared Substitution Check:
      • Test x=7: 4(7)+21​=49​=7=RHS ✓ (Valid!)
      • Test x=−3: 4(−3)+21​=9​=+3=−3 (Extraneous—Reject!)
  • Desmos Visual Guarantee: Graph y = sqrt(4x + 21) and y = x. Because x​≥0, the radical curve stays on or above the x-axis and intersects y = x ONLY once, at (7, 7)!
  • Trap Alert: Trap C (Both -3 and 7) is the #1 Advanced Math trap on the entire Digital SAT—never skip checking radical roots!

MATH-D3-Q9 → Correct Answer: C (30)

  • Step-by-Step Dimensional Analysis: Write fraction units explicitly so unwanted units cancel diagonally:
    1 hr1.8 km​×1 km1,000 m​×60 min1 hr​=60 min1,800 m​=30 m/min
  • Trap Alert: Trap D (108) multiplies 1.8×60 without converting kilometers to meters (or multiplies by 60 instead of dividing!).

MATH-D3-Q10 → Correct Answer: C (30%)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Box the phrase percent greater than Control Plot B:
    • Difference =65−50=15 bushels/acre.
    • Reference denominator (after "than") =Control Plot B=50:
      5065−50​×100%=5015​×100%=30%
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (15%) confuses raw bushel difference (15) with percentage; Trap B (23%) divides by 65 (Plot A) instead of 50 (Plot B); Trap D (130%) answers "what percent OF Plot B" rather than "what percent GREATER THAN Plot B."

MATH-D3-Q11 → Correct Answer (SPR): 0.35 (or 7/20)

  • Step-by-Step Solution:
    1. Plug x=2.5 km into the line of best fit to get the predicted boiling point:
      y^​=100−3.3(2.5)=100−8.25=91.75∘C
    2. Subtract predicted from actual (92.1∘C):
      Residual=y−y^​=92.1−91.75=0.35
  • Trap Alert: Entering 91.75 (stopping at the predicted value without subtracting from 92.1).

MATH-D3-Q12 → Correct Answer: B (13/22)

  • Step-by-Step Solution: Read the exact restriction after "selected at random from":
    • Subgroup denominator: those with a lead-free glaze ⟹ Column 1 Total =132 (ignore 240 and 120!).
    • Favorable numerator: porcelain AND lead-free glaze =78.
    • Simplify fraction (or type 78/132 in Desmos and click the fraction button!):
      13278​=132÷678÷6​=2213​
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (13/40) uses grand total 240 (24078​); Trap C (13/20) uses Porcelain row total 120 (12078​, answering "given porcelain, what is the probability of lead-free glaze?"—backwards condition!).

MATH-D3-Q13 → Correct Answer (SPR): 800

  • Step-by-Step Multiplier Equation: Let P = original catalog price.
    • 20% discount multiplies price by (1−0.20)=0.80.
    • 5% freight fee added to that discounted price multiplies by (1+0.05)=1.05:
      P×0.80×1.05=672⟹0.84P=672⟹P=0.84672​=800
  • Forward Check: ✓!
  • Trap Alert: Combining −20%+5%=−15% (672/0.85=790.59 — wrong, because +5% applies to the discounted 0.80P, not to P!), or multiplying .

MATH-D3-Q14 → Correct Answer: D (5,000)

  • Step-by-Step Squared-Unit Solution:
    1. Square the linear conversion 1 km=1,000 m:
      1 km2=(1,000 m)×(1,000 m)=1,000,000 m2
    2. Convert sanctuary area to square meters:
      4.5 km2=4.5×1,000,000 m2=4,500,000 m2
    3. Divide total area by area per quadrat (900 m2):
      900 m24,500,000 m2​=945,000​=5,000
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (5) uses 1 km2=1,000 m2 (9004,500​=5)—off by a factor of 1,000!

MATH-D3-Q15 → Correct Answer: C

  • Step-by-Step Study-Design Evaluation: Check the two SAT Statistical Inference Rules:
    1. Who was randomly sampled? Adult residents of Rotterdam ⟹ scope generalizes to Rotterdam adults (eliminates A "adults worldwide").
    2. Was gardening randomly assigned? No! It was an observational survey of existing habits (maybe retirees or low-stress workers have more free time to garden). Without random assignment to treatments, causation cannot be claimed (eliminates A, B, and D), leaving negative association (Choice C)!

MATH-D3-Q16 → Correct Answer: B (Between 1,980 and 3,060)

  • Step-by-Step Solution:
    1. Form the plausible percentage interval using sample estimate ± margin of error:
      14%−3%=11%to14%+3%=17%
    2. Scale to the entire district population of 18,000 mature ash trees:
      • Lower bound: 0.11×18,000=1,980
      • Upper bound: 0.17×18,000=3,060
  • Trap Alert: Trap A (33 to 51) multiplies [11%,17%] by sample size 300 instead of population 18,000; Trap D forgets to subtract the 3% margin of error on the lower bound!

errorLab.beforeKeyHtml:
Part A: Morning Cold Re-Solve Verification (Day 1–2 Trap Check — 5 Minutes)

Confirm you completed both disguised Day 1–2 checks cleanly during 09:00–09:20 without checking old keys:

  1. Day 2 Modifier + Comma-Splice Check: Fix if needed: "Carved from dense Anatolian boxwood, luthiers prize Turkish oud pegs for holding pitch through desert temperature swings." → Dangling modifier! Luthiers aren't carved from boxwood: "Carved from dense Anatolian boxwood, Turkish oud pegs are prized by luthiers for holding pitch..."
  2. Day 2 Strict-Inequality Modeling Check: Plan X costs ; Plan Y costs . Minimum integer n for Plan Y to cost strictly less than Plan X? → 150+1.5n<90+3n⟹60<1.5n⟹n>40⟹41 (NOT 40!).

Part B: Classify Five Day 3 Student Mistakes (EL-D3-CASE-1 to EL-D3-CASE-5)

For each realistic student mistake below, assign (1) Primary Error Code (E1–E10), (2) Vocabulary/Language Label (V1–V7, if R&W), and (3) a 1-sentence Prevention Rule:
errorLab.caseKeyHtml:
• EL-D3-CASE-1: E3 (Passage misread — Old-View Reversal Trap) + V3 (Missed participial concession structure) — Prevention Rule: Never treat "Long framed as X..." or "Traditionally assumed to be X..." as the author's thesis; read past the main clause verb to capture the revision!
  • EL-D3-CASE-2: E5 (Incorrect inference) + V7 (Failed to connect evidence to the claim — True-Fact / Wrong-Column Trap) — Prevention Rule: Verify logical sufficiency against every condition in the boxed thesis (morning dew + energy harvesting = light transmission), not merely whether numbers match a table cell.
  • EL-D3-CASE-3: E1 / E7 / E9 (Skipped mandatory un-squared radical check) — Prevention Rule: Whenever an equation contains x​, substitute every candidate back into the un-squared original (or check Desmos intersection) to eliminate negative extraneous roots.
  • EL-D3-CASE-4: E7 (Linear vs. squared unit conversion error) — Prevention Rule: Whenever units carry an exponent (km2,ft2,m3), raise the conversion factor to that exact same exponent ((1,000)2=106).
  • EL-D3-CASE-5: E4 (Misread conditional probability denominator) — Prevention Rule: Circle the exact phrase right after "selected at random from..." (those with a lead-free glaze = 132) and write that number in the denominator BEFORE looking for the numerator.
errorLab.afterKeyHtml:
Part C: Personal Day 3 Error-Log & 3+ Escalation Audit (10 Minutes)

Record every missed or guessed item from today's R&W comprehension set (RW-D3-Q1..18), Math set (MATH-D3-Q1..16), and College Board Question Bank blocks in SAT-Error-Log-and-Daily-Reflections.md. Check your 3-day cumulative counts:

  • Have E3/E5 (evidence/pivot misreads), E4 (wording/denominator traps), or V4 (context clue misses) hit 3+ total entries? Flag them in your Priority Weakness Escalation Table before tomorrow's Hard-Module Simulation Day!

cases.promptHtml: Reading quickly under time pressure, Kenji read Sentence 1's opening phrase ("Long framed by older maritime histories as an enterprise driven primarily by European appetite for Asian silks and porcelain...") and chose an answer stating European luxury demand was the sole driver of the Manila Galleon trade, missing the pivot to Ming China's silver tax.
cases.answerHtml: E3 (Passage misread — Old-View Reversal Trap) + V3 (Missed participial concession structure) — Prevention Rule: Never treat "Long framed as X..." or "Traditionally assumed to be X..." as the author's thesis; read past the main clause verb to capture the revision!

cases.promptHtml: On the solar-panel table, Sofia noticed Choice C (41% vs. 38% dry dust removal) matched the exact numbers in Column 1 of the table, saw it favored hydrophobic silica, and picked C without checking why the prompt talked about morning dew and energy-harvesting suitability.
cases.answerHtml: E5 (Incorrect inference) + V7 (Failed to connect evidence to the claim — True-Fact / Wrong-Column Trap) — Prevention Rule: Verify logical sufficiency against every condition in the boxed thesis (morning dew + energy harvesting = light transmission), not merely whether numbers match a table cell.

cases.promptHtml: Solving 4x+21​=x, Tariq squared both sides cleanly, factored (x−7)(x+3)=0, got −3 and 7, and immediately selected Choice C (Both -3 and 7).
cases.answerHtml: E1 / E7 / E9 (Skipped mandatory un-squared radical check) — Prevention Rule: Whenever an equation contains x​, substitute every candidate back into the un-squared original (or check Desmos intersection) to eliminate negative extraneous roots.

cases.promptHtml: Seeing "4.5 square kilometers" and "1 kilometer = 1,000 meters," Mei multiplied 4.5×1,000=4,500, divided by 900, and selected Choice A (5).
cases.answerHtml: E7 (Linear vs. squared unit conversion error) — Prevention Rule: Whenever units carry an exponent (km2,ft2,m3), raise the conversion factor to that exact same exponent ((1,000)2=106).

cases.promptHtml: On the ceramic glaze two-way table, Lukas saw 78 porcelain lead-free vessels and divided by 120 (total porcelain vessels) instead of 132 (total lead-free vessels), picking Choice C (13/20).
cases.answerHtml: E4 (Misread conditional probability denominator) — Prevention Rule: Circle the exact phrase right after "selected at random from..." (those with a lead-free glaze = 132) and write that number in the denominator BEFORE looking for the numerator.

mastery.introHtml: Complete all 10 synthesis questions below closed-notes in 9 minutes:

masteryItems.promptHtml: Fill both blanks accurately: "Whereas critics claimed the sensor glitch would ______ the satellite's credibility, engineers argued the rapid software patch actually ______ the mission's resilience."
masteryItems.answerHtml: First blank = undermine (weaken); Second blank = underscored (strongly emphasized).

masteryItems.promptHtml: On a Cross-Text question, Text 2 says "Although Dr. Patel accurately calculates solar panel manufacturing emissions, she overlooks 30 years of grid coal displacement." Does Text 2 completely refute Dr. Patel's emission calculation, or concede it while qualifying her broader conclusion?
masteryItems.answerHtml: Concedes her emission calculation while qualifying/challenging her broader conclusion (±)—never pick "completely refutes her calculation"!

masteryItems.promptHtml: In "Geologists attributed the canyon's terraces to glacial outburst floods," which noun is the cause and which noun is the effect?
masteryItems.answerHtml: Cause: glacial outburst floods (after to); Effect: the canyon's terraces.

masteryItems.promptHtml: Fill both blanks: "String theorists ______ extra spatial dimensions mathematically, though physicists are still designing ______ experiments to detect them."
masteryItems.answerHtml: First blank = posit; Second blank = empirical.

masteryItems.promptHtml: If a claim states "Species M outcompetes Species N only in high-salinity marshes," why must supporting table data include low-salinity marsh numbers in addition to high-salinity numbers?
masteryItems.answerHtml: Without low-salinity data showing Species M does not outcompete Species N there, Species M might outcompete Species N everywhere—which would falsify "only"!

masteryItems.promptHtml: If f(x) has maximum point (−3,10), what is the maximum point of h(x)=f(x+4)−7?
masteryItems.answerHtml: Shift left 4 (−3−4=−7) and down 7 (10−7=3) ⟹(−7,3).

masteryItems.promptHtml: What is the sum of the real solutions to 4x2+28x−15=0?
masteryItems.answerHtml: Check D=282−4(4)(−15)=784+240>0; Sum =−ab​=−428​=−7.

masteryItems.promptHtml: Find all real solutions to 2x+15​=x.
masteryItems.answerHtml: Squaring gives x2−2x−15=0⟹(x−5)(x+3)=0. Check x=5: 25​=5 ✓; check x=−3: 9​=+3=−3 (reject!). Solution: 5 only.

masteryItems.promptHtml: Convert 0.03 km2 into square meters (1 km=1,000 m).
masteryItems.answerHtml: 0.03×(1,000)2=0.03×1,000,000=30,000 m2.

masteryItems.promptHtml: City A has 72 tram stops and City B has 60 tram stops. City A has what percent more tram stops than City B?
masteryItems.answerHtml: 6072−60​×100%=6012​×100%=20%.

mastery.keyHtml:
1. First blank = undermine (weaken); Second blank = underscored (strongly emphasized).
  2. Concedes her emission calculation while qualifying/challenging her broader conclusion (±)—never pick "completely refutes her calculation"!
  3. Cause: glacial outburst floods (after to); Effect: the canyon's terraces.
  4. First blank = posit; Second blank = empirical.
  5. Without low-salinity data showing Species M does not outcompete Species N there, Species M might outcompete Species N everywhere—which would falsify "only"!
  6. Shift left 4 (−3−4=−7) and down 7 (10−7=3) ⟹(−7,3).
  7. Check D=282−4(4)(−15)=784+240>0; Sum =−ab​=−428​=−7.
  8. Squaring gives x2−2x−15=0⟹(x−5)(x+3)=0. Check x=5: 25​=5 ✓; check x=−3: 9​=+3=−3 (reject!). Solution: 5 only.
  9. 0.03×(1,000)2=0.03×1,000,000=30,000 m2.
  10. 6072−60​×100%=6012​×100%=20%.

mastery.matrixHtml:

Multi-Day Spaced Retrieval (SR-D3-Q1..12) >= 10 / 12 (83%+) Carry any missed Day 1 or Day 2 word into Day 4's "Priority 3-Touch Vocabulary Box".
Day 3 Vocab Recall (Exercise 4C-5) >= 8 / 10 (80%+) Re-write personal context sentences for missed words (posit, entail, underscore, tenuous, caveat) before bed.

objectives.html:
By 15:00 today, you will demonstrate:

  1. Vocabulary Independence Under Uncertainty: Solve Medium/Hard Words in Context questions accurately even when 1–2 answer choices are unfamiliar, using strict polarity/scope elimination rather than guessing familiar-looking traps.
  2. Cumulative 30-Word Retention (>=80% on SR-D4-Q1..15): Retrieve and discriminate nuanced academic vocabulary from Days 1–3 under mixed testing conditions, while adding 10 Hard-tier concession, skepticism, and precision words (#31–#40, bringing your structured bank to 40 words).
  3. Expression of Ideas Speed Banking (>=85% at <=45 sec/Q): Solve Transitions via twin-elimination and Rhetorical Synthesis by reading only the goal prompt first (skipping bullet notes whenever choice grammar/content suffices).
  4. Hard Module-2 Math Gatekeepers (>=75% across MATH-D4-Q1..16): Apply D=b2−4ac=0 for tangency, rewrite a(1.21)t/2 into annual percent growth, convert xmnxp​, complete the square on circles, and scale similar volumes/areas (s3 vs. s2).
  5. Tactical Pacing & Bailout Discipline: Classify every Math item within 5 seconds (Desmos vs. Manual vs. Plug-In) and enforce the 75-second R&W / 90-second Math mark-and-return bailout rule with zero >2.5-minute freezes.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.1: Vocabulary Independence — Scoring Accurately When 1–2 Answer Choices Are Unknown
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 4.1: Vocabulary Independence — Scoring Accurately When 1–2 Answer Choices Are Unknown
lessons.html:
Every international student eventually reaches a Harder Module 2 Words in Context question where two choices are familiar and one or two choices are completely unknown. Native-speaker intuition will not save you here—probability and logical discipline will.

A. The Four Non-Negotiable Rules for Unknown Answer Choices

Suppose you have predicted your own simple English fill-in (Prediction = "avoid / get around an obstacle"), and the choices are:

  • A) corroborate (known — confirm)
  • B) proliferate (known — multiply rapidly)
  • C) circumvent (suppose unknown today)
  • D) ameliorate (suppose unknown today)

Follow this exact sequence every time:

  1. Rule 1 — Test Every KNOWN Word Against Your Context Prediction First:
    Never stare at unknown words first! Check A (confirm) → wrong logic, cross out! Check B (multiply rapidly) → wrong logic, cross out! You just jumped from a 25% guess to a 50% shot in 12 seconds.
  2. Rule 2 — NEVER Pick a Known Word That Violates Context Just Because You Recognize It (Familiarity Bias):
    This is the single costliest error international students make on Hard R&W: picking Choice A (corroborate) simply because "I studied corroborate on Day 1!" If a word you know 100% does not fit the sentence's logic, it has a 0% chance of being right—eliminate it ruthlessly!
  3. Rule 3 — NEVER Eliminate an Unknown Word Just Because It Looks Strange:
    If all three words you DO know fail your context prediction, pick the remaining unknown word with 100% confidence and move on in 5 seconds! You do not need to define Choice C if A, B, and D are provably false.
  4. Rule 4 — When Down to Two Unknowns, Use Directional Word Parts (Prefix + Suffix Check):
    • Look at circum- (circle / around, like circumference) in circumvent vs. -melior- in ameliorate → circum- matches "go around an obstacle"!
    • Watch negative/privative prefixes (in-, un-, im-, dis-, pre-clude) vs. positive/together prefixes (con-, co-, sym-).

B. Secondary Academic Polysemy (Everyday Word, Uncommon Academic Job)

Hard SAT Words in Context loves ordinary 5-letter English words used in formal scientific/historical senses (V2 trap):

Familiar Word Everyday Meaning (Usually Trap!) High-Frequency SAT Academic Meaning Contextual Example
arrest (v.) Police handcuff a suspect Stop, halt, or freeze a physical, biological, or economic process "Rapid freeze-drying arrests enzymatic decay in berry tissues."
yield (v./n.) Traffic sign ("let cars pass") (v.) Produce / generate data or crops; (v.2) give way under force; (n.) output "Spectroscopy yielded unexpected methane signatures."
afford (v.) Have enough money to buy Provide, supply, or grant an opportunity or view "High limestone bluffs afford ornithologists unobstructed views."
harbor (v.) Port where ships dock (noun) Hold privately (a doubt/hope) OR shelter (microbes/species) "Deadwood snags harbor rare saproxylic beetles."

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 4.1 (Check answers in Section 8)

  • CC-D4-RW1: Your context prediction is "rule out / make impossible." You know Choice A (substantiate = prove), Choice B (bolster = strengthen), and Choice D (concede = admit), and none of those three fit "make impossible." You have never seen Choice C (preclude) in your life. Which choice MUST you select, and why?
  • CC-D4-RW2: What does arrested mean in "Introducing dry nitrogen gas into the bronze display case arrested chloride corrosion across the helmet's rim"?

B. Secondary Academic Polysemy (Everyday Word, Uncommon Academic Job)
Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 4.1 (Check answers in Section 8)

You know Choice A (substantiate = prove), Choice B (bolster = strengthen), and Choice D (concede = admit), and none of those three fit "make impossible." You have never seen Choice C (preclude) in your life. Which choice MUST you select, and why?

lessons.title: Lesson 4.2: Expression of Ideas Speed Bank (<45 Seconds/Q) — Transitions & Rhetorical Synthesis
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 4.2: Expression of Ideas Speed Bank (<45 Seconds/Q) — Transitions & Rhetorical Synthesis
lessons.html:
In Harder Module 2, Inferences and Command of Evidence passages demand 90–105 seconds of deep focus. Where do you earn that extra time? By solving the 5–7 Transitions and Rhetorical Synthesis questions at the end of the module in 30–45 seconds each with 90%+ accuracy!

A. Transitions — Read Before & After With the Blank Covered!

Never read the transition word currently sitting in Choice A first—it poisons your ear! Cover the blank, label Idea 1 (before blank) and Idea 2 (after blank), and pick the exact logical bridge:

Logical Relationship Core SAT Transition Markers Exact Test
1. Contrast / Concession (+ vs. -) However, Nevertheless, Nonetheless, Even so, Still, Conversely, By contrast, On the other hand, Regardless Idea 2 pushes against, surprises, or reverses Idea 1. (Note: Conversely requires a symmetrical two-sided flip, whereas Nevertheless / Still means "despite that fact"!)
2. Cause → Effect Therefore, Consequently, Thus, Hence, Accordingly, As a result Idea 1 is the reason/evidence; Idea 2 is the logical outcome.
3. Continuation / Addition Moreover, Furthermore, In addition, Similarly, Likewise Idea 2 adds a second point in the exact same direction (Similarly/Likewise = parallel case on a new subject; Moreover/Furthermore = stronger/extra point on same argument).
4. Example / Specification For instance, For example, Specifically, In particular, Fittingly Idea 2 gives a concrete named case or zoomed-in detail proving Idea 1 (Fittingly = appropriately matching a name or theme!).
5. Restatement / Clarification In other words, That is, Indeed That is / In other words = exact rephrasing; Indeed = emphatic confirmation escalating Idea 1.

5-Second "Functional Twin" Shortcut on Transitions:
When two answer choices perform the exact same logical job in context (e.g., A) However, and B) Nevertheless, where no subtle concession distinction exists, or C) Furthermore, and D) Moreover,), eliminate BOTH twins immediately!

B. Rhetorical Synthesis ("Student Notes") — Goal-First Protocol (35 Seconds!)

International students waste 90+ seconds reading all 5 bullet notes slowly before reading the question! Reverse the order:

  1. Step 1 — Read ONLY the Final Question Stem ("The student wants to...") FIRST (8 Seconds):
    Underline every required constraint in the goal:
    • "emphasize a similarity between X and Y" (must name BOTH + state shared trait—cross out any choice mentioning "whereas / unlike"!)
    • "present the study's methodology and primary finding to an audience unfamiliar with [Term T]" (must define Term T + state HOW tested + state RESULT!)
    • "specify the reason why X occurred" (must contain causal logic because / due to / to prevent, NOT just a date or description!)
  2. Step 2 — Filter Choices A–D Directly Against Your Boxed Goal Constraints (15 Seconds):
    On 80% of SAT Rhetorical Synthesis items, 3 choices fail the goal constraints outright without you ever needing to read the bullet list!
  3. Step 3 — Glance at the Bullet Notes ONLY to Break a Tie or Verify One Number/Fact (10 Seconds).

Worked Example 4.2 (Goal-First Rhetorical Synthesis Without Reading Bullets First!)

Question Stem Only: The student wants to contrast the regeneration speed of tropical seagrass meadows with that of subarctic eelgrass beds.

  • A) Both tropical seagrass meadows and subarctic eelgrass beds anchor coastal sediments and store marine carbon. (Similarity—fails contrast + misses speed!)
  • B) Tropical seagrass meadows can regrow disturbed shoots within six weeks, whereas subarctic eelgrass beds often require four to seven years to recover. (Contrasts whereas + both species + regeneration speed!)
  • C) Subarctic eelgrass beds, which grow in cold North Atlantic estuaries, require four to seven years to recover from anchor scarring. (Missing tropical seagrass entirely!)
  • D) Marine botanists measured shoot regrowth across twelve tropical seagrass meadows and nine subarctic eelgrass beds. (Methodology only—states zero regeneration speeds!)
    Solved in 22 seconds (Choice B)—then 5-second glance at bullets confirms "six weeks" and "four to seven years" match the notes!

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 4.2

  • CC-D4-RW3: Sentence 1 states that Roman concrete seawalls have endured pounding waves for two millennia. Sentence 2 states that modern Portland-cement piers often crack within fifty years in saltwater. Which transition family connects Sentence 1 to Sentence 2, and why would Consequently, be wrong?
  • CC-D4-RW4: What is the exact difference between That is, and Moreover, at the start of Sentence 2?
  • CC-D4-RW5: If a Rhetorical Synthesis prompt asks to "introduce the architect and her most famous bridge to an audience unfamiliar with her work," why must you eliminate a choice beginning "Like her earlier bridges in Zurich, Salginatobel Bridge..." if it never explains who she is?

checks.promptHtml: Sentence 1 states that Roman concrete seawalls have endured pounding waves for two millennia. Sentence 2 states that modern Portland-cement piers often crack within fifty years in saltwater. Which transition family connects Sentence 1 to Sentence 2, and why would Consequently, be wrong?
checks.answerHtml: Contrast (However, / By contrast,) — Sentence 1 highlights 2,000-year Roman concrete durability (+), while Sentence 2 contrasts 50-year modern concrete cracking (-). Consequently, fails because Roman durability did not cause modern piers to crack!

checks.promptHtml: What is the exact difference between That is, and Moreover, at the start of Sentence 2?
checks.answerHtml: That is, restates the exact same idea from Sentence 1 in clearer or more specific words (Sentence 2 = Sentence 1), whereas Moreover, introduces a brand-new, additional supporting point (Sentence 2 = Extra Point #2).

checks.promptHtml: If a Rhetorical Synthesis prompt asks to "introduce the architect and her most famous bridge to an audience unfamiliar with her work," why must you eliminate a choice beginning "Like her earlier bridges in Zurich, Salginatobel Bridge..." if it never explains who she is?
checks.answerHtml: Because an audience unfamiliar with the architect has no idea who "her" is or what "her earlier bridges in Zurich" refers to! For an unfamiliar audience, the correct choice must introduce her full name/identity explicitly rather than presupposing prior knowledge.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.3: Surviving Harder Module 2 Passages & the 75-Second Bailout Rule
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 4.3: Surviving Harder Module 2 Passages & the 75-Second Bailout Rule
lessons.html:
A. Deconstructing Skeptical & Double-Negative Academic Framing

Hard Module-2 passages frequently layer skepticism markers (ostensibly, purportedly, nominally) or litotes / double negatives (not implausible, hardly inconsequential, far from unambiguous):

  • Double-Negative Cancellation Trick: Cross out both negative halves and read the core tone:
    • "hardly inconsequential" = NOT + NOT important ⟹ significantly important (+)!
    • "not implausible" = NOT + unbelievable ⟹ reasonable / believable (+)!
    • "ostensibly designed to protect small weavers" ⟹ on the surface claimed to protect them, signaling that in reality it did NOT!

B. The Non-Negotiable 75-Second R&W Bailout Rule

On Harder Module 2, every question counts roughly the same tier weight—nobody gets bonus points for spending 3 minutes on one brutal literary inference while rushing 3 easy grammar/transition questions at the end!

  • If you hit 75 seconds on a dense passage (Q11–Q14) and two choices still look plausible:
    1. Cross out the 2 clearly wrong choices,
    2. Click your stronger evidence match of the remaining two,
    3. Click "Mark for Review", and move immediately so you never run out of time!

Short Comprehension Check — Lesson 4.3

  • CC-D4-RW6: Translate "The archival gap is far from trivial" into 4 plain English words with zero negatives.
  • CC-D4-RW7: Fix the Hard SEC boundary/modifier error if one exists: "Celebrated for calculating comet orbits accurately, Halley's 1705 treatise predicted the return of a bright periodic comet in 1758." (Careful: can a treatise/book calculate comet orbits, or did Edmond Halley calculate them?!)
