checks.promptHtml: Why should you jot ?Q12 on your scratch paper during the exam even if you end up guessing Q12 correctly?
checks.answerHtml: On Bluebook's score summary, a lucky 50-50 guess gets the exact same green checkmark as a question you knew with 100% certainty—hiding fragile vocabulary or reasoning. Jotting ?Q12 on your scratch paper captures unstable guesses so tomorrow morning's Day 7 Blind Cold Re-Solve repairs the underlying skill before December 5.

checks.promptHtml: Why do we forbid reading Bluebook's answer explanations on Day 6 afternoon and save them until after Day 7's morning blind cold re-solve?
checks.answerHtml: Reading official explanations immediately after a 2.5-hour full test while mentally fatigued creates passive recognition ("the illusion of competence": "Oh, Choice C makes sense now") and permanently spoils the question. Waiting until tomorrow morning lets you re-solve every missed question blind and untimed with a fresh brain, separating careless/timing slips from genuine comprehension gaps and doubling long-term retention.

checks.promptHtml: On Practice Test 5, you encounter two unfamiliar words: (1) pishtaq (an architectural arch term in a single passage) and (2) vindicate (an answer choice in Words in Context). Which word belongs in your Vocabulary Notebook, and why?
checks.answerHtml: Log vindicate ("to prove someone or a doubted claim right after earlier criticism") because it is a reusable, cross-topic academic verb tested repeatedly across SAT Words in Context and science/history passages. Skip pishtaq because narrow architectural or technical nouns are explained by context inside that single passage and almost never reappear.

checks.promptHtml: During R&W Module 2, you notice the passages have much denser academic vocabulary than Module 1. What does that tell you about your Module 1 performance, and how should you react emotionally?
checks.answerHtml: Denser academic vocabulary and subtler distractors in R&W Module 2 are great news: they confirm your strong Module 1 accuracy routed you into Harder Module 2, unlocking the 650–800 scaled score ceiling! React calmly, trust your Split-Order pacing (Q15–27 → Q1–14), and enforce the 75-second bailout rule so one ultra-hard item never steals points from four reachable questions.

subSections.titleHtml: B. Day 6 Exam-Tier Academic Vocabulary (Words #49–#54 — Complete During 13:15–13:35 Block!)
subSections.html:
Study these 6 high-frequency SAT exam words (#49–#54) during your afternoon R&W triage block, then add 6–10 personal unfamiliar words from your Bluebook Practice Test 5 right below them in Vocabulary-Notebook-and-Spaced-Review.md (Rows 61–70).

49. exacerbate (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To make a problem, bad situation, or harmful condition worse or more severe.
  • Master SAT Triad (Memorize Together!): Mitigate (Day 2 #18 = lessen harm) & Ameliorate (Day 4 #39 = make better) ⟷ Exacerbate (= make worse!).
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: worsen, aggravate, intensify, compound · Ant: mitigate, ameliorate, alleviate.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Draining peatlands for timber plantations exacerbates regional wildfire risk because dried sphagnum moss ignites readily and smolders underground for weeks."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Drying out wet peat bogs makes wildfire danger much worse (exacerbates it).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing exacerbate with exaggerate ("overstate in speech"). Overstating a storm on TV exaggerates it; warm ocean water exacerbates (physically worsens) the storm!
  • Short Application Activity: Choose exaggerated or exacerbated: "Prolonged summer drought ______ bark-beetle tree mortality across Sierra Nevada pine forests." (exacerbated).

50. unprecedented (adjective)

  • Simple English Definition: Never done, seen, or experienced before; having zero earlier historical example.
  • Root Clue: un- (not) + precede (come before) = "nothing like this ever came before!"
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: unmatched, novel, unparalleled, unheard-of · Ant: conventional (Day 2 #15), routine, customary, familiar.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Ice-core bubbles spanning eight hundred thousand years show that modern atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations have risen at an unprecedented pace since industrialization."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Across 800,000 years of trapped air, no earlier period ever matched today's speed of increase (unprecedented).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing unprecedented with unpredictable ("hard to forecast") or unimportant!
  • Short Application Activity: If a museum exhibition draws unprecedented attendance, what happened? (More visitors came than ever before in the museum's history!)

51. impede (verb) / impediment (noun)

  • Simple English Definition: To slow down, obstruct, or get in the way of movement or progress.
  • Degree Precision (impede vs. preclude): Impede = slow down / hinder (progress is harder, though maybe still possible); Preclude (Day 4 #33) = make 100% impossible!
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: hinder, obstruct, hamper, retard · Ant: facilitate, catalyze (Day 5 #42), expedite.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Low-head nineteenth-century mill dams impede upstream Atlantic shad migrations without completely blocking floods during spring high water."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Notice "without completely blocking"—the dams obstruct and slow down (impede) fish passage rather than making it 100% impossible.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing impede with stampede or speed. Remember Latin ped = foot (im-pede = tangle someone's feet so they walk slowly!).
  • Short Application Activity: Scale from partial hindrance (1) to total impossibility (2): preclude, impede. (1 = impede, 2 = preclude).

52. vindicate (verb)

  • Simple English Definition: To prove that someone—or a doubted theory—was right and justified all along after earlier criticism or disbelief.
  • Classic SAT Passage Arc: Scientist X was mocked in 1920 -> 1960s data proved Scientist X right = "vindicated Scientist X!"
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: justify, validate, exonerate, bear out · Ant: refute (Day 3 #25), discredit, disprove.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Decades after geologists dismissed Alfred Wegener's continental-drift hypothesis, mid-ocean ridge paleomagnetic stripes vindicated his core insight that continents move horizontally."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Seafloor magnetic data proved Wegener right after years of dismissal (vindicated him).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing vindicate ("prove right / clear of doubt" — positive!) with vindictive ("spiteful / seeking revenge" — negative!)! Watch the ending carefully: vindicate (+) vs. vindictive (-)!
  • Short Application Activity: Did Barbara McClintock's Nobel Prize for "jumping genes" after decades of skepticism vindicate or repudiate her early maize experiments? (Vindicate!)

53. discrepancy (noun)

  • Simple English Definition: An unexpected mismatch or difference between two numbers, reports, or facts that ought to agree.
  • Cross-Section Utility: Appears constantly in SAT science anomalies ("account for the discrepancy between predicted and observed orbits") and historical source comparisons.
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: mismatch, inconsistency, divergence, disparity · Ant: agreement, concordance, consistency.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "A persistent two-percent discrepancy between customs export ledgers in Mocha and import manifests in Marseille alerted historians to widespread Mediterranean coffee smuggling."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Export numbers and import numbers failed to match (discrepancy), revealing off-the-books smuggling.
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Confusing discrepancy with discretion ("careful judgment/privacy").
  • Short Application Activity: Connect Day 1 + Day 6: When scientists find a discrepancy between two datasets, they design experiments to ______ (Day 1 #7: bring into harmony) them! (reconcile).

54. feasible (adjective) / feasibility (noun)

  • Simple English Definition: Possible, workable, and realistic to carry out practically with available time, money, and technology.
  • Difference from plausible (Day 1 #4): Plausible = believable as a true explanation/hypothesis; Feasible = practically doable as an engineering/policy project!
  • Synonym / Antonym: Syn: workable, viable, practicable, achievable · Ant: unfeasible, impractical, unworkable, prohibitive.
  • Original SAT-Style Contextual Sentence: "Advances in directional drilling made subsea power cables across deep Norwegian fjords economically feasible for the first time in the 1990s."
  • Explanation of Contextual Meaning: Better drilling technology made underwater fjord cables practically and financially doable (feasible).
  • Common International-Student Misunderstanding: Mixing up plausible (truth of an explanation) vs. feasible (practicality of an action). You don't call a fossil theory "feasible" or a bridge construction budget "plausible"!
  • Short Application Activity: Pick plausible or feasible: "Solar desalination proved technically ______ on the arid island, offering a ______ explanation for why villagers stayed." (feasible = doable project / plausible = believable explanation!).

Exercise 4C-1: Contextual Calibration MCQs (VOC-D6-Q1 to VOC-D6-Q4)

VOC-D6-Q1 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Medium]
Although laboratory fuel cells using pure platinum anodes achieved high electrical efficiency, platinum's extreme scarcity rendered city-scale deployment economically ______ until engineers developed iron-nitrogen-carbon catalysts at one-hundredth the cost.
A) unprecedented · B) unfeasible · C) equivocal · D) vindicated

VOC-D6-Q2 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Medium]
Dense mats of invasive water hyacinth ______ riverboat navigation along Lake Victoria bays by tangling propellers and blocking wooden landing piers.
A) vindicate · B) corroborate · C) impede · D) ameliorate

VOC-D6-Q3 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Hard]
In the 1970s, cell biologist Lynn Margulis faced widespread skepticism for proposing that mitochondria evolved from engulfed free-living bacteria; subsequent DNA sequencing of mitochondrial genomes decisively ______ her endosymbiotic theory by confirming close kinship with alpha-proteobacteria.
A) exacerbated · B) repudiated · C) circumvented · D) vindicated

VOC-D6-Q4 [Original SAT-Style Practice — Hard]
To resolve a puzzling forty-arcsecond ______ between Uranus's mathematically predicted orbit and telescopic sky charts, Urbain Le Verrier calculated the gravitational pull of an unseen outer planet—leading Berlin astronomers directly to Neptune in 1846.
A) reciprocity · B) discrepancy · C) caveat · D) catalyst

Exercise 4C-2: High-Precision Nuance & Lookalike Match (VOC-D6-Q5 to VOC-D6-Q10)

Choose the accurate word in parentheses:

  • VOC-D6-Q5 (exacerbate vs. exaggerate): "Removing hillside terrace walls would physically (exacerbate / exaggerate) monsoon mudslides."
  • VOC-D6-Q6 (vindicate vs. vindictive): "New ice-radar maps (vindicated / vindictive) the young glaciologist's subglacial river model."
  • VOC-D6-Q7 (feasible vs. plausible): "Replacing lead water pipes across three winters proved financially (feasible / plausible) once municipal bonds passed."
  • VOC-D6-Q8 (impede vs. preclude): "Strong headwinds (impeded / precluded) the cargo schooner's crossing, delaying arrival in Porto by two days rather than stopping the voyage."
  • VOC-D6-Q9 (unprecedented vs. conventional): "Capturing the first direct horizon-scale radio image of a black hole in 2019 was an (unprecedented / conventional) milestone in interferometry."
  • VOC-D6-Q10 (discrepancy vs. reciprocity): "Auditors flagged a (discrepancy / reciprocity) between warehouse receipts and shipping invoices."

Exercise 4C-3: Closed-Notes Retrieval (VOC-D6-Q11 to VOC-D6-Q16) + Test 5 Harvest Filter (VOC-D6-Q17–Q18)

Write a 3–6 word simple English meaning:

  • VOC-D6-Q11: exacerbate → __________________
  • VOC-D6-Q12: unprecedented → __________________
  • VOC-D6-Q13: impede → __________________
  • VOC-D6-Q14: vindicate → __________________
  • VOC-D6-Q15: discrepancy → __________________
  • VOC-D6-Q16: feasible → __________________
  • VOC-D6-Q17: Suppose on Practice Test 5 today you saw the unfamiliar words coccolithophore (a marine plankton species) and corroborate (in an answer choice). Which one should you log in Rows 61–70 of your Vocabulary Notebook?
  • VOC-D6-Q18: Why should you stop adding new vocabulary words after logging 6–10 high-value Test 5 words today rather than copying 35 words into a giant list?

vocabulary.answerKeyHtml:
Pre-Exam Polarity Activation (SR-D6-Q1 to SR-D6-Q8)

  • SR-D6-Q1 (corroborate): + (confirm with independent evidence)
  • SR-D6-Q2 (preclude): - (rule out / make impossible in advance)
  • SR-D6-Q3 (underscore): + (emphasize / highlight strongly — never confuse with undermine!)
  • SR-D6-Q4 (equivocal): ± (inconclusive / open to two interpretations)
  • SR-D6-Q5 (augment): + (supplement / make greater by adding)
  • SR-D6-Q6 (repudiate): - (firmly reject / disown)
  • SR-D6-Q7 (tentative): ± (provisional / cautious / subject to change)
  • SR-D6-Q8 (bolster): + (strengthen / reinforce)

Exercise 4C-1 (VOC-D6-Q1 to VOC-D6-Q4)

  • VOC-D6-Q1: B (unfeasible) — Contrast clue (Although lab platinum cells had high efficiency ⟷ extreme scarcity blocked city-scale deployment until a 100x cheaper catalyst arrived). City-scale deployment was practically/financially unworkable (economically unfeasible). Unprecedented (A = never seen before), equivocal (C = ambiguous), and vindicated (D = proved right) miss the cost-practicality logic.
  • VOC-D6-Q2: C (impede) — Tangling boat propellers and blocking piers slows down and obstructs (impedes) river navigation. Vindicate (A), corroborate (B), and ameliorate (D = improve) all carry positive polarity.
  • VOC-D6-Q3: D (vindicated) — Classic SAT vindication arc: widespread skepticism in the 1970s → mitochondrial DNA sequencing confirmed kinship with alpha-proteobacteria, proving Margulis right (vindicating her endosymbiotic theory). Exacerbated (A = worsened), repudiated (B = rejected), and circumvented (C = bypassed) contradict the confirming evidence.
  • VOC-D6-Q4: B (discrepancy) — A puzzling forty-arcsecond mismatch (discrepancy) between Uranus's predicted orbit and observed sky charts led Le Verrier to calculate Neptune's pull. Reciprocity (A = mutual give-and-take), caveat (C = warning limitation), and catalyst (D = accelerating spark) do not mean numerical/observational mismatch.

Exercise 4C-2 (VOC-D6-Q5 to VOC-D6-Q10)

  • VOC-D6-Q5: exacerbate (physically worsen mudslides; exaggerate = overstate verbally)
  • VOC-D6-Q6: vindicated (verb = proved right; vindictive = spiteful/revengeful adjective!)
  • VOC-D6-Q7: feasible (practically/financially doable engineering project; plausible = believable claim/explanation)
  • VOC-D6-Q8: impeded ("delaying arrival by two days rather than stopping" = slowed/hindered, whereas precluded = made 100% impossible)
  • VOC-D6-Q9: unprecedented ("first direct horizon-scale radio image" = never achieved before)
  • VOC-D6-Q10: discrepancy ( accounting mismatch between receipts and invoices)

Exercise 4C-3 (VOC-D6-Q11 to VOC-D6-Q18)

  • VOC-D6-Q11 (exacerbate): To make a problem or bad condition worse.
  • VOC-D6-Q12 (unprecedented): Never done, seen, or experienced before.
  • VOC-D6-Q13 (impede): To slow down, hinder, or obstruct progress.
  • VOC-D6-Q14 (vindicate): To prove someone or a doubted claim right.
  • VOC-D6-Q15 (discrepancy): An unexpected mismatch between two numbers or reports.
  • VOC-D6-Q16 (feasible): Practically doable and workable with available resources.
  • VOC-D6-Q17: Log corroborate in Rows 61–70 because it is a high-frequency academic evidence verb that appears across dozens of SAT questions; skip coccolithophore (a specialized plankton species name).
  • VOC-D6-Q18: Capping your Test 5 harvest at 6–10 high-utility academic words lets you complete all 3 vocabulary layers (simple English meaning, context clue, own sentence) and hit 80%+ spaced retrieval tomorrow, whereas dumping 35 random words into a list triggers memorization overload and zero contextual transfer.

  • Part A (RW-D6-Q1–Q3): Solve in 2.5 minutes at 09:05 before launching Bluebook Practice Test 5 to wake up your visual scan!

questions.partTitle: Part A: Morning Pre-Exam Eye-Opener (09:05 — 3 Items)
questions.stemHtml:
Designed by Finnish architect Alvar Aalto in 1933, three-legged bent-birch ______ stack neatly into compact vertical towers without scratching one another's lacquered seats.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: stools,
stools
stools;
stools—

questions.explanationHtml: • Clause-Stripping Analysis: [Designed by Finnish architect Alvar Aalto in 1933,] = introductory participial modifier. Core clause: Subject = three-legged bent-birch stools → Finite Verb = stack. Standard English forbids placing a single comma (A), semicolon (C — left side lacks a finite verb!), or single dash (D) directly between a subject and its verb.

questions.partTitle: Part A: Morning Pre-Exam Eye-Opener (09:05 — 3 Items)
questions.stemHtml:
Fresh pineapple juice contains bromelain, a protease enzyme that snips collagen protein chains into short fragments so gelatin desserts cannot set into firm jelly. Canned pineapple chunks are heated above 80∘C during bottling, denaturing bromelain completely; ______ cooks can fold canned pineapple into gelatin molds without preventing solidification.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.html: however,
consequently,
conversely,
for instance,

questions.explanationHtml:
• Logical Relationship: Sentence 1 explains why fresh pineapple ruins gelatin (active bromelain snips collagen). Sentence 2 Clause 1 states that canning heat above 80∘C denatures bromelain completely (Cause) → Clause 2 states that cooks can safely fold canned pineapple into gelatin molds (Effect). B (consequently,) signals cause-and-effect accurately.
  • Why Distractors Fail: A (however,) and C (conversely,) signal contrast between two clauses that actually agree in cause-effect; D (for instance,) introduces a specific example rather than a causal result.

questions.partTitle: Part A: Morning Pre-Exam Eye-Opener (09:05 — 3 Items)
questions.stemHtml:
Far from treating damaged coral reefs as beyond recovery, marine restoration teams in Sulawesi have demonstrated that anchoring hexagonal steel "reef stars" across loose rubble fields stabilizes shifting fragments and ______ natural branching-coral regrowth within three years.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: impedes
catalyzes
precludes
repudiates

questions.explanationHtml:
• 5-Step Context Prediction: "Far from treating damaged coral reefs as beyond recovery" establishes optimistic, positive restoration polarity: stabilizing shifting rubble sparks/accelerates natural regrowth (B: catalyzes).
  • Why Distractors Fail: A (impedes = slows), C (precludes = makes impossible), and D (repudiates = rejects) all reverse the sentence's positive restoration meaning.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Confidence-Tagging Calibration Mini-Set (13:05 — Mark [C] or [?]!)
questions.stemHtml:
Although eighteenth-century canal charters ______ guaranteed free towpath passage to small village skiffs carrying firewood, lockkeepers routinely scheduled timber-barge convoys across all daylight hours, forcing local villagers either to pay night-lantern fees or abandon canal transport altogether.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: feasibly
ostensibly
stringently
empirically

questions.explanationHtml:
• 5-Step Context Prediction: Although signals a surface-vs.-reality contradiction: canal charters on paper / supposedly guaranteed free passage to village skiffs, yet lockkeepers filled every daylight hour with timber barges so villagers couldn't actually use the canal for free. B (ostensibly) means "outwardly/supposedly on the surface, masking an opposite practical reality."
  • Why Distractors Fail: A (feasibly) means practicably doable; C (stringently) means strictly enforced (if free skiff passage had been stringently guaranteed, lockkeepers could not have blocked villagers all day!); D (empirically) means by experimental observation.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Confidence-Tagging Calibration Mini-Set (13:05 — Mark [C] or [?]!)
questions.stemHtml:
When Swiss chemist Friedrich Miescher isolated phosphorus-rich "nuclein" (DNA) from white blood cell nuclei in 1869, senior biochemists dismissed the discovery as experimental contamination by protein phosphate; seventy-five years later, Oswald Avery's pneumococcal transformation experiments ______ Miescher's insistence that nuclein was a distinct, biologically fundamental macromolecule.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.html: exacerbated
vindicated
mitigated
circumscribed

questions.explanationHtml:
• 5-Step Context Prediction: In 1869, senior biochemists dismissed Miescher's "nuclein" as mere protein contamination; 75 years later, Avery's experiments proved Miescher right after decades of dismissal (B: vindicated).
  • Why Distractors Fail: A (exacerbated) = worsened a problem; C (mitigated) = softened harm; D (circumscribed) = drew restrictive limits around.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Confidence-Tagging Calibration Mini-Set (13:05 — Mark [C] or [?]!)
questions.stemHtml:
Text 1
Urban freight researchers often advocate replacing daytime diesel delivery vans with nighttime electric cargo trams running on existing passenger streetcar tracks between midnight and five a.m., noting that nocturnal track sharing requires zero new tunnel excavation and slashes daytime curb double-parking.

Text 2
While off-peak electric freight trams clearly reduce daytime street congestion without costly tunneling, acoustic monitoring along historic European tramways shows that steel-wheel flange squeal around tight neighborhood curves regularly exceeds sixty-eight decibels indoors—triggering municipal sleep-disturbance lawsuits unless transit agencies first install elastomeric rail dampers and automated curve lubrication.

Based on the texts, how does the author of Text 2 view the proposal described in Text 1?

choices.raw: As completely unworkable because passenger streetcar tracks cannot support the axle weight of cargo trams
choices.html: As completely unworkable because passenger streetcar tracks cannot support the axle weight of cargo trams

choices.raw: As promising in its congestion and infrastructure advantages, albeit contingent on targeted noise-mitigation upgrades in residential corridors
choices.html: As promising in its congestion and infrastructure advantages, albeit contingent on targeted noise-mitigation upgrades in residential corridors

choices.raw: As unnecessary because daytime diesel delivery vans rarely double-park along historic European streets
choices.html: As unnecessary because daytime diesel delivery vans rarely double-park along historic European streets

choices.raw: As financially superior to elastomeric rail dampers for reducing nocturnal street noise
choices.html: As financially superior to elastomeric rail dampers for reducing nocturnal street noise

questions.explanationHtml:
• 6-Word Cross-Text Map:
    • T1: + nocturnal cargo trams (zero tunnels, less double-parking)
    • T2: ± concedes congestion/tunneling perks, BUT >68 dB curve squeal requires rail dampers + lubrication first
  • Evaluation: B captures both the positive concession and the conditional noise-mitigation requirement (albeit contingent on...). A fabricates an axle-weight structural collapse (E5 unsupported inference); C contradicts both texts on double-parking; D nonsensically treats trams and dampers as competing noise-reduction budgets.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Confidence-Tagging Calibration Mini-Set (13:05 — Mark [C] or [?]!)
questions.stemHtml:
Dissolved Oxygen and Juvenile Trout Survival Across Four Bridged Creek Crossings

Crossing Type Summer Midday Water Temp (∘C) Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L) Upstream-to-Downstream Trout Passage (%)
Corrugated Steel Pipe Culvert 21.4 6.1 12
Flat-Bottom Concrete Box Culvert 19.8 7.3 28
Open-Bottom Natural-Gravel Arch 16.5 9.4 89
Unbridged Reference Reach 16.2 9.6 92

Fisheries engineers evaluating road-stream crossings concluded that replacing perched corrugated steel pipe culverts with open-bottom natural-gravel arches restores both thermal-oxygen water quality and juvenile trout movement to nearly natural unbridged conditions, whereas flat-bottom concrete box culverts yield only modest partial gains.

Which data comparison from the table most completely substantiates the engineers' conclusion?

choices.raw: Open-bottom natural-gravel arches had lower midday water temperatures ($16.5^\circ\text{C}$) than corrugated steel pipe culverts ($21.4^\circ\text{C}$).
choices.html: Open-bottom natural-gravel arches had lower midday water temperatures (16.5∘C) than corrugated steel pipe culverts (21.4∘C).

choices.raw: Unbridged reference reaches recorded $9.6\text{ mg/L}$ dissolved oxygen and $92\%$ trout passage, the highest values in the table.
choices.html: Unbridged reference reaches recorded 9.6 mg/L dissolved oxygen and 92% trout passage, the highest values in the table.

choices.raw: Whereas concrete box culverts raised dissolved oxygen only from $6.1$ to $7.3\text{ mg/L}$ and passage from $12\%$ to $28\%$, open-bottom gravel arches reached $16.5^\circ\text{C}$, $9.4\text{ mg/L}$ oxygen, and $89\%$ passage—closely approaching the unbridged reference ($16.2^\circ\text{C}$, $9.6\text{ mg/L}$, $92\%$).
choices.html: Whereas concrete box culverts raised dissolved oxygen only from 6.1 to 7.3 mg/L and passage from 12% to 28%, open-bottom gravel arches reached 16.5∘C, 9.4 mg/L oxygen, and 89% passage—closely approaching the unbridged reference (16.2∘C, 9.6 mg/L, 92%).

choices.raw: Juvenile trout passage through concrete box culverts ($28\%$) was more than double passage through corrugated steel pipe culverts ($12\%$).
choices.html: Juvenile trout passage through concrete box culverts (28%) was more than double passage through corrugated steel pipe culverts (12%).

questions.explanationHtml:
• Two-Half Claim Audit: The engineers' conclusion has two distinct claims:
    1. Open-bottom gravel arches restore temperature, oxygen, and trout passage nearly to unbridged natural levels (16.5∘C vs. 16.2∘C, 9.4 vs. 9.6 mg/L, 89% vs. 92%).
    2. Flat-bottom concrete box culverts yield only modest partial gains over steel pipes (6.1→7.3 mg/L oxygen; 12%→28% passage).
  • Why Distractors Fail: A omits concrete culverts, oxygen, passage, and the unbridged baseline; B mentions only the reference reach; D compares only concrete vs. steel passage without showing how close gravel arches get to natural conditions (V7 Partial Evidence-to-Claim Mismatch). Only C proves the entire comparative conclusion.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Confidence-Tagging Calibration Mini-Set (13:05 — Mark [C] or [?]!)
questions.stemHtml:
Ancient Roman glassmakers colored ceremonial Lycurgus cage cups with trace gold-silver alloy nanoparticles (50–70 nm wide) dispersed at just forty parts per million: under reflected front light the glass glows opaque jade green, whereas light shining through the cup from behind scatters short blue-green wavelengths and transmits deep ruby red. Because ordinary wood-fired Roman glass furnaces fluctuated wildly in oxygen levels—which causes silver ions to clump into dull black soot rather than uniform 60-nm particles—archaeometallurgists infer that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.raw: Roman glassmakers imported pre-manufactured ruby-red cage cups from twentieth-century laboratories.
choices.html: Roman glassmakers imported pre-manufactured ruby-red cage cups from twentieth-century laboratories.

choices.raw: the remarkably few intact dichroic cage cups surviving from antiquity likely reflect a low-yield, tightly guarded workshop technique rather than routine mass production across ordinary Roman furnaces.
choices.html: the remarkably few intact dichroic cage cups surviving from antiquity likely reflect a low-yield, tightly guarded workshop technique rather than routine mass production across ordinary Roman furnaces.

choices.raw: *Lycurgus* cage cups appear opaque jade green only when illuminated from behind in dark rooms.
choices.html: Lycurgus cage cups appear opaque jade green only when illuminated from behind in dark rooms.

choices.raw: increasing silver concentrations from forty parts per million to four thousand parts per million would prevent black soot formation in wood-fired kilns.
choices.html: increasing silver concentrations from forty parts per million to four thousand parts per million would prevent black soot formation in wood-fired kilns.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Deductive Chain: Premise 1 = Dichroic Lycurgus glass requires uniform 50–70 nm gold-silver alloy nanoparticles at 40 ppm. Premise 2 = Ordinary Roman wood-fired furnaces fluctuated wildly in oxygen, clumping silver into dull black soot instead. Strict inference = Producing true dichroic glass could not happen routinely in ordinary fluctuating furnaces; the tiny surviving number of intact cups likely reflects a low-yield, specialized workshop method (B).
  • Why Distractors Fail: A is a comical anachronism (ancient Romans importing from 20th-century labs!); C flips reflected front light (jade green) and transmitted back light (ruby red); D invents an unsupported 4,000 ppm recipe change.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Confidence-Tagging Calibration Mini-Set (13:05 — Mark [C] or [?]!)
questions.skill: Form, Structure, and Sense (Hard Parallel Comparison + Possessive)
questions.stemHtml:
Wind-tunnel force-plate recordings demonstrate that a gliding colugo's patagium—a furred skin membrane stretching from wrist to ankle—generates lift-to-drag ratios exceeding ______ smaller arboreal gliding mammals such as sugar gliders.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.html: that of
those of
them of
any

questions.explanationHtml:
• Parallel Comparison Check (Day 2 Lesson 2.2): Ask two questions: (1) What noun is being compared? "lift-to-drag ratios" (plural!). (2) Singular or plural pronoun? Plural = those of ("generates lift-to-drag ratios exceeding those of [= the lift-to-drag ratios of] smaller arboreal gliding mammals").
  • Why Distractors Fail: A (that of) is singular—the single most common SAT comparison trap when a plural noun (ratios) sits right next to a verb! C (them of) is ungrammatical in English; D (any) illogically compares lift-to-drag ratios directly to smaller mammals instead of to those mammals' ratios!

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Confidence-Tagging Calibration Mini-Set (13:05 — Mark [C] or [?]!)
questions.stemHtml:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Silent films projected in the 1910s and 1920s were rarely monochromatic black-and-white: over eighty percent of surviving nitrate prints feature chemical color treatments.
  • Tinting dipped an entire developed film strip into colored dye so pale highlights turned amber (daylight), blue (night), or red (firelight) while dark shadows stayed black.
  • Toning chemically replaced silver grains inside dark shadow areas with colored metal salts (such as Prussian blue or sepia brown) while leaving clear highlights untinted.
  • Film archivists must scan nitrate prints in full RGB color before digital restoration, or subtle tinting and toning emotional cues are permanently erased.

The student wants to contrast the visual effects of tinting and toning in silent-era cinema. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.raw: Over eighty percent of surviving $1910\text{s}$ and $1920\text{s}$ silent nitrate prints feature tinting or toning, requiring archivists to scan prints in full RGB color.
choices.html: Over eighty percent of surviving 1910s and 1920s silent nitrate prints feature tinting or toning, requiring archivists to scan prints in full RGB color.

choices.raw: In silent-era film processing, tinting dyed a print's light areas while keeping shadows black, whereas toning colored the dark silver shadow grains while leaving clear highlights uncolored.
choices.html: In silent-era film processing, tinting dyed a print's light areas while keeping shadows black, whereas toning colored the dark silver shadow grains while leaving clear highlights uncolored.

choices.raw: Tinting used colored dyes such as amber, blue, or red to signal daylight, night, or firelight in $1920\text{s}$ silent cinema.
choices.html: Tinting used colored dyes such as amber, blue, or red to signal daylight, night, or firelight in 1920s silent cinema.

choices.raw: Both tinting and toning added color to silent-era nitrate film strips long before modern three-strip color photography became standard.
choices.html: Both tinting and toning added color to silent-era nitrate film strips long before modern three-strip color photography became standard.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Goal-First Synthesis Audit: Target = contrast the visual effects of tinting and toning.
  • Evaluation: B names both processes and contrasts their exact visual effects (tinting = dyed light areas while keeping shadows black; whereas toning = colored dark silver shadow grains while leaving clear highlights uncolored). A focuses on archival scanning; C omits toning completely; D states a general similarity without contrasting how they look.

lessons.title: Lesson 6.3: Exam-Morning Execution Playbook for Bluebook Math & the Official 10-Minute Break
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 6.3: Exam-Morning Execution Playbook for Bluebook Math & the Official 10-Minute Break
lessons.html:
A. The Official 10-Minute Break Script (10:19–10:29 — Do Not Improvise!)

Right after R&W Module 2 ends at 10:19, Bluebook starts a 10:00 break screen:

  1. Minutes 0–3: Stand up immediately, walk to the restroom/kitchen, drink water, and eat a steady-glucose snack (half a banana, almonds, or oat bar—avoid pure candy sugar spikes that crash at Math Module 2 Q15!).
  2. Minutes 3–7: Roll your shoulders, look out a distant window (20+ meters away) to relax ciliary eye muscles after 64 minutes of close reading, and do NOT replay R&W questions in your head! R&W is locked in the vault; let it go 100%.
  3. Minutes 7–9: Sit back down with 2:00 to spare, lay out 2 fresh sheets of folded 4-quadrant scratch paper for Math Module 1, and take three slow breaths before clicking "Resume Testing".

B. The 4-Quadrant Scratch-Paper Habit (Saves 3 Minutes & Powers Afternoon Triage!)

Fold each blank sheet once vertically and once horizontally (4 boxes per side = 8 clean boxes per sheet). Write Q1, Q2, Q3 inside each box instead of scribbling chaotic numbers diagonally across the page:

  • During Final 02:00 Review: You can inspect your Q7 algebra in 5 seconds instead of starting over from scratch!
  • During Afternoon Triage (13:45): Looking at Box Q19 shows you instantly whether you made a sign slip (QS) or didn't know the concept (CU)—without peeking at Bluebook's solution!

lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 6.4: The 4-Tag Sustainable Post-Test Math Triage System (13:45–14:30)
lessons.html:
When you inspect your Bluebook Practice Test 5 Math results after lunch, do NOT click "Show Explanation"! Compare your missed/[?] question numbers against your numbered scratch-paper boxes and assign one of 4 Triage Tags in Section 9B:

Triage Tag Meaning Scratch-Paper Signature Tomorrow's Day 7 Action
QS (Quick Slip) Knew the exact method; lost the point to sign, arithmetic, or target-box misread (x vs. 2x+5, radius vs. diameter) Work in box is 90% right; final step slipped You will crush this in 30 sec during tomorrow's blind re-solve → add 1-line firewall rule!
TR (Timing Rush) Ran short on clock at Q19–Q22 and guessed in <30 sec Box is empty or half-started Test untimed tomorrow morning first to see if you already know the math!
DM (Desmos Missed) Did 3 minutes of messy hand algebra on a system/slider/circle that Desmos graphs in 15 sec Box is crammed with crossed-out algebra Tomorrow morning, solve exclusively in Desmos in <20 seconds!
CU (Concept Unknown) Genuinely unsure what theorem, formula, or setup applied Question mark in box; stuck even with time Priority #1 teaching & 6-question consolidation target on Day 7 afternoon!

Short Comprehension Check — Lessons 6.3 & 6.4 (Check answers in Section 8)

  • CC-D6-M1: Why does numbering 8 clean boxes per scratch sheet help you both during the last 2 minutes of Math Module 1 and during afternoon triage?
  • CC-D6-M2: On Practice Test 5 Math M2-Q20, you spent 3 minutes expanding (x−3)2+(y+4)2=25 and y=2x−1 by hand, made a quadratic-formula error, and missed it. Which of the 4 Triage Tags (QS, TR, DM, CU) fits best?
  • CC-D6-M3: Why should you avoid checking your phone messages or looking up an R&W vocabulary word in a dictionary during the 10-minute break between R&W and Math?
  • CC-D6-M4: On an SPR problem asking "In A=kπ, what is the value of k?", you find A=25π. What exact characters do you type into Bluebook?

outline.text: Short Comprehension Check — Lessons 6.3 & 6.4 (Check answers in Section 8)

checks.promptHtml: Why does numbering 8 clean boxes per scratch sheet help you both during the last 2 minutes of Math Module 1 and during afternoon triage?
checks.answerHtml: Numbering 8 clean boxes per folded sheet (Q1, Q2, ...) lets you audit your exact algebra in 5 seconds during the final 02:00 module check (instead of re-solving from scratch) and lets you see immediately during afternoon triage whether a miss came from a last-step sign/target slip (QS), clock rush (TR), skipped graphing (DM), or an unknown theorem (CU)—without peeking at Bluebook's solution!

checks.promptHtml: On Practice Test 5 Math M2-Q20, you spent 3 minutes expanding (x−3)2+(y+4)2=25 and y=2x−1 by hand, made a quadratic-formula error, and missed it. Which of the 4 Triage Tags (QS, TR, DM, CU) fits best?
checks.answerHtml: DM (Desmos Missed). Typing (x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 = 25 and y = 2x - 1 directly into Desmos displays both intersection coordinates in 12 seconds with zero binomial-expansion or quadratic-formula arithmetic risk.

checks.promptHtml: Why should you avoid checking your phone messages or looking up an R&W vocabulary word in a dictionary during the 10-minute break between R&W and Math?
checks.answerHtml: First, touching a phone or dictionary during the official December 5 test-center break is a testing violation that cancels your score. Second, looking up an R&W word mid-break traps your brain in emotional rumination over a locked section instead of resting your eyes and stabilizing blood glucose for 70 minutes of Math.

checks.promptHtml: On an SPR problem asking "In A=kπ, what is the value of k?", you find A=25π. What exact characters do you type into Bluebook?
checks.answerHtml: Type 25 only! Because π is already printed in A=kπ, 25π=kπ⟹k=25. Never type pi into a Bluebook SPR box.

questions.partTitle: Part A: Morning Pre-Exam Math Eye-Opener (09:10 — 3 Items)
questions.stemHtml: If 4(x−2)=20, what is the value of 3x−5?

choices.html: 7
10
16
21

questions.explanationHtml:
• Step 1 (Box Target): Box 3x - 5 before touching algebra!
  • Step 2: Divide 4(x−2)=20 by 4⟹x−2=5⟹x=7.
  • Step 3: Substitute into boxed target: 3(7)−5=21−5=16 (C).
  • Trap Alert: Choice A (7) is the classic Module 1 QS trap for students who stop at x!

questions.partTitle: Part A: Morning Pre-Exam Math Eye-Opener (09:10 — 3 Items)
questions.stemHtml: If 15% of n is equal to 42, what is the value of n?
questions.explanationHtml: • Translate Directly: "15% of n is equal to 42" ⟹0.15n=42⟹n=0.1542​=280. Quick mental check: 10% of 280 is 28, plus 5% (14) =42. Confirmed!

questions.partTitle: Part A: Morning Pre-Exam Math Eye-Opener (09:10 — 3 Items)
questions.stemHtml: In right triangle JKL, ∠L is a right angle and cosJ=257​. What is the value of sinK?

choices.html: 257​
2524​
247​
725​

questions.answerHeadlineHtml: Correct Answer: A (257​)
questions.explanationHtml:
• 5-Second Complementary Trig Identity: Because ∠L=90∘ in right △JKL, acute angles J and K satisfy J+K=90∘. The side adjacent to ∠J is the exact same leg opposite ∠K, so sinK=cosJ=257​ (A) with zero Pythagorean calculation needed!
  • Trap Alert: Choice B (2524​) wastes 30 seconds finding the other leg (24) and accidentally computes cosK!

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Triage Calibration Mini-Set (14:05 — 7 Items)
questions.stemHtml:
21​(8x−10)=kx+3
In the given equation, k is a constant. If the equation has no solution, what is the value of k?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Simplify Left Side: 21​(8x−10)=4x−5.
  • Apply No-Solution Rule (Day 2 Lesson 2.4): A linear equation 4x−5=kx+3 has no solution when the x-coefficients (slopes) are identical (k=4) and the constants (y-intercepts) differ (−5=3). Check k=4: 4x−5=4x+3⟹−5=3 (never true). Type 4.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Triage Calibration Mini-Set (14:05 — 7 Items)
questions.stemHtml:
5x2+35x−18=0
What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?

choices.html: −35
−7
7
518​

questions.explanationHtml:
• 5-Second Vieta Shortcut: For ax2+bx+c=0 (a=5,b=35,c=−18):
    1. Confirm real roots exist: D=352−4(5)(−18)=1,225+360=1,585>0 (two distinct real solutions).
    2. Sum of solutions =−ab​=−535​=−7 (B).
  • Trap Alert: A (-35) forgets to divide by a=5; C (7) drops the negative sign in −b/a.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Triage Calibration Mini-Set (14:05 — 7 Items)
questions.stemHtml:
B(t)=1,250(1.06)t
The function B models the balance, in dollars, in an endowment certificate t years after deposit, with no additional deposits or withdrawals. Which statement is the best interpretation of 1.06 in this context?

choices.raw: The balance increases by $\$1.06$ each year.
choices.html: The balance increases by each year.

choices.raw: The balance increases by $106\%$ each year.
choices.html: The balance increases by 106% each year.

choices.raw: Each year's balance is $1.06$ times the preceding year's balance.
choices.html: Each year's balance is 1.06 times the preceding year's balance.

choices.raw: It takes $1.06$ years for the initial $\$1{,}250$ deposit to double.
choices.html: It takes 1.06 years for the initial deposit to double.

questions.explanationHtml:
• Exponential Anatomy: In B(t)=1,250(1.06)t, 1,250 is the initial deposit at t=0, and 1.06=1+0.06 is the annual growth factor: each year, the balance is multiplied by 1.06 (C), which equals a 6% annual increase.
  • Why Distractors Fail: A treats an exponential base like a linear slope (/year); B confuses a 1.06 multiplier (+6%) with +106% (which would be a 2.06 multiplier!); D confuses base with doubling time.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Triage Calibration Mini-Set (14:05 — 7 Items)

Transit Mode and Fare-Payment Method of 180 Surveyed Commuters

Transit Mode Monthly Pass Pay-Per-Ride Total
Regional Rail 65 35 100
Express Bus 45 35 80
Total 110 70 180

If one commuter is selected at random from those who use a monthly pass, what is the probability that the selected commuter rides regional rail?

choices.html: 3613​
2213​
2013​
1811​

questions.answerHeadlineHtml: Correct Answer: B (2213​)
questions.explanationHtml:
• Conditional Denominator Firewall (Day 3 Lesson 3.5): Underline "selected at random from those who use a monthly pass." That phrase locks your denominator to the Monthly Pass column total = 110!
  • Numerator: Commuters in that column who ride Regional Rail = 65.
  • Simplify: 11065​=110÷565÷5​=2213​ (B).
  • Trap Alert: A (18065​=3613​) uses the grand total 180; C (10065​=2013​) divides by the Regional Rail row total 100 instead of the Monthly Pass column total!

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Triage Calibration Mini-Set (14:05 — 7 Items)
questions.stemHtml:
yy​=(x−2)2−4=2x−5​
If (x1​,y1​) and (x2​,y2​) are the two real solutions to the system of equations above and x1​>x2​, what is the value of x1​?
questions.explanationHtml:
• Desmos Method (12 Seconds — Zero Sign Risk!):
    1. Line 1: y = (x - 2)^2 - 4
    2. Line 2: y = 2x - 5
    3. Click both intersection dots: (1,−3) and (5,5). Since x1​>x2​, x1​=5. Type 5.
  • Algebra Backup: (x−2)2−4=2x−5⟹(x2−4x+4)−4=2x−5⟹x2−6x+5=0⟹(x−5)(x−1)=0⟹x=5 or 1⟹x1​=5.

questions.partTitle: Part B: Afternoon Triage Calibration Mini-Set (14:05 — 7 Items)
questions.stemHtml:
x2+y2+6x−10y+9=0
In the xy-plane, what is the area of the circle defined by the equation above?

choices.html: 5π
10π
25π
43π

questions.answerHeadlineHtml: Correct Answer: C (25π)
questions.explanationHtml:
• Step 1 (Box Target): Box area (πr2, NOT radius r!).
  • Step 2 (Complete the Square): Move +9 to the right side and add (6/2)2=9 and (−10/2)2=25 to both sides:
    (x2+6x+9)+(y2−10y+25)=−9+9+25
    (x+3)2+(y−5)2=25
  • Step 3: Here r2=25, so Area=πr2=25π (C).
  • Trap Alert: A (5π) plugs in r=5 instead of r2=25; B (10π) finds circumference 2πr; D (43π) forgets to flip the sign of +9 when moving it across the equals sign (+9+9+25=43).

questions.stemHtml:
kx2−8x+2=0
In the given equation, k is a nonzero constant. If the equation has exactly one real solution, what is the value of k?

choices.html: −8
2
4
8

questions.explanationHtml:
• Discriminant Tangency Rule (Day 4 Lesson 4.4): A quadratic kx2−8x+2=0 (k=0) has exactly one real solution if and only if its discriminant equals zero:
    b2−4ac=(−8)2−4(k)(2)=64−8k=0⟹8k=64⟹k=8 (D)

subSections.title: A. Lesson Comprehension Checks (CC-D6-RW1–RW4 & CC-D6-M1–M4)
subSections.titleHtml: A. Lesson Comprehension Checks (CC-D6-RW1–RW4 & CC-D6-M1–M4)
subSections.html:
• CC-D6-RW1: On Bluebook's score summary, a lucky 50-50 guess gets the exact same green checkmark as a question you knew with 100% certainty—hiding fragile vocabulary or reasoning. Jotting ?Q12 on your scratch paper captures unstable guesses so tomorrow morning's Day 7 Blind Cold Re-Solve repairs the underlying skill before December 5.
  • CC-D6-RW2: Reading official explanations immediately after a 2.5-hour full test while mentally fatigued creates passive recognition ("the illusion of competence": "Oh, Choice C makes sense now") and permanently spoils the question. Waiting until tomorrow morning lets you re-solve every missed question blind and untimed with a fresh brain, separating careless/timing slips from genuine comprehension gaps and doubling long-term retention.
  • CC-D6-RW3: Log vindicate ("to prove someone or a doubted claim right after earlier criticism") because it is a reusable, cross-topic academic verb tested repeatedly across SAT Words in Context and science/history passages. Skip pishtaq because narrow architectural or technical nouns are explained by context inside that single passage and almost never reappear.
  • CC-D6-RW4: Denser academic vocabulary and subtler distractors in R&W Module 2 are great news: they confirm your strong Module 1 accuracy routed you into Harder Module 2, unlocking the 650–800 scaled score ceiling! React calmly, trust your Split-Order pacing (Q15–27 → Q1–14), and enforce the 75-second bailout rule so one ultra-hard item never steals points from four reachable questions.
  • CC-D6-M1: Numbering 8 clean boxes per folded sheet (Q1, Q2, ...) lets you audit your exact algebra in 5 seconds during the final 02:00 module check (instead of re-solving from scratch) and lets you see immediately during afternoon triage whether a miss came from a last-step sign/target slip (QS), clock rush (TR), skipped graphing (DM), or an unknown theorem (CU)—without peeking at Bluebook's solution!
  • CC-D6-M2: DM (Desmos Missed). Typing (x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 = 25 and y = 2x - 1 directly into Desmos displays both intersection coordinates in 12 seconds with zero binomial-expansion or quadratic-formula arithmetic risk.
  • CC-D6-M3: First, touching a phone or dictionary during the official December 5 test-center break is a testing violation that cancels your score. Second, looking up an R&W word mid-break traps your brain in emotional rumination over a locked section instead of resting your eyes and stabilizing blood glucose for 70 minutes of Math.
  • CC-D6-M4: Type 25 only! Because π is already printed in A=kπ, 25π=kπ⟹k=25. Never type pi into a Bluebook SPR box.

subSections.title: B. Vocabulary Polarity Activation & Post-Exam Exercises (SR-D6-Q1–Q8 & VOC-D6-Q1–Q18)
subSections.titleHtml: B. Vocabulary Polarity Activation & Post-Exam Exercises (SR-D6-Q1–Q8 & VOC-D6-Q1–Q18)
subSections.html:
Pre-Exam Polarity Activation (SR-D6-Q1 to SR-D6-Q8)

  • SR-D6-Q1 (corroborate): + (confirm with independent evidence)
  • SR-D6-Q2 (preclude): - (rule out / make impossible in advance)
  • SR-D6-Q3 (underscore): + (emphasize / highlight strongly — never confuse with undermine!)
  • SR-D6-Q4 (equivocal): ± (inconclusive / open to two interpretations)
  • SR-D6-Q5 (augment): + (supplement / make greater by adding)
  • SR-D6-Q6 (repudiate): - (firmly reject / disown)
  • SR-D6-Q7 (tentative): ± (provisional / cautious / subject to change)
  • SR-D6-Q8 (bolster): + (strengthen / reinforce)

Exercise 4C-1 (VOC-D6-Q1 to VOC-D6-Q4)

  • VOC-D6-Q1: B (unfeasible) — Contrast clue (Although lab platinum cells had high efficiency ⟷ extreme scarcity blocked city-scale deployment until a 100x cheaper catalyst arrived). City-scale deployment was practically/financially unworkable (economically unfeasible). Unprecedented (A = never seen before), equivocal (C = ambiguous), and vindicated (D = proved right) miss the cost-practicality logic.
  • VOC-D6-Q2: C (impede) — Tangling boat propellers and blocking piers slows down and obstructs (impedes) river navigation. Vindicate (A), corroborate (B), and ameliorate (D = improve) all carry positive polarity.
  • VOC-D6-Q3: D (vindicated) — Classic SAT vindication arc: widespread skepticism in the 1970s → mitochondrial DNA sequencing confirmed kinship with alpha-proteobacteria, proving Margulis right (vindicating her endosymbiotic theory). Exacerbated (A = worsened), repudiated (B = rejected), and circumvented (C = bypassed) contradict the confirming evidence.
  • VOC-D6-Q4: B (discrepancy) — A puzzling forty-arcsecond mismatch (discrepancy) between Uranus's predicted orbit and observed sky charts led Le Verrier to calculate Neptune's pull. Reciprocity (A = mutual give-and-take), caveat (C = warning limitation), and catalyst (D = accelerating spark) do not mean numerical/observational mismatch.

Exercise 4C-2 (VOC-D6-Q5 to VOC-D6-Q10)

  • VOC-D6-Q5: exacerbate (physically worsen mudslides; exaggerate = overstate verbally)
  • VOC-D6-Q6: vindicated (verb = proved right; vindictive = spiteful/revengeful adjective!)
  • VOC-D6-Q7: feasible (practically/financially doable engineering project; plausible = believable claim/explanation)
  • VOC-D6-Q8: impeded ("delaying arrival by two days rather than stopping" = slowed/hindered, whereas precluded = made 100% impossible)
  • VOC-D6-Q9: unprecedented ("first direct horizon-scale radio image" = never achieved before)
  • VOC-D6-Q10: discrepancy ( accounting mismatch between receipts and invoices)

Exercise 4C-3 (VOC-D6-Q11 to VOC-D6-Q18)

  • VOC-D6-Q11 (exacerbate): To make a problem or bad condition worse.
  • VOC-D6-Q12 (unprecedented): Never done, seen, or experienced before.
  • VOC-D6-Q13 (impede): To slow down, hinder, or obstruct progress.
  • VOC-D6-Q14 (vindicate): To prove someone or a doubted claim right.
  • VOC-D6-Q15 (discrepancy): An unexpected mismatch between two numbers or reports.
  • VOC-D6-Q16 (feasible): Practically doable and workable with available resources.
  • VOC-D6-Q17: Log corroborate in Rows 61–70 because it is a high-frequency academic evidence verb that appears across dozens of SAT questions; skip coccolithophore (a specialized plankton species name).
  • VOC-D6-Q18: Capping your Test 5 harvest at 6–10 high-utility academic words lets you complete all 3 vocabulary layers (simple English meaning, context clue, own sentence) and hit 80%+ spaced retrieval tomorrow, whereas dumping 35 random words into a list triggers memorization overload and zero contextual transfer.

subSections.title: C. Reading & Writing Practice Questions (RW-D6-Q1 to RW-D6-Q10)
subSections.titleHtml: C. Reading & Writing Practice Questions (RW-D6-Q1 to RW-D6-Q10)
subSections.html:
Question Answer Domain & Skill Key Strategic Takeaway
RW-D6-Q1 B SEC · Boundaries Never place a comma, semicolon, or dash between subject (stools) and verb (stack)!
RW-D6-Q2 B EOI · Transitions Heat denatures enzyme → consequently, canned fruit doesn't ruin gelatin
RW-D6-Q3 B C&S · Words in Context "Far from beyond recovery" → positive spark (catalyzes regrowth)
RW-D6-Q4 B C&S · Words in Context Paper guarantee vs. daylight lock blockade = ostensibly (supposedly on the surface)
RW-D6-Q5 B C&S · Words in Context Early dismissal (1869) → later proof (Avery) = vindicated
RW-D6-Q6 B C&S · Cross-Text Qualified endorsement (±): accepts congestion/cost perks, adds >68 dB damper condition
RW-D6-Q7 C I&I · Quant Evidence Must prove BOTH halves: gravel arch ≈ reference AND concrete box = modest gain
RW-D6-Q8 B I&I · Inferences Finicky furnace oxygen → low-yield specialized craft explains why few cups survive
RW-D6-Q9 B SEC · Parallel Comparison Plural "lift-to-drag ratios" requires plural pronoun those of (not singular that of!)
RW-D6-Q10 B EOI · Rhetorical Synthesis Contrasts BOTH visual effects: tinting dyes light areas vs. toning colors dark shadow silver

Detailed Distractor-by-Distractor Teaching Explanations

  1. RW-D6-Q1 — Correct Answer: B (stools)

    • Clause-Stripping Analysis: [Designed by Finnish architect Alvar Aalto in 1933,] = introductory participial modifier. Core clause: Subject = three-legged bent-birch stools → Finite Verb = stack. Standard English forbids placing a single comma (A), semicolon (C — left side lacks a finite verb!), or single dash (D) directly between a subject and its verb.

  2. RW-D6-Q2 — Correct Answer: B (consequently,)

    • Logical Relationship: Sentence 1 explains why fresh pineapple ruins gelatin (active bromelain snips collagen). Sentence 2 Clause 1 states that canning heat above 80∘C denatures bromelain completely (Cause) → Clause 2 states that cooks can safely fold canned pineapple into gelatin molds (Effect). B (consequently,) signals cause-and-effect accurately.
    • Why Distractors Fail: A (however,) and C (conversely,) signal contrast between two clauses that actually agree in cause-effect; D (for instance,) introduces a specific example rather than a causal result.

  3. RW-D6-Q3 — Correct Answer: B (catalyzes)

    • 5-Step Context Prediction: "Far from treating damaged coral reefs as beyond recovery" establishes optimistic, positive restoration polarity: stabilizing shifting rubble sparks/accelerates natural regrowth (B: catalyzes).
    • Why Distractors Fail: A (impedes = slows), C (precludes = makes impossible), and D (repudiates = rejects) all reverse the sentence's positive restoration meaning.

  4. RW-D6-Q4 — Correct Answer: B (ostensibly)

    • 5-Step Context Prediction: Although signals a surface-vs.-reality contradiction: canal charters on paper / supposedly guaranteed free passage to village skiffs, yet lockkeepers filled every daylight hour with timber barges so villagers couldn't actually use the canal for free. B (ostensibly) means "outwardly/supposedly on the surface, masking an opposite practical reality."
    • Why Distractors Fail: A (feasibly) means practicably doable; C (stringently) means strictly enforced (if free skiff passage had been stringently guaranteed, lockkeepers could not have blocked villagers all day!); D (empirically) means by experimental observation.

  5. RW-D6-Q5 — Correct Answer: B (vindicated)

    • 5-Step Context Prediction: In 1869, senior biochemists dismissed Miescher's "nuclein" as mere protein contamination; 75 years later, Avery's experiments proved Miescher right after decades of dismissal (B: vindicated).
    • Why Distractors Fail: A (exacerbated) = worsened a problem; C (mitigated) = softened harm; D (circumscribed) = drew restrictive limits around.

  6. RW-D6-Q6 — Correct Answer: B

    • 6-Word Cross-Text Map:
      • T1: + nocturnal cargo trams (zero tunnels, less double-parking)
      • T2: ± concedes congestion/tunneling perks, BUT >68 dB curve squeal requires rail dampers + lubrication first
    • Evaluation: B captures both the positive concession and the conditional noise-mitigation requirement (albeit contingent on...). A fabricates an axle-weight structural collapse (E5 unsupported inference); C contradicts both texts on double-parking; D nonsensically treats trams and dampers as competing noise-reduction budgets.

  7. RW-D6-Q7 — Correct Answer: C

    • Two-Half Claim Audit: The engineers' conclusion has two distinct claims:
      1. Open-bottom gravel arches restore temperature, oxygen, and trout passage nearly to unbridged natural levels (16.5∘C vs. 16.2∘C, 9.4 vs. 9.6 mg/L, 89% vs. 92%).
      2. Flat-bottom concrete box culverts yield only modest partial gains over steel pipes (6.1→7.3 mg/L oxygen; 12%→28% passage).
    • Why Distractors Fail: A omits concrete culverts, oxygen, passage, and the unbridged baseline; B mentions only the reference reach; D compares only concrete vs. steel passage without showing how close gravel arches get to natural conditions (V7 Partial Evidence-to-Claim Mismatch). Only C proves the entire comparative conclusion.

  8. RW-D6-Q8 — Correct Answer: B

    • Deductive Chain: Premise 1 = Dichroic Lycurgus glass requires uniform 50–70 nm gold-silver alloy nanoparticles at 40 ppm. Premise 2 = Ordinary Roman wood-fired furnaces fluctuated wildly in oxygen, clumping silver into dull black soot instead. Strict inference = Producing true dichroic glass could not happen routinely in ordinary fluctuating furnaces; the tiny surviving number of intact cups likely reflects a low-yield, specialized workshop method (B).
    • Why Distractors Fail: A is a comical anachronism (ancient Romans importing from 20th-century labs!); C flips reflected front light (jade green) and transmitted back light (ruby red); D invents an unsupported 4,000 ppm recipe change.

  9. RW-D6-Q9 — Correct Answer: B (those of)

    • Parallel Comparison Check (Day 2 Lesson 2.2): Ask two questions: (1) What noun is being compared? "lift-to-drag ratios" (plural!). (2) Singular or plural pronoun? Plural = those of ("generates lift-to-drag ratios exceeding those of [= the lift-to-drag ratios of] smaller arboreal gliding mammals").
    • Why Distractors Fail: A (that of) is singular—the single most common SAT comparison trap when a plural noun (ratios) sits right next to a verb! C (them of) is ungrammatical in English; D (any) illogically compares lift-to-drag ratios directly to smaller mammals instead of to those mammals' ratios!

  10. RW-D6-Q10 — Correct Answer: B

    • Goal-First Synthesis Audit: Target = contrast the visual effects of tinting and toning.
    • Evaluation: B names both processes and contrasts their exact visual effects (tinting = dyed light areas while keeping shadows black; whereas toning = colored dark silver shadow grains while leaving clear highlights uncolored). A focuses on archival scanning; C omits toning completely; D states a general similarity without contrasting how they look.

MATH-D6-Q1 C (16) MC Manual (15 sec) Linear solve + Box the Target (3x−5, not x=7!)
MATH-D6-Q2 280 SPR Manual/Calc (15 sec) Percent translation (0.15n=42)

Step-by-Step + Desmos Teaching Solutions

  1. MATH-D6-Q1 — Correct Answer: C (16)

    • Step 1 (Box Target): Box 3x - 5 before touching algebra!
    • Step 2: Divide 4(x−2)=20 by 4⟹x−2=5⟹x=7.
    • Step 3: Substitute into boxed target: 3(7)−5=21−5=16 (C).
    • Trap Alert: Choice A (7) is the classic Module 1 QS trap for students who stop at x!

  2. MATH-D6-Q2 — Correct Answer: 280 (SPR)

    • Translate Directly: "15% of n is equal to 42" ⟹0.15n=42⟹n=0.1542​=280. Quick mental check: 10% of 280 is 28, plus 5% (14) =42. Confirmed!

  3. MATH-D6-Q3 — Correct Answer: A (257​)

    • 5-Second Complementary Trig Identity: Because ∠L=90∘ in right △JKL, acute angles J and K satisfy J+K=90∘. The side adjacent to ∠J is the exact same leg opposite ∠K, so sinK=cosJ=257​ (A) with zero Pythagorean calculation needed!
    • Trap Alert: Choice B (2524​) wastes 30 seconds finding the other leg (24) and accidentally computes cosK!

  4. MATH-D6-Q4 — Correct Answer: 4 (SPR)

    • Simplify Left Side: 21​(8x−10)=4x−5.
    • Apply No-Solution Rule (Day 2 Lesson 2.4): A linear equation 4x−5=kx+3 has no solution when the x-coefficients (slopes) are identical (k=4) and the constants (y-intercepts) differ (−5=3). Check k=4: 4x−5=4x+3⟹−5=3 (never true). Type 4.

  5. MATH-D6-Q5 — Correct Answer: B (-7)

    • 5-Second Vieta Shortcut: For ax2+bx+c=0 (a=5,b=35,c=−18):
      1. Confirm real roots exist: D=352−4(5)(−18)=1,225+360=1,585>0 (two distinct real solutions).
      2. Sum of solutions =−ab​=−535​=−7 (B).
    • Trap Alert: A (-35) forgets to divide by a=5; C (7) drops the negative sign in −b/a.

  6. MATH-D6-Q6 — Correct Answer: C

    • Exponential Anatomy: In B(t)=1,250(1.06)t, 1,250 is the initial deposit at t=0, and 1.06=1+0.06 is the annual growth factor: each year, the balance is multiplied by 1.06 (C), which equals a 6% annual increase.
    • Why Distractors Fail: A treats an exponential base like a linear slope (/year); B confuses a 1.06 multiplier (+6%) with +106% (which would be a 2.06 multiplier!); D confuses base with doubling time.

  7. MATH-D6-Q7 — Correct Answer: B (2213​)

    • Conditional Denominator Firewall (Day 3 Lesson 3.5): Underline "selected at random from those who use a monthly pass." That phrase locks your denominator to the Monthly Pass column total = 110!
    • Numerator: Commuters in that column who ride Regional Rail = 65.
    • Simplify: 11065​=110÷565÷5​=2213​ (B).
    • Trap Alert: A (18065​=3613​) uses the grand total 180; C (10065​=2013​) divides by the Regional Rail row total 100 instead of the Monthly Pass column total!

  8. MATH-D6-Q8 — Correct Answer: 5 (SPR)

    • Desmos Method (12 Seconds — Zero Sign Risk!):
      1. Line 1: y = (x - 2)^2 - 4
      2. Line 2: y = 2x - 5
      3. Click both intersection dots: (1,−3) and (5,5). Since x1​>x2​, x1​=5. Type 5.
    • Algebra Backup: (x−2)2−4=2x−5⟹(x2−4x+4)−4=2x−5⟹x2−6x+5=0⟹(x−5)(x−1)=0⟹x=5 or 1⟹x1​=5.

  9. MATH-D6-Q9 — Correct Answer: C (25π)

    • Step 1 (Box Target): Box area (πr2, NOT radius r!).
    • Step 2 (Complete the Square): Move +9 to the right side and add (6/2)2=9 and (−10/2)2=25 to both sides:
      (x2+6x+9)+(y2−10y+25)=−9+9+25
      (x+3)2+(y−5)2=25
    • Step 3: Here r2=25, so Area=πr2=25π (C).
    • Trap Alert: A (5π) plugs in r=5 instead of r2=25; B (10π) finds circumference 2πr; D (43π) forgets to flip the sign of +9 when moving it across the equals sign (+9+9+25=43).

  10. MATH-D6-Q10 — Correct Answer: D (8)

    • Discriminant Tangency Rule (Day 4 Lesson 4.4): A quadratic kx2−8x+2=0 (k=0) has exactly one real solution if and only if its discriminant equals zero:
      b2−4ac=(−8)2−4(k)(2)=64−8k=0⟹8k=64⟹k=8 (D)

mastery.keyHtml:
• MA-D6-Q1: Mitigate (+ lessen/soften harm) and ameliorate (+ make a bad condition better) are antonyms of exacerbate (- make a problem worse). Vindicate (verb, +) = prove someone or a doubted theory right; vindictive (adj., -) = spiteful / seeking revenge.
  • MA-D6-Q2: feasible ("practically/technically doable as an engineering project"; plausible applies to believable explanations/claims, not cable construction).
  • MA-D6-Q3: those of — replaces plural "thermal conductivities"! (That of is singular and fails number agreement.)

When you open Bluebook Practice Test 5 at 09:20, cover the "Correct Answer" letter with your hand or a sticky note, navigate to the first question number on your Day 6 Section 9B R&W Queue, and solve it untimed using your full toolkit (3-Step Clause Stripping, 5-Step Context Prediction, 6-Word Cross-Text Map, Two-Half Evidence Check).

Only after committing to a new untimed letter do you click "Show Explanation". Compare your two attempts using this diagnostic matrix:

Day 6 Timed Result Day 7 Untimed Cold Result Exact Diagnostic Meaning Primary Error Codes (E1–E10 / V1–V7) Mandatory Repair Action
Wrong [X] Right Cold [✓] Execution / Pressure Leak: You already own the English/logic skill! Time pressure, rushing the stem, or skipping clause stripping caused the miss. E4 (Misread stem), E7 (Careless click), E8 (Timing rush), or V3/V4 (Skipped bracket/pivot under speed) Do not watch basic concept videos! Write a 5-second habit trigger (e.g., "Underline contrast word BEFORE reading A–D").

E1 (Concept), E2+V1/V2/V5 (Vocab), E3+V3 (Syntax), E5+V7 (Inference/Evidence), E6 (Grammar rule) Highest-value goldmine! lessons.title: Lesson 7.2: The 7-Step Vocabulary Error Repair Protocol & Master R&W Firewalls
lessons.titleHtml: Lesson 7.2: The 7-Step Vocabulary Error Repair Protocol & Master R&W Firewalls
lessons.html:
Whenever E2 (V1, V2, V4, or V5) contributed to a Practice Test 5 miss or [?] guess, run all 7 Repair Steps (3 minutes per word — far more effective than staring at flashcards!):

  1. Step 1 — Isolate the Exact Blocking Word: Was it in the passage, the question stem (substantiate, undermine, qualify), or the answer choices?
  2. Step 2 — Write a 5-Word Simple English Meaning: Strip dictionary jargon down to everyday English (e.g., circumscribe = draw strict limits around).
  3. Step 3 — Re-Read the Original SAT Context & Circle the Logical Clue: Find the exact colon, semicolon, although, far from, or parallel verb that forced that meaning—even if you hadn't known the word!
  4. Step 4 — Map Polarity (+ / - / ±) + 2 Synonyms & 1 Contrast: Anchor the word inside an existing cluster (e.g., mitigate/ameliorate [+] vs. exacerbate [-]).
  5. Step 5 — Guard Against Lookalike / Polysemy Traps: Note any treacherous twin (circumscribe = restrict limits = circumvent = bypass; underscore = emphasize = undermine = weaken; afford = provide/supply = buy).
  6. Step 6 — Write One Original Sentence About Science, History, or Daily Life: Active generation cements neural retrieval (3x stronger than silent reading).
  7. Step 7 — Schedule 48-Hour & 7-Day Spaced Retrieval Dates: Enter Nov 22 and Nov 27 in Column 7 of Vocabulary-Notebook-and-Spaced-Review.md.

Quick-Reference Master R&W Firewalls (Review Before RW-D7-Q1–Q12)

  • Firewall 1 (SEC Boundaries): IC , IC is ALWAYS WRONG (even with , however, or , therefore,!). Only ., ;, :, —, or , + FANBOYS can legally join two independent clauses.
  • Firewall 2 (SEC Finite Verb vs. Modifier): Cross out [prepositional phrases], [participial -ing/-ed phrases], and [who/which/that clauses]. Every main clause MUST have at least one finite tense-bearing verb (is/was/have/writes/wrote — NEVER bare writing or to write!).
  • Firewall 3 (SEC Parallel Comparisons & Introductory Modifiers): Check singular that of vs. plural those of against the exact compared noun; and verify that the noun immediately after [Introductory -ing/-ed phrase], is the actual doer of that action!
  • Firewall 4 (Polysemy Alert): Common English words often wear academic disguises on Hard SAT items: qualify ("limit/add conditions to"), check ("restrain/slow"), arrest ("stop/halt"), yield ("produce" or "surrender"), afford ("provide/offer access to"), weather ("endure/survive safely").

Short Comprehension Check — Lessons 7.1 & 7.2 (Check answers in Section 8)

  • CC-D7-RW1: On Practice Test 5 M2-Q11, you picked A under time pressure (wrong). This morning at 09:30, before viewing Bluebook's explanation, you re-solve M2-Q11 untimed and confidently pick D (correct). What does Cold Right prove about your skill vs. your test execution?
  • CC-D7-RW2: Why is writing "Pay closer attention to answer choices" in Column 7 of your Error Log ineffective compared to writing an IF -> THEN rule?
  • CC-D7-RW3: In the sentence "Vaulted cedar ceilings afford chamber musicians warm acoustic resonance without artificial amplification," what does afford mean?
  • CC-D7-RW4: What is Step 3 of the 7-Step Vocabulary Repair Protocol, and why does it build vocabulary independence even for words you never see again?
  • CC-D7-RW5: Is "The excavation uncovered bronze weights, however, no written tablets survived" grammatically valid in Standard English? How do you fix it?
